0.title: The Magna Carta of Christian Liberty: Paul’s Letter to the Galatians
0.overview:
The message. Galatians says that a sinner is right with God through faith in Christ alone, and that to add anything to Christ is to lose him. Young churches were being told that Gentile believers must also be circumcised and keep the law of Moses to belong fully to God’s people. Paul answers that this is “a different gospel” (1:6), and no gospel at all: “if righteousness were through the law, then Christ died for no purpose” (2:21). The freedom Christ won is not a licence to sin but the only ground of a life of love by the Spirit. Paul writes in controlled fury, angry not for himself but for them and for the gospel.

Background: the writer. The letter names Paul as its author (1:1; 5:2), and he takes the pen himself at the end: “See with what large letters I am writing to you with my own hand” (6:11). Hardly anyone doubts that he wrote it. Every other letter he wrote to a church opens with thanksgiving or blessing to God; Galatians has neither. He moves in the first verse to defend his calling as an apostle “not from men nor through man” (1:1), and by verse 6 he is in open astonishment.

Galatia and its churches. “Galatia” could mean two things: the highlands of central Asia Minor, modern Turkey, where Celtic tribes had settled in the third century BC; or the larger Roman province, formed in 25 BC, which reached south to take in Pisidian Antioch, Iconium, Lystra and Derbe. Paul and Barnabas founded churches in those southern cities on their first journey (Acts 13–14). Pisidian Antioch and Lystra were Roman colonies; their synagogues had Gentile God-fearers attached, among whom the gospel first took hold (Acts 13:14–48). The country people worshipped the old gods: at Lystra a crowd took Barnabas and Paul for Zeus and Hermes, and soon afterwards, stirred up by Jews from elsewhere, stoned Paul and left him for dead (Acts 14:8–19). Paul had first preached to them “because of a bodily ailment”, and they had received him “as an angel of God, as Christ Jesus” (4:13–14). The churches were mostly converted pagans with Jewish believers among them, and that mixture is what the dispute was about.

When and to whom? Some think Paul wrote to ethnic Galatians in the north, whom he may have visited later (Acts 16:6; 18:23), and date the letter in the mid-50s, near Romans. The more likely view, and this commentary’s, is that he wrote to the southern churches: Paul normally used Roman provincial names, and Acts tells us about those churches and nothing about any in the north. He then wrote probably about AD 48–49, perhaps from Syrian Antioch, just before the Jerusalem Council of Acts 15, which would explain why he never cites its decision on this very question. It may well be his earliest letter. Its message does not depend on the answer.

What prompted it. After Paul left, teachers arrived, probably Jewish Christians with ties to Judea, like the men who came to Antioch teaching, “Unless you are circumcised according to the custom of Moses, you cannot be saved” (Acts 15:1). They are often called the Judaizers. They did not deny Christ; they added to him circumcision, the food laws and the sacred calendar (4:10), and they belittled Paul as a second-hand apostle. It seemed a small addition. But if anything besides Christ is required for justification, being declared righteous by God, even something God-given like circumcision, then Christ is no longer sufficient, grace is no longer free, and the cross is no longer enough. Some recent scholars stress that “works of the law” means above all the marks that set Jews apart from Gentiles; that is part of the picture, but Paul’s deeper question is how a sinner stands before God, and his answer is “through faith in Jesus Christ” (2:16).

How the letter makes its case. Chapters 1–2 tell Paul’s story. His gospel came by “a revelation of Jesus Christ” (1:12), not from Jerusalem; the leaders there added nothing to it and did not compel Titus, a Greek, to be circumcised (2:1–10); and at Antioch he opposed Peter to his face, because Peter had stopped eating with Gentile believers and so put the gospel itself at stake (2:11–14). The story becomes doctrine in 2:15–21, the centre of the letter: justified by faith in Christ, not by works of the law, and living by faith in the Son of God, “who loved me and gave himself for me” (2:20). Chapters 3–4 argue from experience and Scripture. The Galatians received the Spirit by hearing with faith (3:1–5). Abraham believed God and was counted righteous, and the promise came 430 years before the law, which cannot cancel it (3:6–18). The law was a guardian until Christ came (3:19–29); now slaves have become sons and heirs (4:1–7). After a personal plea (4:8–20), Paul reads the story of Hagar and Sarah as a picture of two covenants, slavery and freedom (4:21–31). Chapters 5–6 are practical. “For freedom Christ has set us free” (5:1), but freedom is a call to serve one another in love (5:13), walking by the Spirit and bearing his fruit (5:16–26). Such a church restores the fallen and bears burdens (6:1–10), and Paul ends boasting only in the cross (6:11–18).

Where it leads: to Christ. Christ “gave himself for our sins to deliver us from the present evil age” (1:4). He is the one offspring of Abraham to whom the promises were made (3:16), so that all who are his are “heirs according to promise” (3:29). Born under the law, he redeemed those under the law (4:4–5); he bore its curse, “becoming a curse for us” (3:13), so that Abraham’s blessing might reach the Gentiles. In him “you are all one in Christ Jesus” (3:28), Jew and Greek, slave and free, one family of faith that Paul finally calls “the Israel of God” (6:16). What counts is “a new creation” (6:15), the new age that began when Christ rose.

In the church’s history. Martin Luther’s commentary on Galatians (1535) became one of the best-loved books of the Reformation. He called the letter his “Katie von Bora”, after his wife: the letter he was married to. For Luther it said most clearly what the Reformation was about: the righteousness God requires is not a standard we must reach but a free gift we receive, by grace alone, through faith alone, in Christ alone. Anything added to that takes away from it.

For us. Everyone who feels that their standing before God depends on their performance needs to hear Galatians. Every church that drifts towards moralism, self-improvement in place of trust in Christ’s finished work, needs to sit with it until the gospel is clear again. The threat usually comes from the same direction: the wish to make grace a little less free and human effort a little more decisive. Galatians says no. The cross is enough; Christ is enough; grace is enough. And because it is enough, believers are free: not to please themselves, but to love, with “faith working through love” (5:6). “Far be it from me to boast except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ” (6:14).

1.title: No Other Gospel: The Divine Origin of Paul’s Message
1.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 1 opens the letter and its first movement (chapters 1–2), in which Paul tells his own story to show where his gospel came from, before he argues it from Scripture in chapters 3–4.

The message. There is only one gospel, Christ’s giving of himself for our sins, and it came from God, not from men, so no one may change it: not the teachers in Galatia, not Jerusalem, not Paul himself, not an angel from heaven. Hence the double curse (vv. 8–9). If the gospel could be revised by human authority, by apostles, tradition or church consensus, it would be a human message, and a human message cannot save. Paul preaches the same gospel as the other apostles, but its authority rests on the Christ who gave it, not on their endorsement.

Why it was said. Teachers had come to the young Galatian churches adding circumcision and the law of Moses to faith in Christ, and belittling Paul as a second-hand apostle who had got his message from Jerusalem and trimmed it to please Gentiles (see the introduction).

How the chapter makes its case. The greeting already answers the crisis (vv. 1–5): Paul was sent by the risen Christ and the Father, and Christ gave himself for our sins to rescue us, so all the glory is God’s. In place of thanksgiving comes astonishment (vv. 6–10): another gospel means deserting the God who called them, and whoever preaches it, even an angel, is accursed. Then Paul’s life becomes the evidence (vv. 11–24): his gospel came by a revelation of Jesus Christ (vv. 11–12). He was the last man to invent it, a zealot who tried to destroy the church (vv. 13–14). God set him apart, called him by grace and revealed his Son to him (vv. 15–16). For years he was far from Jerusalem, apart from a fortnight with Peter (vv. 17–22), while the Judean churches glorified God because of him (vv. 23–24).

Where it leads. The chapter rests on two acts of Christ. He gave himself for our sins (v. 4), and he stopped his enemy on the road and revealed himself to him (vv. 12, 16). The gospel is news of what God has done in his Son, and the persecutor turned preacher shows how far that grace reaches. The curse Paul pronounces on a false gospel is the curse Christ himself bore to buy the true one (3:13).

For us. Test every message, however impressive its messenger, by the gospel the apostles gave once for all. Refuse every “Christ plus”, however respectable the plus. And take heart from Saul of Tarsus: no past is beyond the grace that called him.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul’s authority and his message both come from God, and the message is Christ’s rescue of sinners, for the Father’s glory. Paul is an apostle sent by the risen Christ and God the Father, not by any human authority, the very point his opponents disputed (vv. 1–2). His greeting of grace and peace then gives the gospel in a phrase: Christ gave himself for our sins to rescue us from the present evil age, as the Father willed, and the glory is God’s for ever (vv. 3–5).
verseByVerse.theology:
Grace begins with God

Verses 3–5 are among the earliest summaries of the gospel in the New Testament, and they show that salvation starts wholly with God. The Son gives himself for our sins and rescues us out of an evil age, by the Father’s will. That rules out a cross improvised late and a Father who had to be talked into mercy (see the note on vv. 3–5). Grace is God’s own first move, and it ends in glory to God (v. 5).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The Galatians had received a complete gospel and were being told it was only a foundation that needed a second storey. Paul’s opening answers that before the argument starts: the gospel of vv. 3–5 leaves no gap for a human contribution.

Now: The same instinct survives wherever the gospel is treated as the way in and something else as the real substance of the Christian life: a sacramental record, a moral achievement, an intense spiritual experience. Christ gave himself, the Father willed it, and nothing remains to be added.

verseByVerse.quote: Paul, an apostle—not from men nor through man, but through Jesus Christ and God the Father, who raised him from the dead— and all the brothers who are with me, To the churches of Galatia:
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul writes as an apostle sent by the risen Christ and by God the Father, not by any human authority, and everything in the letter depends on that claim. Someone in Galatia was saying otherwise, so he answers in his first sentence.

No warm-up. The credentials arrive in the first breath, and they are not modest. An apostolos is one who is sent, an envoy carrying the authority of the one who sent him. A king’s messenger does not soften the message to suit the room; he answers to the throne, not to the audience.

Not from men nor through man. “Not from men”: no human authority is the source of what he preaches. “Nor through man”: no human being was even the channel of his appointment. The teachers in Galatia were evidently calling him a second-hand apostle, who got his gospel from Jerusalem and dropped the awkward parts, and Paul refuses the description before he has finished his name.

Through Jesus Christ. Christ commissioned him directly on the Damascus road (Acts 9:15; 26:16–18). Having denied that any man was the source, Paul names Jesus Christ, side by side with the Father. He does not argue that Christ is God; he assumes it, setting Jesus on God’s side of the line and not on the side of “men”.

Who raised him from the dead. Paul’s whole claim rests on this phrase. The Twelve were commissioned by a Jesus they had walked beside for some three years. Paul was commissioned on a road outside Damascus by a Jesus he had never met, and the only thing that makes that a commissioning and not a hallucination is that the man is alive. Take the resurrection out of the sentence and Paul is a zealot with a story (Acts 9:3–6; 1 Corinthians 9:1).

To the churches of Galatia. The brothers with him say it too, so this is not one man’s grievance dressed up as doctrine. And the address is bare: no “to the saints”, no “beloved”, just the destination, as on an envelope. These were young churches, very likely those of Paul’s first journey (see the introduction), and at Lystra he had been stoned and left for dead (Acts 14:19). He had bled for these people.

The throne behind the letter. Before any argument, the letter has shown us the throne. The Father raised the Son from the dead; the risen Son stopped his enemy on a road and made him an envoy; and the message that envoy carried has crossed twenty centuries without needing a human endorsement once.

Why does it matter where Paul got his gospel? Because a message is only as reliable as its source. If Paul’s gospel came from the Jerusalem church, Jerusalem could correct it, and the teachers in Galatia could claim to bring the fuller, official version. If it came from the risen Christ, nobody may correct it: not Jerusalem, not a council, not a modern scholar, not your own feelings on a bad day. Galatians is not one early Christian’s opinion among many, but the message the Lord gave his apostle, and it carries his authority over you.
verseByVerse.note: Galatia was a Roman province in central Asia Minor. Many think the letter went to the churches Paul founded on his first journey (Pisidian Antioch, Iconium, Lystra and Derbe); others think of ethnic Galatians farther north.

verseByVerse.quote: Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ, who gave himself for our sins to deliver us from the present evil age, according to the will of our God and Father, to whom be the glory forever and ever. Amen.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul’s greeting already holds the whole gospel: grace from the Father and the Son, because Christ gave himself for our sins to rescue us, as the Father willed, so that all the glory is God’s. In a letter about to fight for grace, grace is the first word of blessing.

Grace to you and peace. A Greek letter opened with chairein, greetings; a Jew said shalom, peace. Paul seems to bend the first word into its cousin charis, grace, God’s free and undeserved favour, and set the Hebrew blessing beside it. The order never reverses. Peace, the wholeness of being right with God, is not something we bring to earn grace; it is what grace gives.

From God and the Lord Jesus. One source, two persons. Grace is something only God can give, and Paul names Jesus as its giver alongside the Father without any sense of saying something daring.

Who gave himself. Not “who was given” or “who was taken”. In the garden more than twelve legions of angels were within reach, and the arresting party drew back and fell to the ground at his word, and still he handed himself over (Matthew 26:53; John 18:6). No one took his life from him; he laid it down of his own accord (John 10:18).

For our sins. Not for our disadvantages, our wounds or our unrealised potential, but for the thing that is actually wrong. The little word “for” carries the whole weight of the cross: to atone for them, in our place, the innocent standing where the guilty should have stood (1 Corinthians 15:3). This is exactly what the teachers in Galatia were quietly undermining. If Christ gave himself for our sins, nothing remains to be added; if something must be added, he did not finish what he gave himself to do. Paul puts the answer in his greeting before he has stated the problem.

To deliver us from the present evil age. To snatch out, to rescue (exaireō), the word Peter used when the Lord rescued him from Herod’s prison (Acts 12:11): a rescue party pulling a man out of a burning building, not a renovation crew. Much Jewish teaching divided history into this present age and the age to come, when God would put everything right. Paul says the age to come has already broken in, in the risen Christ, and believers have been hauled out of the old one while still walking around inside it. The present evil age is this world under sin, Satan and death (Ephesians 2:2): the age in which a scan comes back with bad news, vows end with lawyers, and old men die alone in wards; the age in which your own heart quietly prefers itself to God on a Tuesday morning. Christ gave himself to pull us out of its guilt and its grip, not only its sorrows. And the law, as a way of being right with God, belonged to that old age: going back to it is going back into the building Christ pulled you out of.

According to the will of our God and Father. The cross was not a rescue plan improvised late, nor did a reluctant Father have to be talked round by a loving Son; it was the Father’s plan from before the foundation of the world (Acts 2:23; 1 Peter 1:20). There is no reluctance anywhere in the Trinity towards sinners.

To whom be the glory. Before a line of argument, the greeting breaks into worship, and this doxology (a short burst of praise to God) is the argument in miniature. Salvation by grace gives all the glory to God. Salvation by works, even partly, would share it with us, and a gospel that lets man take a bow has stopped being this gospel.

In everyday life. When your conscience accuses you, notice which way you instinctively look: back at your own week, to see whether it was good enough, or up at the one who gave himself for your sins. You come to God after a bad week exactly as you came the first time.

If Christ has rescued me from the present evil age, why is my life still so hard? Because the rescue comes in two stages, and you live between them. You have been delivered from the age’s guilt, condemnation and claim on you: sin is no longer your master, and death no longer your end. You have not yet been delivered from its presence: illness, grief and temptation remain. The age to come has begun in you by the Spirit and will arrive in full when Christ returns. Your hardships do not mean the rescue failed; they mean the rescuer has not finished, and he will.

Does “for our sins” really mean in our place? Yes. Paul says it outright in 3:13: Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us, bearing the penalty our sins deserved. This is called penal substitution (penal because it concerns the penalty, substitution because he bore it in our place), and it is not one theory among many but the heart of what Scripture says the cross accomplished (Isaiah 53:5–6; 2 Corinthians 5:21). Some sincere Christians are uneasy with it, fearing it pictures an angry Father punishing an unwilling Son; but this verse rules that out, since the Son gave himself according to the will of our God and Father, one in love and purpose. Christ’s death also defeated the powers and showed us God’s love, but it does those things precisely because it first paid for sin.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: There is only one gospel, and to change it is to desert God himself. In place of his usual thanksgiving, Paul is astonished that the Galatians are so quickly turning from the God who called them in grace to “a different gospel”, which is no gospel but a distortion (vv. 6–7). Anyone who preaches another, even Paul or an angel from heaven, is under God’s curse, and Paul says it twice (vv. 8–9). A man who says that is plainly not courting human approval; he is Christ’s servant (v. 10).
verseByVerse.theology:
The gospel stands over the church that preaches it

The double curse of vv. 8–9 means the gospel is not the church’s property, to be developed by councils or refined by consensus. Luther saw in these verses the controversy of his own century.

Why the curse does not fall on every disagreement among Christians, and why no one may edit a gospel that was bought rather than drafted, is set out in the note on vv. 8–9.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The troublers in Galatia were very probably sincere (on who they were, see vv. 6–7). Their error was that they had turned the relation of law and grace upside down, which is why the test of vv. 8–9 matters: it asks whether the message is the gospel first received, not whether the teacher is sincere.

Now: A different gospel rarely announces itself. It presents itself as the fuller, more serious version. How to tell it from a secondary disagreement, and what the curse means for a mother or brother in such a church, are taken up in the note on vv. 8–9.

verseByVerse.quote: I am astonished that you are so quickly deserting him who called you in the grace of Christ and are turning to a different gospel— not that there is another one, but there are some who trouble you and want to distort the gospel of Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
To turn from the gospel of grace to a gospel of Christ plus the law is not an upgrade but a desertion of God himself, for there is no other gospel, only a distortion of the one. And Paul is astonished at how fast it is happening.

The loudest silence. Every other letter Paul wrote to a church opens with thanksgiving or blessing. The Corinthians were tolerating a man sleeping with his father’s wife and getting drunk at the Lord’s Table, and they still got a thanksgiving. The Galatians get “I am astonished”, and the first readers would have heard the silence at once.

I am astonished. The word (thaumazō) can mean wonder at something glorious or bewilderment at something absurd; here it is plainly the second. It was also a standing formula of rebuke in ancient letters.

So quickly. He had preached, they had believed, the Spirit had come, and already they were most of the way to something else. The gospel’s hold on a heart is more fragile than we assume, and a church can be evangelical on paper and drifting in practice inside a year.

Deserting. The word (metatithēmi) is used of changing sides: a soldier crossing to the enemy lines. And it is in the present tense: they are in the act of deserting. The door is still open behind them.

Him who called you. They are not deserting a doctrine but a person: God himself. You cannot leave the gospel of grace behind and keep the God of grace; he does not come apart from his message. Every step away from grace is a step away from the one whose grace it is, however religious the walk looks from outside.

A different gospel, not that there is another one. What they are moving to is not a second version of the good news, nor good news at all. Paul corrects himself at once: there is only ever one gospel.

Trouble and distort. “Trouble” means to stir up, unsettle; “distort” means to turn a thing inside out. Adding law-keeping to grace does not top grace up; it inverts it. The moment my acceptance depends even one per cent on my performance, God is no longer the one who justifies the ungodly but the one who audits the diligent, and I am back keeping score.

Who were the troublers? They are usually called Judaizers (see the introduction): Jewish Christians who professed faith in Jesus and taught that Gentile believers must also take on circumcision, the food rules and the sacred calendar to be counted full members of God’s people and truly saved (Acts 15:1, 5). Not Christ instead of Moses, but Christ plus Moses. They would have called themselves the conservative party, the ones taking the Old Testament seriously.

The grace of Christ. Grace here has a face. Paul has already said what the grace of Christ is: he gave himself for our sins (v. 4). To be called in it is to be summoned into the shelter of a finished gift, a cross already borne and a debt already paid. That is why Christ plus anything distorts the gospel instead of supplementing it: every addition says his self-giving left something undone, and asks the Galatians to complete what the Son of God, dying, declared was finished (John 19:30). Grace was not a stage on the way to something better. It was the best thing God had, and he gave it first. There is no gospel above this one to graduate to, because there is no greater gift than Christ, and he is already given.

What it does not mean. The false teachers did not deny Christ; they added to him. The most dangerous error is rarely the one that throws Christ out. It is the one that keeps him and gives him a partner.

What does Christ-plus look like today? Rarely circumcision. More often something a Christian must also do or be before he is properly accepted: a particular experience, a particular church, a sacrament treated as the ground of salvation, a standard of devotion, cultural rules about dress, drink, music or schooling. Many are good in their place. The question is whether they have quietly moved from being the fruit of acceptance to its condition. Ask what you think of a believer who lacks them. If the answer is second-class Christian, the plus has arrived.

Does this mean that true believers can desert Christ and be lost? No. Paul writes to the Galatians as to people he believes are Christ’s: “I have confidence in the Lord that you will take no other view” (5:10). Their danger was real, and the warning is the means God uses to bring them back: those who are truly his do not finally fall away (John 10:28–29; Philippians 1:6), and the warnings of Scripture are one of the ways he keeps them. Paul is warning of the danger a church is in when it keeps the Christian words and changes the gospel, not saying these believers are already lost.
verseByVerse.note: Teachers had come insisting that Gentile believers be circumcised and keep the law of Moses.

verseByVerse.quote: But even if we or an angel from heaven should preach to you a gospel contrary to the one we preached to you, let him be accursed. As we have said before, so now I say again: If anyone is preaching to you a gospel contrary to the one you received, let him be accursed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Anyone who preaches a gospel contrary to the one the apostles preached, however impressive he is, stands under God’s curse, because the gospel is God’s and no one may change it. Paul says it twice, so that no one can put it down to temper.

Let him be accursed. Accursed is anathema. In the Old Testament an anathema was something placed under the ban, devoted to God for destruction: Jericho and everything in it, Achan and the silver under his tent (Leviticus 27:28–29; Joshua 7). To be anathema is to be handed over to the judgment of God. Paul does not use the word about the immorality in Corinth; in that letter it falls on anyone who has no love for the Lord (1 Corinthians 16:22). He uses it here, because a false gospel does not merely damage lives; it destroys souls.

Even if we or an angel. The two examples are chosen to be impossible. “Even if we”: Paul puts himself first in the line of fire. “Or an angel from heaven”: not a demon in disguise, but a real messenger from heaven in all his glory. The gospel does not take its authority from whoever carries it. It stands over its messengers, and Paul is one of them.

I say again. Verse 8 could be dismissed as a man saying something enormous in the heat of the moment, so he says it again in cold blood, and drops the hypothetical: not “even if”, but “If anyone is preaching”. Someone is. And the test is not novelty, eloquence or results, but “the one you received”: the apostolic gospel, now preserved for us in Scripture, which measures all Christian preaching and is measured by nothing.

Why the gospel cannot be revised. The gospel is not a philosophy that later minds might improve. It is news: the report of something God has done in history. Christ died for our sins in accordance with the Scriptures, he was buried, he was raised on the third day (1 Corinthians 15:3–4). An angel can no more amend that than roll the stone back across an empty tomb. So Paul can curse a rival message without quoting it: any gospel that adds to Christ’s finished work announces something that never took place, a Christ whose death was not enough. Nor is insisting on one gospel arrogance. Reporting what happened is not boasting, and this report humbles the one who carries it, because it says he could not save himself either.

The anathema that fell on the Son. Why such severity? Because of what the message cost. There was already an anathema in this story, and it did not fall on a false teacher. It fell on the Son. Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us (3:13). He stood where the ban falls, to buy this gospel for sinners at the price of himself. Nobody may edit it: it was paid for, and it is perfect.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Christians may curse people personally. Our response to false teachers is to warn, refute and pray for their repentance, remembering that Paul himself was once a persecutor of the gospel and received mercy.

Does every doctrinal disagreement fall under this curse? No, and Paul’s own practice proves it: he allowed real latitude on food, holy days and other matters where believers see differently (Romans 14). What he anathematises is a gospel contrary to the one received, and the letter tells us which question he means: on what ground is a sinner accepted by God? Christians have long argued over church government, the last days and baptism without either side being outside the faith. Change the ground of acceptance from Christ’s finished work to anything a person contributes, and the argument is no longer inside Christianity.

Does this include those who claim new revelation from an angel? Yes; it is the plainest test the Bible gives. Joseph Smith said the angel Moroni led him to the Book of Mormon; Islam teaches that Gabriel gave the Qur’an to Muhammad. Paul anticipated exactly this. No later revelation, whatever its claimed source, an angel or a church authority, may contradict the gospel the apostles preached. Even Satan disguises himself as an angel of light (2 Corinthians 11:14).

And what of churches like Rome? The test is the one Paul gives. The Council of Trent taught that a person is justified by a righteousness God pours into him, received in baptism and increased by good works, and it condemned those who teach that we are justified by faith alone. That teaching falls on the wrong side of Paul’s line. Yet the Roman Catholic and Orthodox churches also confess the Trinity, Christ’s deity, his atoning death and bodily resurrection, and many of their members trust Christ alone in spite of what their church teaches. The curse falls on the false gospel and those who preach it, not on everyone who sits under it, and our part is to make the true gospel plain to them.

Is Paul saying my mother is accursed? This is the question that keeps people awake: a mother in a church that teaches something like this, a brother who has joined a group that adds requirements to Christ. Read the sentence again: “let him be accursed”, the one preaching. The anathema falls on the teacher who corrupts the gospel, not on the troubled congregation being taught. Paul calls the Galatians themselves “my little children, for whom I am again in the anguish of childbirth” (4:19): the words of a mother in labour, not of a man consigning them to destruction. The severity is aimed at the wolves because he loves the sheep. Pray for your mother, love her, and gently show her Christ alone.

Should I leave a church that preaches a different gospel? If a church has made something other than Christ’s finished work the ground of a sinner’s acceptance, and its leaders will not be corrected, then yes: you and your children need to be fed, not starved. Do it without bitterness, after honest conversation, and not over a secondary matter. A church with weak preaching, poor music or a pastor you disagree with on the millennium is not under this verse. A church that has changed the gospel is.

Where Christians differ: how serious is false teaching? Many today treat doctrinal differences as unimportant, as long as people are sincere. This commentary’s view: Paul shows that changing the gospel itself, especially adding works to faith as the ground of justification, is a matter of eternal life and death. Not every disagreement is a matter of the gospel; Christians may differ charitably on secondary matters (Romans 14). But on the way of salvation there is no room for compromise. Justification by grace alone through faith alone in Christ alone is the article on which the church stands or falls.

Uncertain wording. “As we have said before” could point back to verse 8, a moment earlier, or to a warning Paul and his companions gave while they were in Galatia. The tense, a saying made and still standing, fits an earlier visit a little better. Either way the repetition is a settled verdict, not a slip of temper.
verseByVerse.note: “Accursed” is anathema: handed over to God’s judgment.

verseByVerse.quote: For am I now seeking the approval of man, or of God? Or am I trying to please man? If I were still trying to please man, I would not be a servant of Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A man who pronounces a curse even on angels for changing the gospel is plainly not courting human approval: he is Christ’s slave, and serves one Master. Living for people’s approval and serving Christ cannot be combined.

Am I now seeking the approval of man, or of God? The question probably echoes his critics: that Paul was a crowd-pleaser who had noticed circumcision was a hard sell in a Gentile town and quietly dropped it to fill his meetings. His answer is what they have just read. A crowd-pleaser does not curse angels in his third paragraph. The verb is peithō, to win someone over: am I canvassing for human votes or for God’s?

Or am I trying to please man? “Please” (areskō) means to make oneself agreeable. And the word “still” in the next phrase is a confession. There was a time when he did live to please people, arranging everything around the approval of his teachers and his nation’s leaders (v. 14). Not any more.

The scars are the argument. He gives a second answer later, which settles the matter: “if I, brothers, still preach circumcision, why am I still being persecuted?” (5:11). Keeping circumcision would have delighted the synagogue and kept him out of prison; that was the man-pleasing option, and he refused it. The stones of Lystra left marks on him, and such scars he calls the marks of Jesus (6:17).

I would not be a servant of Christ. A slave (doulos): owned, not employed, with one master. To need the approval of the room is to have taken a second owner, and no one can serve two masters (Matthew 6:24). This Master first took the form of a servant and went down to a slave’s death on a cross (Philippians 2:7–8). A man owned by him has no need to buy approval anywhere else.

How the crisis actually worked. Bad theology usually travels on the back of a longing for approval. What moved a Gentile believer in Galatia was not an argument but the ache of being told, by impressive men from the mother church, that he was a second-class Christian, and the relief on offer if he would just be circumcised and be counted properly.

A verdict already given. Paul’s freedom does not come from a tough personality but from grace. A man whose acceptance is still being decided must manage everybody’s opinion of him, because any one of them might be the verdict. A man accepted in Christ has had the verdict handed down in advance, in his favour, at the cost of the cross, and every other opinion is now only an opinion (1 Corinthians 4:3–4). The Son of God, who stood before Caiaphas and Pilate and the crowd and would not trade a syllable of the truth for their favour, was condemned by all of them so that the only Judge whose verdict counts could say over sinners: no condemnation.

Living by radar. In The Lonely Crowd (1950) the sociologist David Riesman argued that earlier generations had been steered from within, as if by a gyroscope set early by parents and tradition, while a new kind of person was steered by radar, scanning those around him for signals of approval. Now we carry the radar in our pockets, and it never switches off. The usual cure on offer is to trust your inner gyroscope and stop caring what anyone thinks, but that only makes the self the judge instead of the crowd, and the self is a harsh and fickle judge (see the note on Romans 1:24–25). Paul has neither radar nor gyroscope. He has a Master. And the people-pleaser is not the most loving person in the room: he needs people too much to tell them the truth, so in the end he is using them. Only someone who no longer needs your approval is free to serve you at the cost of your frown, as Paul serves the Galatians in this letter, and as Christ, who “did not please himself” (Romans 15:3), served us all.

What it does not mean. Not that Paul did not care about people. He became all things to all people, that by all means he might save some (1 Corinthians 9:22): he adapted his manner, never the message. He tells Christians to please their neighbours for their good, to build them up (Romans 15:2). The line is crossed when someone’s approval becomes the thing you cannot live without, and the truth bends to keep it.

How do I get free from the fear of what people think? Not mainly by trying harder to stop caring, which usually makes you anxious about your anxiety. Name the specific person and the specific thing you have softened or left unsaid to keep their approval. Bring it to the cross, and remind yourself what God has already said about you in Christ: accepted, forgiven, his child, not on probation. The more that verdict fills your sight, the smaller every other one becomes. Then take one small step of obedience you have been avoiding, and notice that you survive their frown.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul’s gospel came from the risen Christ, not from men, and his own life proves it. He states the claim: he was not handed it or taught it, but received it by a revelation of Jesus Christ (vv. 11–12). The evidence follows in order of time: a zealous persecutor, the last man to invent such a message (vv. 13–14); God’s call by grace (vv. 15–16); years far from Jerusalem, with a fortnight with Peter and a sight of James (vv. 17–22); and the churches of Judea, who never saw his face, glorifying God for the persecutor turned preacher (vv. 23–24).
verseByVerse.theology:
Chosen, called and shown the Son

Verses 15–16 are among Paul’s most compact statements of God’s free grace. Three acts of God stand in order, and Paul starts none of them: God set him apart before birth, called him by grace, and was pleased to reveal his Son in him (the call that does what it says, and the revelation in him, are opened in the note on vv. 15–16). Grace that reaches a man riding the other way with warrants in his bag is not a reward for seeking (Romans 8:29–30; Ephesians 1:4–5).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Paul’s critics could point to his absence from Jesus’ earthly ministry and his late arrival among the apostles. His answer is the record of vv. 17–22: three years in Arabia and Damascus, a fortnight in Jerusalem where he met only two of the leaders, then far-off Cilicia.

Now: A shameful history made into evidence for the gospel (vv. 13–14), a calling that began before the one called was looking (v. 15), and hidden years that turn out to be part of God’s work (vv. 17, 21–22): each of these reaches an ordinary believer directly.

verseByVerse.quote: For I would have you know, brothers, that the gospel that was preached by me is not man’s gospel. For I did not receive it from any man, nor was I taught it, but I received it through a revelation of Jesus Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The gospel Paul preached is not a human product: he was neither handed it nor taught it, but received it when the risen Christ revealed himself to him. The rest of chapters 1 and 2 argue this claim, and the letter leans on it: if justification by faith (2:16) were Paul’s idea, it could be bargained over; because it is Christ’s revelation, it cannot.

I would have you know, brothers. A formula that flags what he most wants remembered. He has just spoken of angels under a curse, and the next word is a family word. He is fighting for them, not with them.

Not man’s gospel. The claim comes in three parts, and each closes a door. Not man’s gospel: literally not according to man, not shaped to human taste or invented by a human mind. Then not received from any man, and not taught.

The vocabulary of the rabbis. Those last two verbs belong to the world Paul came from. Receiving and being taught were how a rabbi was made: tradition passed hand to hand, master to pupil, from the school of Hillel to Gamaliel to Saul of Tarsus (Acts 22:3), every link named and verifiable. Paul had that pedigree, and the machinery that made him a Pharisee had nothing whatever to do with this.

A revelation of Jesus Christ. “Revelation” is unveiling. On the Damascus road the risen Christ pulled back the curtain, and what was behind it was himself. The gospel did not rise from below, out of human wisdom or piety. It came down, out of the mouth of the risen Son, and the one who spoke it is still the one who keeps it.

In everyday life. Nobody in the discussion outranks Jesus Christ. So when the culture, a bestseller or your own doubts suggest that the old message needs revising for modern people, you are free to say no.

Received, or not received? A careful reader will feel a problem. To Corinth Paul writes, “I delivered to you as of first importance what I also received” (1 Corinthians 15:3): that Christ died, was buried, was raised and appeared. Received, plainly, from the church before him. Both are true. What Paul received from others were the facts: the burial, the names of the witnesses, things he very likely heard from Peter over those fifteen days (v. 18). He knew before Damascus that a man called Jesus had been crucified; he was persecuting people over it. What no one gave him, and no one could teach him, was the meaning: that this crucified man is the Son of God, that his death ends the law as a way of being accepted by God, and that Paul was to take that news to the nations.

Should I expect God to reveal his truth to me directly, as he did to Paul? Not in that way. The revelation given to the apostles was foundational: given once and now written down for the whole church (Ephesians 2:20; Jude 3). The canon, the list of books that make up Scripture, is closed. The Spirit does not give you new revelation but opens your eyes to the revelation already given, so that you see Christ in the Scriptures and believe (1 Corinthians 2:12; 2 Corinthians 4:6). That is not a lesser thing. The Christ who unveiled himself to Paul on the road unveils himself to you in the pages Paul wrote.

Uncertain wording. “A revelation of Jesus Christ” can mean a revelation given by Jesus Christ or one whose content is Jesus Christ; the Greek allows either. Verse 16, where God reveals “his Son”, favours the second, but Paul most likely means both, because on the Damascus road they were one event: the one who revealed was the one revealed.

verseByVerse.quote: For you have heard of my former life in Judaism, how I persecuted the church of God violently and tried to destroy it. And I was advancing in Judaism beyond many of my own age among my people, so extremely zealous was I for the traditions of my fathers.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul’s own past refutes the charge that his gospel was a softened Judaism: he was a rising zealot who tried to destroy the church, the last man on earth to invent a gospel of grace. He now produces as evidence the past everyone knew about.

My former life in Judaism. Judaism here means the Jewish religion and way of life as he had practised it, in its strictest form.

Persecuted the church of God violently. “Violently” is literally “beyond measure” (the Greek gives us our word hyperbole), and “tried to destroy it” uses the word for what an army does to a city it means to leave uninhabitable. And it was the church of God. He was not fighting a sect. He was fighting God.

The pictures Luke supplies. Saul dragging off men and women to prison (Acts 8:3), casting his vote when believers were put to death, and pursuing them to foreign cities in raging fury, as he told Agrippa (Acts 22:4; 26:10–11). There were families in Judea who still lived with what he had done.

Advancing in Judaism. The verb is used of a career going well. He was not a failing religious man looking for something gentler; trained under Gamaliel (Acts 22:3) and ahead of his contemporaries, he was winning. That is the uncomfortable point for every respectable person: religious success can keep a heart further from God than open rebellion, because a man who is winning sees no need to be rescued. Paul later counted all his gains as loss for Christ (Philippians 3:4–8).

Extremely zealous for the traditions of my fathers. “Zealous” is the word for a zealot (zēlōtēs), and it had a history: Phinehas with his spear, Elijah at Carmel, the Maccabees in the hills. The traditions were the oral law of the Pharisees, rules built like a fence around the law of Moses (Mark 7:3). To the charge that his gospel was Judaism trimmed down for people who could not manage the whole thing, his answer is: look at who I was. Nobody leaves the top of a system he is winning at, for a message that gets him flogged, because he wants an easier life.

Why are you persecuting me? On the Damascus road the risen Lord did not ask why Saul was persecuting the disciples, but “Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?” (Acts 9:4). A blow at the least of his people lands on him. And he stopped the man wounding him not to repay him but to call him. Paul said it later: “Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners, of whom I am the foremost” (1 Timothy 1:15). The foremost of sinners was made an apostle, so that no one afterwards could say his own case was too far gone. The patience of Christ has never yet met a sinner it could not outlast.

What it does not mean. Zeal is not bad; Paul was zealous before and after. But zeal for the wrong cause is deadly, and sincerity is no guarantee of truth. Saul was entirely sincere on the road to Damascus. He was also entirely wrong, and he had blood on his hands to prove it.

In everyday life. Think of the most hostile unbeliever you know, the one who mocks your faith or has hurt people you love, and pray for his salvation today. Saul was the last man the church expected to see converted. Stephen died praying that this sin would not be held against his killers (Acts 7:60), and Saul was standing there.

Does my past disqualify me from serving God? No. Some reader carries a history he has never said out loud: something done at twenty-two, something a family still lives with, something that surfaces at three in the morning and argues that whatever else grace is for, it is not for that. Paul had helped to kill Christians, and God made him an apostle. Your past may have real consequences that must be faced honestly; some offences rightly bar a man from certain offices, and wrongs must be put right where they can be. But your past cannot put you beyond forgiveness or stop God using you. Often he uses the very history you are ashamed of to show others what his mercy can do.

verseByVerse.quote: But when he who had set me apart before I was born, and who called me by his grace, was pleased to reveal his Son to me, in order that I might preach him among the Gentiles, I did not immediately consult with anyone;
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul’s conversion and calling were God’s work from first to last: God set him apart before birth, called him by grace and revealed his Son to him, to send him to the Gentiles. The sentence that began in verse 13 now turns: before, Paul was the one acting; from here God is the subject of every verb, and Paul contributed nothing but the opposition.

Set apart before I was born. Literally, from my mother’s womb: before the zeal, before the persecution, before there was a person there at all to be either good or bad. The language echoes the prophets: “Before I formed you in the womb I knew you, and before you were born I consecrated you” (Jeremiah 1:5), and the Servant of Isaiah 49:1, called from the womb. Here the setting apart is Paul’s appointment as an apostle. Saul of Tarsus did not take heaven by surprise; heaven had made arrangements for him before his mother knew she was carrying him.

The separated man. There may be a play on words: Pharisee most likely comes from a root meaning the separated ones. Paul had spent his adult life separating himself, from Gentiles, the unclean and the careless, by rigorous effort, and it had made him the most dangerous man the church knew. God’s reply is that he had been set apart before he separated himself from anything at all, and set apart, of all things, to go to the Gentiles.

Called me by his grace. Not because of his zeal, or in spite of his record, or on account of anything visible at the time. The call had no cause outside God, and Paul deserved the opposite. And this call does what it says: not an invitation left on the table but a summons that itself brings the dead man to life (Romans 8:30). Grace has never once been embarrassed by the material it was given to work with.

Was pleased to reveal his Son. The Father took pleasure in showing this man his Son. Read it with Acts 9 in view: while Paul is still breathing threats and murder against the disciples, God is glad. And it was not only a light on a road but something opened on the inside: God shone in his heart “to give the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ” (2 Corinthians 4:6). He had known the facts about Jesus for years and hated them. Now the Son himself was unveiled to him, and everything he knew rearranged itself around a living person.

In order that I might preach him among the Gentiles. The commission arrives in the same breath as the conversion (Acts 9:15; 26:17–18): he was not saved and then, later, given something to do. And he was to preach him: not a system or a programme, but the Son.

I did not immediately consult with anyone. Literally, I did not confer with flesh and blood. He did not go to human authorities for interpretation or approval. The revelation needed no second opinion.

In everyday life. On the days you doubt that God could want you, go back to the verbs. Not one of them depends on you. He set you apart before you were born; he called you by his grace; he was pleased to reveal his Son to you. It rests on his pleasure, and his pleasure does not come and go.

Is this about every believer, or only Paul? It is first Paul’s call to be an apostle, but the pattern holds for every believer: God chose his people in Christ before the foundation of the world (Ephesians 1:4) and calls them by grace (Romans 8:29–30). Not every Christian is called to be an apostle; every Christian was chosen before he was born and called by grace.

Did I choose God, or did God choose me? Ask a simpler question: on the day it happened, was I looking for him? Paul was not merely uninterested; he was riding in the opposite direction with authority to arrest the people who loved the name. If grace reached him there, it is not a reward handed to the seekers, and you need not audit the sincerity of your first steps to find out whether you are safe. You did choose Christ, really and gladly; but you chose him because he first chose you (John 15:16). Who moved first is not in doubt.

If God chose people before birth, why should I evangelise? Because God’s choosing works through the preaching of his Son, as this verse says: he revealed his Son to Paul in order that Paul might preach him among the Gentiles. Election is not a reason to keep quiet; it is the reason preaching works. You do not know who the elect are, so you tell everyone, and with confidence, because God has people he intends to reach, and the hardest heart in your street is no harder than Saul’s was.

Where Christians differ: did God choose those he foresaw would believe? Some Christians hold that God’s choice rests on his foreknowledge of who would freely trust Christ. Others hold that it rests on his own free grace alone, and that faith is the result of election, not its cause. This commentary’s view: election is unconditional. Paul’s own case is the strongest answer: what God foresaw in Saul was a persecutor, and grace called him anyway. Elsewhere Paul says God chose us that we should be holy, not because we were (Ephesians 1:4–5), and that the choice was made not because of works but because of him who calls (Romans 9:11). Brothers who hold the other view love the same Christ; but the verse in front of us puts the whole initiative with God.

Uncertain wording. Paul writes literally that God was pleased to reveal his Son “in me”. The ESV takes it as “to me”, a common use of the Greek preposition; others read “within me”, an inward unveiling, or “through me”, to others. The vision on the road and the opening of his eyes went together (2 Corinthians 4:6), so both “to me” and “in me” are true of what happened.

parallels.desc: the LORD called me from the womb

verseByVerse.quote: nor did I go up to Jerusalem to those who were apostles before me, but I went away into Arabia, and returned again to Damascus.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Instead of going to the Jerusalem apostles to be taught, Paul went away to Arabia and then back to Damascus, so his gospel cannot have come from them. Every instinct says go to headquarters; he went the other way.

Those who were apostles before me. “Before me” is about time, not rank: they were apostles earlier, not higher.

Into Arabia. The Nabataean kingdom, south and east of Damascus: a real state with towns, trade routes and a capital at Petra, ruled by King Aretas (2 Corinthians 11:32). Why Arabia? Perhaps for prayer and rethinking the Scriptures in the light of Christ. Perhaps to preach, and Paul lets slip what may have followed: the governor under King Aretas guarded Damascus to seize him, and he escaped through a window in the wall, lowered in a basket (2 Corinthians 11:32–33). Kings do not post guards for men who have been quietly meditating.

And returned again to Damascus. There he preached boldly in the synagogues that Jesus is the Christ, until a plot forced him to flee (Acts 9:19–25).

Three silent years. Three years (v. 18) passed before he met Peter, and Scripture does not say what happened in them. But the Paul who wrote Romans did not have Romans in his head on the Damascus road. Somewhere between the light and the letters, the whole Old Testament was rebuilt around Christ in that mind, and Paul names no teacher but Jesus Christ himself (v. 12). The nearest picture is the Emmaus road, where the risen Lord, beginning with Moses and all the Prophets, interpreted to two disciples the things concerning himself (Luke 24:27). The Pharisee now found the Scriptures full of the one he had been hunting.

The hidden years are part of the work. Some believers’ lives feel like a waiting room, or illness took the decade that was supposed to count. Scripture’s pattern runs the other way: Moses had forty years in Midian, David years in caves, Joseph a pit and a prison. The Son of God himself spent about thirty years in a workshop in a town of no consequence, and about three in public. The hidden years are not the delay before the work; they are part of it. The God who set Paul apart was no less at work in the silent years than in the light on the road. He has never wasted a year of a life he owns, and the apostle who wrote “I have learned in whatever situation I am to be content” (Philippians 4:11) did not learn it by accident.

What should I do in a season when I feel unused? Do the next faithful thing in front of you, as to the Lord. Read Scripture and pray, not to earn the next assignment but because the God preparing you is worth knowing for his own sake. Serve in the small ways that are open: the visit, the meal, the child in Sunday school, the colleague who needs a kind word. Ask mature believers whether there is something you are not seeing. And refuse the lie that God has mislaid you: he is often doing in you what he will later do through you.
verseByVerse.note: Arabia here is the Nabataean kingdom, south and east of Damascus.

verseByVerse.quote: Then after three years I went up to Jerusalem to visit Cephas and remained with him fifteen days. But I saw none of the other apostles except James the Lord’s brother.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul’s first visit to Jerusalem came three years after his conversion, lasted fifteen days and brought him face to face with only Peter and James: far too little to make him their pupil. Three years, fifteen days, two men: Paul is counting.

Then after three years. Probably about AD 35–36: three years, not three weeks.

To visit Cephas. Cephas is Peter’s name in Aramaic; both mean rock (John 1:42). The rare verb, from which we get “history”, means to go and get to know someone, not to be examined, trained or commissioned by him. Paul may well have learned about Jesus’ earthly ministry from this eyewitness, but he did not receive his gospel from him.

Fifteen days. The length is the argument: long enough for two men to talk themselves hoarse, nothing like long enough to train an apostle. A rabbinic apprenticeship took years, not a fortnight.

James the Lord’s brother. Jesus’ own brother, raised in the same house in Nazareth, did not believe during the ministry: “For not even his brothers believed in him” (John 7:5). Then his brother was killed, and then, in a single line, the risen Jesus “appeared to James” (1 Corinthians 15:7). That meeting turned an unbeliever into the leader of the Jerusalem church (Acts 15:13; 21:18), who would call himself a servant of God and of the Lord Jesus Christ (James 1:1).

One would like to have been in that house. Peter had denied the Lord three times beside a charcoal fire and been restored beside another one (John 18:18; 21:9). Paul had hunted down the people Peter was pastoring. James had once thought his brother out of his mind (Mark 3:21). Those fifteen days very likely contained Peter’s eyewitness accounts, and a man who had never seen any of it listening to every word. The risen Christ had gathered all three, the coward, the enemy and the sceptic, and there is no one his mercy cannot turn into a witness.

Did Paul and Peter preach the same gospel? Yes: “Whether then it was I or they, so we preach and so you believed” (1 Corinthians 15:11). A fisherman and a Pharisee received the same gospel independently from the same risen Lord, and when they compared notes they were preaching the same Christ. That is one of the strengths of the evidence.

Does Paul contradict Acts? Luke says Barnabas brought him to the apostles, plural, and that he went in and out among them at Jerusalem (Acts 9:27–28); Paul says he saw none except James. The best explanation is ordinary speech, not special pleading. Luke summarises the visit in two verses and uses “the apostles” as a collective term for that circle’s recognised leadership, Peter and James; a man who met the Prime Minister and the Chancellor says he met the government. Paul, whose argument depends on the precise number, gives it. The other apostles were probably elsewhere. Both accounts can be true, even if we cannot reconstruct every detail.

Was James Jesus’ full brother? The plain reading is that he was a son of Mary and Joseph, born after Jesus, and so his half-brother, since Jesus had no human father. The early church developed other views, that he was Joseph’s son by an earlier marriage or a cousin, to protect the belief that Mary remained a virgin, but the New Testament never suggests either. Many Christians through the centuries, including some of the Reformers, held one of those views, and faithful believers still differ; nothing in the gospel turns on it.

Uncertain wording. “I saw none of the other apostles except James” can mean that James was the one other apostle Paul saw, or that Paul saw no other apostle, only James. The first is the more natural reading: Paul probably counted James an apostle in a wider sense, one to whom the risen Christ had appeared (1 Corinthians 15:7). The argument is the same either way.
verseByVerse.note: Cephas is Peter. James the Lord’s brother led the church in Jerusalem.

verseByVerse.quote: (In what I am writing to you, before God, I do not lie!)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul swears before God that his account is true, because the truth of the gospel hangs on the facts of where it came from. Halfway through a plain account of dates and names he stops and calls God as witness.

He was being called a liar. Nobody swears like this unless something is at stake. A rival account of his life was circulating in Galatia: apparently that he had been taught and authorised by Jerusalem and had then departed from their teaching.

What he protects shows what is at stake. Paul does not defend his character: no wounded paragraph about years of service, no list of what these churches owe him. He swears to one thing only, the facts of where the gospel came from, and lets his name take whatever damage it takes. If the Galatians conclude that Paul is unimpressive, nobody is lost. If they conclude that the gospel is a human product, everything is.

The faithful witness. Behind Paul’s oath stands his Lord’s. When the high priest said, “I adjure you by the living God, tell us if you are the Christ, the Son of God,” the Lord who had forbidden careless oaths answered under oath, and his true answer sent him to the cross (Matthew 26:63–66). A lie would have saved his life. He is the faithful and true witness (Revelation 3:14), and Paul, under accusation, walks where his Master walked, telling the truth before God when it costs him.

In everyday life. Speak the truth as before God, always, because you always are before God, and the Spirit of truth lives in you. Notice the small untruths that ease a day along: the exaggeration, the flattering excuse, the “I’m fine”.

Did Jesus not forbid oaths? The Lord said, “Do not take an oath at all”, and “Let what you say be simply ‘Yes’ or ‘No’” (Matthew 5:34–37), and James repeats it (James 5:12). But look at what he was forbidding. Oaths had become a sliding scale of honesty: swear by the temple and you may wriggle out; swear by the gold of the temple and you are held to it (Matthew 23:16–22). A man could signal how much of what he said he meant to stand behind, so his ordinary word was worth nothing. Christ abolishes the scale: a disciple’s plain yes carries the full weight of an oath. Paul is not grading his truthfulness; under formal accusation, he is testifying to a matter on which souls depend. Scripture is not embarrassed by that kind of solemn witness. Paul does it more than once (Romans 1:9; 2 Corinthians 1:23), and God, having no one greater to swear by, swore by himself to guarantee a promise (Hebrews 6:13–17).

May a Christian take an oath in court? Yes. The Reformed confessions, the 1689 London Baptist Confession as well as Westminster, teach that a lawful oath is part of religious worship, in which a person solemnly calls God to witness what he asserts, and that it may rightly be taken when lawful authority requires it in a weighty matter (Westminster 22.1–3; 1689 23.1–3). Swear only to what you know is true, and only when the matter is serious. Some Christians, from tender conscience, prefer to affirm, and most courts allow it. Either way, you are speaking before God, as you do every day.

verseByVerse.quote: Then I went into the regions of Syria and Cilicia. And I was still unknown in person to the churches of Judea that are in Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For years after that visit Paul worked far from Jerusalem, in Syria and Cilicia, so unknown to the churches of Judea that they would not have recognised his face. The point is still his distance from the supposed source of his gospel.

Syria and Cilicia. Syria included Antioch; Cilicia was Paul’s home province, with its capital at Tarsus, where he was born (Acts 22:3). Luke says why he went home: the Hellenists in Jerusalem were seeking to kill him, so the brothers brought him down to Caesarea and sent him off to Tarsus (Acts 9:29–30). Acts then carries on without him until Barnabas fetches him to Antioch (Acts 11:25–26).

The years nobody reported. They may add up to as many as ten, with no recorded sermon, no named convert, no letter. He was preaching (v. 23), and he may have founded the churches of Syria and Cilicia that the Jerusalem Council later wrote to (Acts 15:23, 41). Those years produced no headline, but they produced the apostle to the Gentiles.

Unknown in person. Literally, unknown by face. The churches of Judea, closest to Jerusalem and once hunted by him, would not have recognised him in the street; had Paul absorbed his gospel there, they would at least have known his face. To them he was a name in a story. But the Lord of the church sees in secret, counts the hairs of heads no one else looks at, and was himself unknown by face to almost the whole world while he did the work that saved it.

That are in Christ. Not the churches of Jerusalem’s region, or of the apostles, but the churches of Judea that are in Christ. Being in Christ means being joined to him by faith, so that what is true of him is counted true of everyone joined to him: his death is their death to sin, his righteousness their standing before God, his Father their Father (Romans 6:4–5; 2 Corinthians 5:21). Only there could what happened next have happened. The families Saul had broken and the man who broke them now stood before God on exactly the same ground, and it was not their own.

Someone who hurt me has become a Christian. Must I now be close to him? You must forgive him, and you should rejoice that God has saved him, as the Judean churches did. But forgiveness is not the same as restored trust, and it does not require you to put yourself back in harm’s way. God did not send Saul to live among the families he had wronged. Where a wrong was serious, and especially where there has been abuse, it is right to keep a wise distance, to let the church and, where needed, the authorities deal with what must be dealt with, and to let trust be rebuilt slowly, if at all. You can bless a man from a distance, and God often heals both sides without asking you to stand in the same room.
verseByVerse.note: Cilicia was Paul’s home province, with its capital at Tarsus.

verseByVerse.quote: They only were hearing it said, “He who used to persecute us is now preaching the faith he once tried to destroy.” And they glorified God because of me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The churches Paul had persecuted heard that he now preached the faith he had tried to destroy, and they glorified God because of him. Their worship settled, years before this letter, the question the Galatians were now asking.

They only were hearing it said. Paul preserves the sentence they kept repeating; the tense is continuous, the report going round the villages of Judea the way a church tells the story it cannot get over.

He who used to persecute us. Mark the word “us”. The report passed between the very people he had hunted: families who had lost someone, congregations that had scattered. “The faith” here means the gospel itself. The man who set out to make sure it did not survive is now carrying it across the empire. One line shows what the gospel does: a before and an after, a total change the man did not manage himself, with the evidence in what he now does, not in what he says.

The question already settled. Paul has spent the chapter arguing that his gospel did not come from men; the Judean churches settled it years earlier, on the strength of one report, without weighing his credentials: no committee produces a man like that. And they were Jewish Christians who did not oppose Paul’s gospel but praised God for it. If the churches nearest Jerusalem glorified God for Paul’s ministry, how can the Galatians reject it on the say-so of men claiming to speak for Jerusalem?

They glorified God because of me. Not: they admired my transformation. Literally, they glorified God “in me”, the words Paul used of his conversion: God was pleased to reveal his Son in me (v. 16). Looking at what had become of Saul of Tarsus, the churches of Judea did not see a reformed character; they saw Christ living in a former persecutor, and knew that no one but God could have put him there. That is what a converted life is: not a self improved, but a life in which Christ has taken up residence and begun to show, giving by his Spirit new desires, so that the man who wanted the church destroyed now spends himself for it (Ezekiel 36:26–27). Paul will say it outright: “It is no longer I who live, but Christ who lives in me” (2:20).

What he does with his enemies. A chapter that opened with a curse pronounced on angels closes with worship rising from villages that had suffered at the hands of the man being spoken of. This is what the risen Christ does with his enemies when he means to have them: he does not merely stop them; he turns them into the reason his people worship. And the glory is not Paul’s.

What if my conversion was not dramatic? Your story still ends the same way: with God glorified. Most Christians were not struck down on a road; many cannot remember a time when they did not trust Christ. That is not a lesser grace. A child kept from the far country by God’s mercy is as much a wonder as a prodigal brought home from it. If you love Christ and live for him, however quietly, the same God has done the same work in you, and it is right for others to give thanks for it.

Should I tell my story? Yes, simply and honestly, with Christ at the centre. Paul tells his story so that the gospel can be seen, not so that Paul can be admired. Tell what you were, what Christ did and what he is to you now, without making the before more lurid or the after more impressive. People can argue with your theology. It is much harder to argue with what God has evidently done to you.

1.text: <sup>1</sup>Paul, an apostle—not from men nor through man, but through Jesus Christ and God the Father, who raised him from the dead—<sup>2</sup>and all the brothers who are with me, To the churches of Galatia:<sup>3</sup>Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ,<sup>4</sup>who gave himself for our sins to deliver us from the present evil age, according to the will of our God and Father,<sup>5</sup>to whom be the glory forever and ever. Amen.<sup>6</sup>I am astonished that you are so quickly deserting him who called you in the grace of Christ and are turning to a different gospel—<sup>7</sup>not that there is another one, but there are some who trouble you and want to distort the gospel of Christ.<sup>8</sup>But even if we or an angel from heaven should preach to you a gospel contrary to the one we preached to you, let him be accursed.<sup>9</sup>As we have said before, so now I say again: If anyone is preaching to you a gospel contrary to the one you received, let him be accursed.<sup>10</sup>For am I now seeking the approval of man, or of God? Or am I trying to please man? If I were still trying to please man, I would not be a servant of Christ.<sup>11</sup>For I would have you know, brothers, that the gospel that was preached by me is not man’s gospel.<sup>12</sup>For I did not receive it from any man, nor was I taught it, but I received it through a revelation of Jesus Christ.<sup>13</sup>For you have heard of my former life in Judaism, how I persecuted the church of God violently and tried to destroy it.<sup>14</sup>And I was advancing in Judaism beyond many of my own age among my people, so extremely zealous was I for the traditions of my fathers.<sup>15</sup>But when he who had set me apart before I was born, and who called me by his grace,<sup>16</sup>was pleased to reveal his Son to me, in order that I might preach him among the Gentiles, I did not immediately consult with anyone;<sup>17</sup>nor did I go up to Jerusalem to those who were apostles before me, but I went away into Arabia, and returned again to Damascus.<sup>18</sup>Then after three years I went up to Jerusalem to visit Cephas and remained with him fifteen days.<sup>19</sup>But I saw none of the other apostles except James the Lord’s brother.<sup>20</sup>(In what I am writing to you, before God, I do not lie!)<sup>21</sup>Then I went into the regions of Syria and Cilicia.<sup>22</sup>And I was still unknown in person to the churches of Judea that are in Christ.<sup>23</sup>They only were hearing it said, “He who used to persecute us is now preaching the faith he once tried to destroy.”<sup>24</sup>And they glorified God because of me.

keyVerse.quote: who gave himself for our sins to deliver us from the present evil age, according to the will of our God and Father
keyVerse.note: Before Paul states the problem, he gives the answer: this is the gospel the rest of the chapter defends. Christ gave himself, freely and completely, for the very thing that is wrong with us, and the Father willed it. Because the rescue is finished, anything added to it does not complete the gospel but contradicts it.

1.reflection:
Paul’s greeting already contains the gospel: Christ “gave himself for our sins to deliver us from the present evil age” (v. 4). In what sense have believers already been rescued from the present evil age, and in what sense are we still waiting? How does that help on a hard day?

The teachers in Galatia did not deny Christ; they added to him (vv. 6–7). What “Christ plus” might tempt Christians today, and you in particular? How can you tell when something good has become a condition of acceptance?

Paul says he would not be a servant of Christ if he were still trying to please people (v. 10). Where do you feel the pull of others’ approval most strongly, and how does the verdict God has already given in Christ set you free from it?

The churches Saul had persecuted “glorified God because of me” (v. 24). Who seems to you beyond the reach of grace? How does Paul’s story change the way you pray for them, and the way you think about your own past?

2.title: Justified by Faith: The Gospel Confronts the Church
2.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 2 completes Paul’s account of where his gospel came from and how it was tested (1:11–2:21), and then turns that story into the doctrine the rest of the letter defends.

The message. A sinner is put right with God through faith in Christ, not by works of the law, and no one, however highly placed, may add to that gospel, or deny it at a meal table any more than in a sermon. Jew and Gentile come by the same road, sit at the same table and live by the same faith in the Son of God.

Why it was said. The teachers troubling Galatia claimed Jerusalem’s backing for their demand that Gentile believers be circumcised, and hinted that Paul’s gospel was a second-hand, cut-down version (see the introduction). So Paul tells what actually happened when his gospel met the Jerusalem leaders, and when it met Peter.

How the chapter makes its case. In Jerusalem (vv. 1–10) Paul laid his gospel before the leaders with the uncircumcised Greek Titus at his side; Titus was not compelled to be circumcised, and the pillars added nothing and gave Paul the right hand of fellowship. At Antioch (vv. 11–14) the same truth was tested in practice: Peter drew back from eating with Gentile believers for fear of the circumcision party, even Barnabas followed, and Paul opposed him before them all. Then Paul states the truth at stake (vv. 15–21): even Jews by birth are justified only through faith in Christ; going back to the law, not trusting Christ, is what makes a transgressor; through the law Paul died to the law and now lives by faith in the Son of God; otherwise Christ died for nothing.

Where it leads. The whole dispute was whether Christ’s death is enough: if righteousness could come any other way, “Christ died for no purpose” (v. 21). He did not die for nothing. His cross is wide enough for Jew and Gentile together, and personal enough for Paul, once his enemy, to write that he “loved me and gave himself for me” (v. 20).

For us. Few now argue about circumcision, but the pull to add something to Christ, a rule, a background, a performance, and to keep a slightly separate table for those who lack it, is as strong as ever. This chapter calls us to rest our whole standing before God on his finished work, to welcome every believer on the same terms, and to live each ordinary day by faith in him.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–10 — Paul Accepted by the Apostles
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The Jerusalem leaders added nothing to Paul’s gospel and welcomed him as a partner, so the troublers in Galatia cannot claim them. Fourteen years on, Paul went up by revelation with Barnabas and the uncircumcised Greek Titus, and laid his gospel privately before the leaders, so that the one church would not become two (vv. 1–2). Titus was not compelled to be circumcised, and the false brothers who came to spy out the believers’ freedom got no ground at all (vv. 3–5). The pillars, whose standing counts for nothing against the truth, added nothing, for they saw that the same God who worked through Peter was working through Paul (vv. 6–8). They gave him the right hand of fellowship and asked only that he remember the poor (vv. 9–10).
verseByVerse.theology:
One gospel, one people, one way in

The decision about Titus (v. 3) settles a question of the first order: Jew and Gentile are justified on the same terms, and no covenant sign such as circumcision is added to faith as a condition of acceptance with God. This is not first a point about cultural inclusion but about what justification is: one covenant of grace, one people, one Saviour, one way in.

Two further principles sit in the passage: the gospel is “entrusted” (v. 7), so neither Paul nor Jerusalem may edit it (see vv. 6–8); and in v. 9 grace is seen before fellowship is given (see vv. 9–10).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Galatia was being told that Gentile believers needed circumcision added to their faith. Paul answers that he took exactly this question to Jerusalem with an uncircumcised Greek beside him (vv. 1–3), and the men whose authority the troublers claimed added nothing (v. 6) and shook his hand (v. 9).

Now: Anything may be done for the gospel; nothing may be added to it (on why Paul circumcised Timothy and refused it for Titus, see vv. 3–5). Where a practice is offered as helpful, Christians may differ; where it is required for full acceptance, the gospel is at stake. And care for the poor is not an addition to the gospel (see the note on vv. 9–10).

verseByVerse.quote: Then after fourteen years I went up again to Jerusalem with Barnabas, taking Titus along with me.
