I went up because of a revelation and set before them (though privately before those who seemed influential) the gospel that I proclaim among the Gentiles, in order to make sure I was not running or had not run in vain.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul went up to Jerusalem at God’s direction, not at the apostles’ summons, and laid his gospel before its leaders so that the church would not split in two.

After fourteen years. The number is the argument: if Paul’s gospel had needed the Jerusalem apostles’ sign-off, it had been working without it for well over a decade. And with Barnabas: the man who had vouched for Paul when the Jerusalem church would not go near him (Acts 9:27).

Taking Titus along with me. Titus was a Greek, an uncircumcised Gentile convert, and Paul walked him into the middle of a meeting about whether Greeks must be circumcised: not only a companion but a deliberate test case.

I went up because of a revelation. Not because he was summoned: God sent him. If this was the famine visit, the revelation may have come through the prophecy of Agabus (Acts 11:28).

Privately. He took it to the leaders first, in a closed room where a thing can be settled, not on a platform where it gets performed. “Those who seemed influential” (hoi dokountes) means those held in repute. Paul is not sneering at Peter and James; he calls them pillars and shakes their hands. He refuses only the idea that reputation is what makes a gospel true, because the Judaizers (the teachers who insisted that Gentile believers be circumcised and keep the law of Moses) had been trading on Jerusalem’s prestige.

Running in vain. Not doubt about his message, which chapter 1 forbids, but the danger that the church might become two churches, circumcised and uncircumcised, each with its own apostle and its own terms. He was not checking his doctrine but protecting the unity it requires.

The gospel among the Gentiles. Paul set on the table not a method of mission but a person: Jesus Christ, crucified for Gentiles exactly as for Jews, and received by faith without the law. Titus standing in the room put the question in flesh and blood: is Christ alone enough for a Greek? Two churches on two sets of terms would mean a Christ cut in half, and Paul’s question to the Corinthians has only one answer: “Is Christ divided?” (1 Corinthians 1:13).

Should I submit my beliefs to church leaders? Submit them to Scripture first, and hold them humbly before the church. Paul would not let Jerusalem’s reputation decide his gospel, but he did not go off alone either: he laid what he preached before mature leaders and was glad to find them agreed. Test your understanding against the Bible, then against wise believers and the historic confessions of the church. If you find yourself believing something no faithful Christian has ever believed, be very slow to trust it. If your leaders ask you to believe what Scripture contradicts, Scripture wins.

Which visit was this? Acts records several. Many take this one to be the Jerusalem Council of Acts 15, where exactly this question was decided. Others take it to be the earlier famine-relief visit of Acts 11:27–30, which would mean Galatians was written before the Council met. That view has strong arguments: Paul describes a private meeting, whereas Acts 15 was a public assembly; and if a formal apostolic ruling on circumcision already existed, it is hard to see why Paul, fighting on precisely that issue, never once quotes it. It fits the southern Galatian churches and the early date this commentary prefers (see the introduction). Nothing in the letter’s argument depends on settling it.
verseByVerse.note: It is debated whether this visit is the famine visit of Acts 11 or the Jerusalem Council of Acts 15.

verseByVerse.quote: But even Titus, who was with me, was not forced to be circumcised, though he was a Greek. Yet because of false brothers secretly brought in—who slipped in to spy out our freedom that we have in Christ Jesus, so that they might bring us into slavery— to them we did not yield in submission even for a moment, so that the truth of the gospel might be preserved for you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jerusalem did not make the Greek Titus be circumcised, and Paul would not give way for a moment to the false brothers who wanted it, because the Gentile believers’ freedom in Christ, and so the gospel itself, was at stake.

Even Titus. Everything came down to one man standing in the room. If the Judaizers were right, Jerusalem had a duty to say so with an uncircumcised Gentile believer in front of them. It said nothing of the kind.

Why circumcise Timothy and not Titus? Paul later circumcised Timothy (Acts 16:3). Timothy’s mother was a Jewish believer (Acts 16:1), so he would probably have been reckoned a Jew by birth who had simply never been marked as one; nobody was demanding it as a condition of his salvation; and Paul did it so that Timothy could get into synagogues and preach. Titus was a Gentile, and the demand was being made as a requirement of acceptance with God. So Paul’s rule is not that circumcision is forbidden, but that anything may be done for the sake of the gospel, and nothing may be added to it. Once a thing stops being free and becomes necessary, he will not move: the man who circumcised Timothy would not let anyone touch Titus.

False brothers. Then the sentence turns dark. Pseudadelphoi claimed to be Christians but were not, and what follows is the vocabulary of espionage: “secretly brought in” (pareisaktos, the word used of smuggling), “slipped in”, and “to spy out”, the word for scouting an enemy position. These were not honest men with a different opinion. They came to find out how free the Gentile churches actually were.

To spy out our freedom. Freedom or slavery (4:9; 5:1): that is the whole letter in brief. What was on offer looked like a promotion, full membership and the marks of the covenant, but it was chains: a performance that decides acceptance with God puts a man on a treadmill he cannot get off, because the performance is never finished and the verdict is never in.

We did not yield. Literally, not for an hour. Compromise never looks like surrender from the inside: it presents itself as a small, reasonable, temporary allowance for the sake of peace.

Preserved for you. Not so that Paul might win, but for Gentile converts hundreds of miles away who would never know the meeting had happened. The truth of the gospel is free grace, kept from being bent into something else. Paul is not a man who enjoys a fight but a man standing in a doorway so that people behind him can stay free, and the freedom of every Gentile believer since, including whoever is reading this, was kept safe in that doorway. Behind Paul stands the one who bought that freedom: Christ, who set us free (5:1), at the cost of his own life.

The circumcision Titus already had. Titus did not need to be circumcised, and the reason is Christ. Paul tells the Colossians that believers have been circumcised with a circumcision made without hands, by the circumcision of Christ, and buried with him (Colossians 2:11–12). The circumcision of Christ most likely means his death: there the old self under sin was cut away, and everyone joined to him by faith shares in it. Everything the sign pointed to, belonging, cleansing, a place in Abraham’s family (3:29), Titus already had in Christ. To demand the sign now would be to say that Christ’s work had not quite reached him.

In everyday life. Notice the small, reasonable allowances: a rule that began as a helpful habit and has quietly become a test of whether someone is a real Christian; a preference about worship, schooling or Bible translation that you now hold over other believers. Ask of each one: is this free, or have I made it necessary?

What exactly is Christian freedom? Freedom from the law as a way of earning God’s acceptance, from its curse on our sins, and from the ceremonies that pointed forward to Christ, such as circumcision, the food laws and the sacrifices. It is not freedom to sin (5:13), but freedom for something: to serve God as sons rather than slaves, gladly, from love. A slave works to avoid punishment; a son works because he belongs to the family. You never again have to wonder whether today’s obedience was enough to keep you in. You are in, and you obey from there.
verseByVerse.note: Titus was a Greek and uncircumcised: a test case for whether Gentile believers must be circumcised.

verseByVerse.quote: And from those who seemed to be influential (what they were makes no difference to me; God shows no partiality)—those, I say, who seemed influential added nothing to me. On the contrary, when they saw that I had been entrusted with the gospel to the uncircumcised, just as Peter had been entrusted with the gospel to the circumcised (for he who worked through Peter for his apostolic ministry to the circumcised worked also through me for mine to the Gentiles),
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Jerusalem leaders, whatever their standing, added nothing to Paul’s gospel, because they saw that the God who worked through Peter among the Jews was working through Paul among the Gentiles.

Added nothing to me. Two words in Greek, and they end the argument. The Judaizers claimed Paul’s gospel was incomplete, an abridgement of the full Jerusalem version. The pillars heard it in full and found nothing missing.

God shows no partiality. Close to an Old Testament formula: God does not lift up faces, does not take the important man’s side because he is important (Deuteronomy 10:17; Acts 10:34). Paul turns it on the apostles themselves. Peter had walked with Jesus and Paul had not, and it makes no difference to the truth of the gospel. Nobody in the room outranks the truth.

Entrusted. They saw what God had plainly been doing in the Gentile world. And “entrusted” is the language of a steward handed something that belongs to someone else. A man entrusted with a message has no authority to revise it: Paul cannot edit this gospel to please Gentiles, and Jerusalem cannot edit it to please Jews, for exactly the same reason. Neither of them owns it.

He who worked through Peter. Verse 8, in brackets, holds the key. Look at who does the work: not Peter, and not Paul. The same God energised both ministries (the verb gives us energy), so the comparison never becomes a competition: two men were used, and one God was working. He does not spend himself heavily on the impressive servants and thinly on the rest; the least of his servants has the same Lord at work in him as the greatest.

One Lord behind both commissions. One gospel, two mission fields: Peter mainly to Jews, Paul mainly to Gentiles, not a senior apostle with a junior assistant. Peter was recommissioned by the risen Christ beside the Sea of Galilee (John 21:15–17); Paul was commissioned by the same risen Christ on the Damascus road and sent to open the eyes of the Gentiles (Acts 26:16–18). So the gospel to the circumcised and to the uncircumcised is one gospel, with one owner and one content, the crucified and risen Christ, the same Lord of Jew and Greek alike (Romans 10:12).

What it does not mean. Not that there are two gospels, one for Jews and one for Gentiles. Peter would say it himself at the Council: “we believe that we will be saved through the grace of the Lord Jesus, just as they will” (Acts 15:11).

Does “God shows no partiality” mean church leaders deserve no respect? No. Paul calls these men pillars and gladly accepts their handshake, and elsewhere tells churches to esteem their leaders very highly in love because of their work (1 Thessalonians 5:12–13). What he refuses is to let their status decide what is true. Respect your pastor, pray for him, and follow his teaching gladly when it is faithful to Scripture. But never believe or dismiss something because of who said it. The question is always whether it is the gospel.

Uncertain wording. “What they were makes no difference to me” renders a compressed phrase. Its small word pote can mean “once” or “formerly”, so that Paul means what they once were, perhaps their years at Jesus’ side; or it can simply strengthen the phrase, “whatever they were”. Either way the point stands: no one’s standing, however it was gained, decides the truth of the gospel.

verseByVerse.quote: and when James and Cephas and John, who seemed to be pillars, perceived the grace that was given to me, they gave the right hand of fellowship to Barnabas and me, that we should go to the Gentiles and they to the circumcised. Only, they asked us to remember the poor, the very thing I was eager to do.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The leaders of the Jerusalem church recognised God’s grace in Paul and shook hands with him as partners in one gospel, asking only that the poor be remembered, which he was already eager to do.

Pillars. The picture is architectural: the men on whom the weight rests, the leaders of the Jerusalem church (Revelation 3:12). James here is not James the brother of John, one of the Twelve, who had already been executed by Herod (Acts 12:2), but James the Lord’s brother. Then Peter, and John the son of Zebedee.

Perceived the grace. The order is the point: first they saw the grace, then they extended the hand. The handshake conferred nothing; it acknowledged what God had already done, as the church always should. Ordination does not manufacture a minister and a handshake does not manufacture a brother. Where grace is evidently at work, the faithful response is to acknowledge it, and where it is not, no ceremony will supply it.

The right hand of fellowship. An ancient pledge of good faith: between us this is settled. The word behind fellowship is koinōnia, partnership: a joint stake in the same enterprise, not merely a truce.

To the Gentiles. A division of labour, not a division of message, and never watertight: Peter opened the Gentile door in the first place (Acts 10), and Paul went to the synagogue first in almost every town he entered.

Remember the poor. After a meeting about the terms of salvation, the one thing Jerusalem asks is that its poor believers not be forgotten, and years of Paul’s life went into the collection for the believers in Judea (Romans 15:25–27; 2 Corinthians 8–9). He has just refused to add one item to the gospel, and he accepts this without a murmur, because it is not an addition. Nothing has been placed between a sinner and God; what has been named is what grace does once it has arrived. A church that has understood justification by faith alone and has no interest in the hungry has not understood it (James 2:15–17; 1 John 3:17).

A company of forgiven enemies. Consider that room. The apostle who had been hunting Christians and the apostle who had denied Christ in a courtyard put their hands together over a gospel neither of them had earned: Peter restored by the risen Lord after his denials, Paul stopped by him on the way to Damascus. Paul uses the same word, fellowship, for what every believer is called into: the fellowship of God’s Son (1 Corinthians 1:9). Nobody in it had a record worth defending, and that is what made it possible. Even the care of the poor is the gospel’s own shape: it comes from the Lord who became poor for our sake (2 Corinthians 8:9), and he did not wait for us to be worth helping.

In everyday life. When you see grace at work in another Christian, especially one from a different background, church or tradition, perceive it and say so: give him the right hand, in words if not in a handshake.

Who are the poor I am to remember, and how? First, needy believers, the household of faith, as Paul will say in 6:10; then everyone in need as we have opportunity. Start near: the widow in your congregation, the family where a job has been lost, the asylum seeker who has turned up on Sunday, the student who cannot afford the trip. Give regularly and deliberately, not only when moved; through your church, so that help is wise and sustained; and with time and friendship as well as money, because the poor are often lonely too. Remember the persecuted and impoverished church abroad. And do it gladly: Paul was eager, not pressured.
verseByVerse.note: Pillars held up a building; these three were the leaders of the Jerusalem church. The poor were the believers in Judea.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The gospel can be denied by conduct as surely as by words, and it must be defended even against an apostle. At Antioch Peter had been eating freely with Gentile believers, but when men came from James he drew back for fear of the circumcision party (vv. 11–12). The other Jewish believers, even Barnabas, followed him. Seeing that they were not in step with the truth of the gospel, Paul challenged Peter before them all: how could he, who lived like a Gentile, force Gentiles to live like Jews (vv. 13–14)?
verseByVerse.theology:
The gospel governs the feet, not only the confession

Peter’s failure was not in his doctrine (see the note on vv. 11–12) but in a life not walking in line with a belief truly held, which is what Paul means by hypocrisy here (see vv. 13–14). The gospel must govern table habits and the pull of social pressure, not only statements of faith.

Scripture also records, without embarrassment, an apostle publicly corrected by another apostle on a matter of the gospel (see the box “Where Christians differ: Peter’s authority” at the end of the note on vv. 11–12).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Peter’s withdrawal at Antioch came from fear, not conviction: verse 12 says he feared the circumcision party. It is the snare Paul named at 1:10, the wish to please people, and it carried the other Jewish believers and Barnabas with it (v. 13).

Now: Two things here reach a reader directly: the company in which he behaves as a slightly different Christian, and the question of when a leader should be corrected in public (both are taken up in the note on vv. 13–14).

verseByVerse.quote: But when Cephas came to Antioch, I opposed him to his face, because he stood condemned. For before certain men came from James, he was eating with the Gentiles; but when they came he drew back and separated himself, fearing the circumcision party.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul opposed Peter to his face at Antioch, because Peter, who had been eating freely with Gentile believers, drew back from them for fear of the circumcision party, and so stood condemned by his own conduct.

I opposed him to his face. The scene moves to Antioch in Syria, the first great Gentile church (Acts 11:19–26), and the agreement just reached is tested, and fails in the most unlikely man. Paul spoke face to face, in front of everybody (v. 14), not behind his back. And a man who could correct Peter by the gospel had not got that gospel from Peter.

Because he stood condemned. A courtroom word: not that Paul condemned him, but that he stood already condemned, by the contradiction between what he believed and what he was doing. Paul did not pass the sentence. He read it out.

Certain men from James. The phrase has been used to blame James, and probably should not be. The Jerusalem church later wrote to Antioch about men who had gone out from them, “although we gave them no instructions” (Acts 15:24); these may have claimed James’s authority without his approval. What is certain is the effect: their arrival was enough.

Eating with the Gentiles. A shared table meant shared life and acceptance, and in the church it may well have included the Lord’s Supper. For a Jew it was charged ground: a Gentile table might serve meat the law called unclean, or meat offered to idols, and many devout Jews would not eat with Gentiles at all. Peter himself had once said it was unlawful for a Jew to associate with a Gentile, and the Jerusalem believers had taken him to task for eating with uncircumcised men (Acts 10:28; 11:3). To sit down to a Gentile meal was to declare that the wall had come down, and Peter had been doing it, meal after meal.

He drew back. The tense pictures him withdrawing bit by bit. “Drew back” is used of troops pulling back from a position; “separated himself” is aphorizō, the word from which the name Pharisee may come. Nobody announced a policy. He simply began sitting elsewhere, and everyone knew what it meant. And it was not conviction: he had not changed his mind about anything, only his seat, because of who was watching. It is the fear of man (Proverbs 29:25).

A table the Lord had opened. Peter was stepping back not only from his own vision but from his Lord. Mark, whose Gospel the early church connected with Peter’s preaching, records Jesus teaching that what goes into a person from outside cannot defile him: “Thus he declared all foods clean” (Mark 7:19). Moving his plate away from Gentile believers, Peter was putting back a wall Christ himself had taken down, as if Christ’s cleansing were not enough to make a Gentile fit company.

He never changed his table. One man in all of Scripture never once changed his table because of who was watching. He ate with tax collectors in front of the Pharisees and with Pharisees in front of the tax collectors, because he lived before the face of his Father. And when Peter failed again, that same Lord did not cast him off; he sent him a brother to tell him the truth. The Lord who restored Peter by a charcoal fire restored him again at Antioch, and he is patient still with every one of us who has changed seats.

How was this possible? This is the man who heard the voice on the rooftop saying, “What God has made clean, do not call common”; who walked into Cornelius’s house and watched the Spirit fall on Gentiles; who defended it all to the Jerusalem church and won the argument (Acts 10–11). He was the leading expert in the room on this very point. That is the hard lesson: knowing a truth and having settled it publicly does not make a man immune to abandoning it when the wrong people walk in. What undid him was what had undone him in the high priest’s courtyard nearly twenty years before: not doubt, not argument, but the sudden weight of watching faces. Fear of man is not a beginner’s sin that maturity leaves behind.

Is it wrong to adapt to the people I am with? Not in itself. Paul became as a Jew to Jews and as one outside the law to those outside the law, to win them (1 Corinthians 9:20–22), and adapting customs, food and manner for love and the gospel is Christlike. Peter differed in two ways: his motive was fear, not love; and his action told fellow believers they were not fully acceptable unless they changed. So ask: am I adapting to serve these people, or to protect myself? And does it tell any brother or sister in Christ that they are second-class?

Where Christians differ: Peter’s authority. The Roman Catholic Church teaches that Peter was the head of the apostles and the first pope, with a primacy passed to his successors, including infallibility in defining doctrine. It limits that infallibility to formal definitions, not conduct; but the point here is wider. This commentary’s view: Peter was a great apostle and leader, but here Paul publicly rebukes him for a serious error affecting the gospel. Peter was neither infallible in practice nor above correction by another apostle. The gospel judges Peter, not Peter the gospel, and that is true of every church leader since. The authority of the church rests on the apostolic teaching recorded in Scripture, not on the succession of one office (Ephesians 2:20).

Uncertain wording. Who were “the circumcision party”? The phrase is literally “those of the circumcision”. They may have been Jewish believers who insisted that Gentile converts be circumcised (compare Acts 11:2; 15:5), or Jews outside the church in Judea whose pressure on the believers there was growing in these years. Either way, Peter feared what would be said when word of his table reached home.
verseByVerse.note: Antioch in Syria was the first great Gentile church. Eating together was the test: strict Jews would not share a table with Gentiles.

verseByVerse.quote: And the rest of the Jews acted hypocritically along with him, so that even Barnabas was led astray by their hypocrisy. But when I saw that their conduct was not in step with the truth of the gospel, I said to Cephas before them all, “If you, though a Jew, live like a Gentile and not like a Jew, how can you force the Gentiles to live like Jews?”
verseByVerse.commentary:
Peter’s withdrawal carried the other Jewish believers with him, even Barnabas, so Paul, seeing that their conduct denied the truth of the gospel, challenged Peter before them all.

Acted hypocritically. The damage spreads in a single verse. The word is synypokrinomai, to play the actor together, from the theatre. Not secret unbelief: they were acting, behaving in a way their convictions did not support, because the audience had changed.

Even Barnabas. The son of encouragement (Acts 4:36), who had stood up for Paul in Jerusalem, fetched him from Tarsus, and travelled the first missionary journey at his side (Acts 11:22–26; 13–14). If one man in Antioch could be counted on, it was Barnabas, and he was carried away too. No word of persuasion is recorded. A few significant people sat at a different table, and the whole church moved.

Not in step. The word pictures walking straight (orthos, straight, and pous, foot). Paul does not say their doctrine was wrong; every man at those tables would have signed the same confession. Their feet were wrong. The gospel is something to be walked in, and it can be denied by a seating plan as effectively as by a sermon.

I said to Cephas before them all. Public sin with public effect required public correction (1 Timothy 5:20). Peter had been living “like a Gentile”, not keeping the Jewish food laws, so he plainly did not believe they still bound him. Yet by withdrawing he was telling Gentile believers, in effect, “To have full fellowship with us, you must become Jews.” Pressure does not have to be spoken to be applied, and this pressure denied the gospel.

A table paid for in full. In Christ Jesus there is neither Jew nor Greek (3:28). His death had made the Gentile believer clean, and his Spirit had made him a son; to leave that man eating alone was to say, without a word, that Christ had not been quite enough to bring him in. The table at Antioch was always meant to be a picture of something bigger: the marriage supper of the Lamb, where people from every tribe and language and nation will sit down together, and no one will ask anyone else to become something first. The one who spreads that table paid for every seat, and he does not move anyone to a lower one.

What it does not mean. Not that Paul relished confronting Peter, nor that it ended the friendship. Years later Peter, writing his last letter, mentioned “our beloved brother Paul”, and the things in his letters that are hard to understand (2 Peter 3:15–16). Two men who both knew what it was to be forgiven could survive being told the truth.

What are the separate tables today? Rarely food laws. More often it is the church where the professionals sit together and the cleaners sit together, the congregation that welcomes newcomers who look like the existing members, the fellowship that is warm to the respectable and cool to the man who has come out of prison or the woman with a messy history. Wherever believers make others feel that full acceptance requires becoming like us, in culture, class or race, the Antioch problem is back. Whoever is in Christ belongs at the table, and the table is the Lord’s, not ours.

Should a Christian confront leaders publicly? Usually not, and Scripture is careful about it. For sin between brothers the Lord says go privately first, and widen the circle only if there is no repentance (Matthew 18:15–17). Paul tells Timothy to admit a charge against an elder only on the evidence of two or three witnesses, but adds: “As for those who persist in sin, rebuke them in the presence of all” (1 Timothy 5:19–20). Four things lined up here, and they rarely all do: the conduct was public, so a private word could not undo it; the matter was the gospel itself, not a preference or a personality; others were already being swept away; and Paul said it to Peter’s face, in the room, at cost to himself, not about him, afterwards, to somebody else. That last test is the one most often failed: much of what calls itself courage in the church is a message to a third party, or a post about a man who will never be in the room. Paul’s way is harder and kinder: he said it where Peter could answer.

What if I am the one who has been rebuked? Do what Peter evidently did: listen, and do not defend yourself first. Ask whether the rebuke is true, even if it was delivered badly. If it is, own it plainly before God and before those affected, without excuses, and change course. “Faithful are the wounds of a friend” (Proverbs 27:6). A believer who can receive correction is resting on Christ’s righteousness rather than his own, because he has nothing to protect.

Uncertain wording. “Not in step” translates a rare verb, orthopodeō, not found in any earlier Greek writing that survives. From its parts it means to walk straight or upright; some take it as to make straight progress towards a goal. Either way, their conduct did not line up with the gospel.
verseByVerse.note: Barnabas had been Paul’s partner on the first journey.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A person is right with God only through faith in Christ, and to add the law to him empties his death of meaning. Even Jews by birth are justified through faith in Christ, not by works of the law (vv. 15–16). That does not make Christ a promoter of sin; going back to the law as the way to God is what makes a person a transgressor (vv. 17–18). Through the law Paul died to the law so that he might live to God: crucified with Christ, he now lives by faith in the Son of God who loved him and gave himself for him (vv. 19–20). If righteousness came through the law, Christ died for no purpose (v. 21).
verseByVerse.theology:
The article by which the church stands or falls

Protestant theology came to call justification by faith the article by which the church stands or falls, a summary of Luther’s own conviction, and vv. 15–21 are the classic passage for it. Justification is a declaration of our standing before God, not goodness poured into us (see the note on vv. 15–16). It is by grace alone, through faith alone, in Christ alone, and these stand or fall together.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Jewish believers had every religious advantage and still came the same way as the Gentiles they were now refusing to eat with (v. 15). And verse 18 lands directly on Antioch, where stones were going back into the wall between Jew and Gentile that the gospel had pulled down.

Now: The person who comes to faith from a respectable life and the person who comes from obvious wreckage stand on the same ground, with the same righteousness, which is Christ’s. The respectability counts for as little in the verdict as the wreckage.

verseByVerse.quote: We ourselves are Jews by birth and not Gentile sinners; yet we know that a person is not justified by works of the law but through faith in Jesus Christ, so we also have believed in Christ Jesus, in order to be justified by faith in Christ and not by works of the law, because by works of the law no one will be justified.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Even Jews by birth, with every advantage, know that no one is put right with God by doing what the law requires, but only through faith in Jesus Christ, and so they too have believed in him. Paul says it three times in one verse, because everything else stands on it: every later argument in Galatians unfolds this verse, from Abraham (3:6) and the curse Christ bore (3:13) to sons not slaves (4:7) and the life of the Spirit (chapters 5 and 6).

Jews by birth. “Gentile sinners” was how Jews commonly spoke: Gentiles were counted sinners simply because they lived outside the law. Paul is echoing that way of speaking, not endorsing it. The most advantaged religious people on earth, with the covenant, the Scriptures, the temple and a lifetime of training, also had to believe in Christ Jesus; if the law could have justified anybody, it would have justified them. The irreligious man is not too far gone to come by faith, and the religious man is not too good to need to.

Not justified. Justified (dikaioō) is a courtroom word. To justify is not to make someone good but to declare someone in the right: acquitted, accepted, the opposite of condemned (Romans 8:33–34). A judge who justifies a defendant does not improve him; he pronounces a verdict, and the man walks out with a status he did not have when he walked in. Many people think of salvation in medical terms, God gradually curing us, with heaven at the end if the treatment works. Justification is the judge’s verdict, given whole, in a moment, at the beginning rather than the end. God does also heal the sinner he acquits, for a lifetime, but he does not acquit him because the healing is going well.

By works of the law. Deeds done in obedience to the law of Moses, especially the visible markers that separated Jew from Gentile: circumcision, the food rules, the holy days, the very issues at Antioch. But Paul’s conclusion is wider than the markers, and the last clause shows it.

But through faith in Jesus Christ. Faith is not a work that earns justification but the empty hand that receives Christ and his righteousness: not what we are justified for, but how we receive the one for whose sake we are justified. So it justifies not because it is strong but because he is, and a weak faith in a strong Saviour is as fully justified as a strong one.

No one will be justified. From Psalm 143:2: “Enter not into judgment with your servant, for no one living is righteous before you.” Not the Gentile without the law, nor the Pharisee who kept it better than his peers, for no one keeps it perfectly (3:10; Romans 3:20); even David begs not to be brought into court. The fault is not in the law, which is holy. The law is a mirror, and a mirror has never washed a face.

Righteous with another’s righteousness. God does not pretend we are good when we are not. He declares us righteous because the righteousness of Christ is counted to us (Romans 4:5–6; 2 Corinthians 5:21; Philippians 3:9): our sins were counted to him at the cross, and his obedience is counted to us. The Judge of all the earth has a verdict to give on every human life, and he has given it in advance for everyone who trusts his Son: righteous. Not because he was deceived about us, nor because he lowered his standard, but because his own Son met the standard in our place and bore the sentence we had earned (Romans 3:26). There is no higher court and no appeal against it, and the one who sits on the bench is our Father.

In everyday life. The verdict on you is not waiting on Friday’s performance (Romans 3:20–24). Begin each day by remembering it, and then obey from it, not towards it.

Do Paul and James contradict each other? James says a person is justified by works and not by faith alone (James 2:24). No. Paul asks how a guilty sinner is declared righteous before God: by faith, apart from works. James asks how a claim to faith is shown to be real: faith without works is dead (James 2:17). Paul opposes works as the ground of acceptance; James opposes a faith that is only words. Paul agrees that true faith works: faith working through love (5:6). We are justified by faith alone, but the faith that justifies is never alone.

If I am justified, why do I still feel guilty? Feelings lag behind facts, and you still sin, and a tender conscience notices. Real conviction of a specific sin is the Spirit’s kindness, calling you to confess it and be cleansed (1 John 1:9). But a general cloud of condemnation that hangs over you after you have confessed is not from God, because there is now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus (Romans 8:1). When that cloud comes, do not argue with it from your record; argue from his. The verdict was given at the cross, on the ground of what Christ did, and it does not move with your moods.

Where Christians differ: what are works of the law? Some scholars of the New Perspective on Paul, such as E. P. Sanders, James Dunn and N. T. Wright, argue that works of the law mean mainly the boundary markers that separated Jews from Gentiles, circumcision, food laws and the Sabbath, so that justification is mainly about who belongs to God’s people, not how a sinner is made right with God. This commentary’s view: works of the law certainly include those boundary markers, as the Antioch incident shows; the New Perspective is right about the occasion. But Paul’s argument goes deeper: no one is justified by the law because no one keeps the whole law (3:10–12; 5:3). Justification is God’s legal declaration that a sinner is righteous, on the ground of Christ’s righteousness, received by faith alone (Romans 4:4–8). It has consequences for who belongs together at the table, but it is first about how a guilty person can stand before a holy God (the Westminster Confession 11.1; the 1689 London Baptist Confession 11.1).

Where Christians differ: declared righteous or made righteous? The Roman Catholic Church teaches (Council of Trent, 1547) that justification is a process in which God pours grace into the soul and makes the person inwardly righteous; it grows through the sacraments and good works, can be lost by mortal sin, and is restored by penance. On that view a person is accepted by God as far as he has been made righteous. The Reformers taught that justification is God’s once-for-all legal verdict, received by faith alone, on the ground of Christ’s righteousness alone; sanctification, the lifelong work of making us holy, always follows it but is distinct from it. This commentary’s view: the Reformation view is right. Paul’s word is a law-court word: God justifies the ungodly (Romans 4:5), which cannot mean he finds them already godly. Justification is complete the moment a person believes (Romans 5:1; 8:1), so it cannot grow or be lost. Works matter greatly, but as the fruit of justification, not its ground (Ephesians 2:8–10; Westminster 11.1–2; 1689 11.1–2). If our acceptance depended on how far we had been made righteous, no one could ever be sure of it, and the cross would be only a beginning; but Christ died for no purpose if righteousness comes by anything we do (v. 21).

Where Christians differ: faith in Christ, or the faithfulness of Christ? The Greek phrase pistis Christou, used twice in this verse, can be read as faith in Christ (our trust in him) or as the faith or faithfulness of Christ (his own faithful obedience to the Father, even to the cross). Some recent scholars prefer the second. This commentary’s view: faith in Christ is the better reading. In this very verse Paul adds, “we also have believed in Christ Jesus,” which shows plainly that our believing is in view. Both truths are biblical: we are saved by Christ’s faithful obedience (Romans 5:19), and we receive it by trusting him. But here Paul’s point is that the way to receive righteousness is believing, not doing. Either way the doing is his; the receiving is ours.

Uncertain wording. Where do Paul’s words to Peter end? Greek has no quotation marks. The ESV closes the quotation at verse 14 but notes that some interpreters hold it runs on through verse 21. Verse 15 reads naturally as still spoken to a fellow Jew, yet by verse 21 Paul is plainly speaking to every reader. Most likely he gives the substance of what he said to Peter and lets it widen into a statement of the gospel for the Galatians.

parallels.desc: no one living is righteous before you

verseByVerse.quote: But if, in our endeavor to be justified in Christ, we too were found to be sinners, is Christ then a servant of sin? Certainly not!
verseByVerse.commentary:
If seeking to be justified in Christ leaves Jewish believers counted as sinners like the Gentiles, that does not make Christ a promoter of sin, and Paul throws the very idea out.

Found to be sinners. Jewish believers who came to Christ stopped keeping the food laws and started eating with Gentiles. By the law’s reckoning they became sinners in the process, sinners like the Gentiles (for another way of reading the phrase, see the end of this note).

Is Christ then a servant of sin? So, the objection has always run, Christ has taken law-keepers and made them law-breakers: does he actively promote sin by freeing people from the law?

Certainly not! May it never be (mē genoito): the phrase Paul reaches for when a suggestion is not to be weighed but thrown out of the room. Justification by faith leads to holiness, not licence (5:13–25). Grace does not leave a sinner where it found him and merely change his paperwork. It joins him to Christ, so that his old self dies and a new life begins. That is why Paul’s answer ends at a cross, “I have been crucified with Christ” (2:20), rather than at a code of conduct.

An insult to a friend. To call Christ a servant of sin is to slander the one who took the whole weight of sin into his own body and went into the dark under it. Paul reacts as anyone does when a friend who is not there to answer is slandered. Christ is not the servant of sin but its executioner. He came to destroy the works of the devil (1 John 3:8), and he did it by letting sin do its worst to him, and rising out from under it.

A strange compliment. Paul faced the same objection in Romans: “Are we to continue in sin that grace may abound?” (Romans 6:1). Only truly free grace provokes it. If a preacher has never once been accused of making grace too free, it is worth asking whether he has actually preached it.

In everyday life. When you notice yourself thinking, “It does not matter, I am forgiven anyway,” stop and look at who forgave you and what it cost him. Then ask him for strength to obey in the very thing you were about to excuse; his Spirit lives in you for exactly this (5:16).

Then why do Christians still sin, and does that make grace a failure? Sanctification, God’s work of making a justified person holy, is lifelong; the old desires are defeated but not yet removed, and the war goes on until we see Christ (5:17; 1 John 3:2). That is not grace failing but grace still at work. The difference between a Christian and an unbeliever is not that one sins and the other does not, but that the Christian has a new master, hates his sin, fights it, confesses it, and is slowly changed. If you are using grace as an excuse to keep a sin you love, do not comfort yourself with this verse; it says “Certainly not!” If you are grieving your sin and running to Christ with it, grace has not failed you. It has hold of you.

Uncertain wording. Paul’s compressed “we too were found to be sinners” can be read in two main ways. It may mean that, by setting aside the food laws and eating with Gentiles, Jewish believers were reckoned sinners by the law’s standard (the reading followed above). Or it may mean that, in seeking justification in Christ, they were shown to be sinners as much as any Gentile, needing the same Saviour (compare v. 15). Either way, Christ is not the cause of sin.

verseByVerse.quote: For if I rebuild what I tore down, I prove myself to be a transgressor. For through the law I died to the law, so that I might live to God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The real transgression is not leaving the law behind as the way to God but going back to it, for through the law Paul died to the law, so that he might live to God.

If I rebuild what I tore down. A man who pulls down a building he has judged unsound and then puts every stone back declares publicly that he was wrong to pull it down. What Paul tore down was the whole structure of acceptance by performance: the life of chapter 1, advancing beyond his peers, building a righteousness of his own. So grace does not make sinners; going back does. And it applies directly to Antioch, where Peter had been living in the freedom of the gospel and had begun laying stones back in place, one meal at a time.

Through the law I died to the law. Not by escaping it: the law itself was the instrument of his death to the law. It is one of Paul’s most compressed sentences, so take it in steps. First, the law demands perfect obedience and pronounces death on every transgressor (3:10). Second, Paul was a transgressor, so the law’s sentence on him was death. Third, Christ took that sentence for him: born under the law (4:4), he died under its curse in his people’s place (3:13). Fourth, Paul was united to Christ by faith, so when Christ died, Paul died with him (v. 20). So the law did carry out its sentence on Paul: in Christ, he died. And a dead man is free from the law’s claim; the law has nothing more to say to someone whose sentence has been fully carried out (Romans 7:1–4, where Paul uses the picture of a marriage ended by death).

How the law kills. There is a second strand too: the law, by exposing his sin, drove him to stop trusting it and to flee to Christ (3:24; Romans 7:9–10). It came to a man doing rather well and kept pressing until it had him. Paul tells us which commandment found him out: you shall not covet, a law about the desire and not only the deed (Romans 7:7–11). Jesus read the whole law the same way: not just murder, but anger (Matthew 5:21–28). So the law did what God gave it to do: it ended his hope in himself. Nobody comes to Christ while he still thinks he can pay his own way, and the ache under religious striving, the sense that it is never enough and the standard keeps moving, is not a malfunction. It is the law doing its work, like a guardian whose last kindness is to hand the child over to Christ (3:24).

So that I might live to God. The demolition was not meant to leave a man in the rubble, but to get him out from under a life spent proving himself and into a life lived towards God. The law could not make him live for God; Christ does. God did not cancel the law’s sentence; he carried it out on his Son and counted us as having died in him. Christ honoured every demand of the law, in his life and in his death, so that sinners could be set free from it without the law being dishonoured at all.

What living to God looks like. To live to God is to have God himself, not your record, as the one you live towards: his pleasure your aim, his presence your home, his glory your end. Under the law even religion kept the self at the centre, every prayer and good deed an entry in your own account. In Christ the account is closed, settled by his death, and you are free at last to look at God instead of yourself. In an ordinary week, you pray as a child speaks to a father, not as a tenant paying rent. You obey because you love him and want what he wants, not to stop him turning away. You confess sin quickly, because a failure can no longer overturn your standing. You can bear criticism without collapsing, because the verdict that matters is not theirs to give. And you begin to enjoy him, not only to serve him. The power for all of it is the next verse: Christ lives in you (v. 20).

What it does not mean. Not lawlessness. Paul died to the law as a way of being right with God and as a master that condemns him, not to God’s will. He is now under the law of Christ (1 Corinthians 9:21), and the Spirit leads him to fulfil the law’s righteous requirement in love (5:14; Romans 8:4).

In everyday life. Notice the stones you keep laying back in place: the private rules by which you measure whether God is pleased with you this week. Put them down, and live towards God today, gladly, as a man let out of prison lives towards the friend who paid his fine.

Do Christians still need to keep the Ten Commandments? Not as a way of being accepted by God, and not under the law’s curse. But the moral will they express has not changed, because it flows from God’s own character. Jesus deepened the commandments rather than abolishing them (Matthew 5:17–48), and the apostles repeat their substance to Christians (Romans 13:8–10; Ephesians 6:1–3): the shape of a life of love, the path the Father marks out for children who are already his. Christians differ on how the fourth commandment applies today, and on how much of the old covenant law carries over; but no Christian is free to steal, lie, covet or commit adultery. The ceremonial laws that pointed to Christ, such as circumcision and the food laws, are fulfilled in him and no longer bind.

verseByVerse.quote: I have been crucified with Christ. It is no longer I who live, but Christ who lives in me. And the life I now live in the flesh I live by faith in the Son of God, who loved me and gave himself for me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Joined to Christ, Paul died with him, and now Christ lives in him, so that his ordinary daily life is lived by trusting the Son of God who loved him and gave himself for him.

I have been crucified with Christ. The summit of the letter begins with a funeral. The tense describes a past act whose results still stand: not a thing Paul tries to do, but a thing that has happened. When Christ died, Paul died, because Christ died as his people’s representative, as Adam acted for the whole race, so that what happened to him happened to everyone joined to him. His old self, under the law’s condemnation, died (Romans 6:6). And he says not died but crucified, what was done to a criminal in public. The old self, with the record and the rising reputation in Judaism, did not retire honourably. It was executed.

Christ who lives in me. Paul has not been erased, personality and all. The next clause says “the life I now live”, so there is still an I doing the living, and the man who wrote this letter is unmistakably himself on every page, angry, tender and affectionate by turns. Grace killed what he was living for and left him more himself than before. What died was the self that had to be somebody. Christ now lives in Paul by his Spirit (Romans 8:9–10; Colossians 1:27), turning his will towards God and growing in him love, joy, peace and patience (5:22–23). This is real power: the Spirit who raised Jesus from the dead dwells in him (Romans 8:11).

In the flesh. Here “the flesh” means ordinary bodily, earthly life, not the sinful nature of 5:16–24: a stomach, a temper and a tentmaking business. This is Monday he is describing.

By faith in the Son of God. Faith is not only the door into the Christian life but the way of living it: not a sensation of Christ’s presence, but trusting a person he cannot see, on days when nothing is felt at all. That Christ lives in the believer is a fact about where Christ is, not a report on how the believer feels.

Who loved me and gave himself for me. Then Paul’s grammar goes suddenly singular. A chapter of councils, delegations and mission fields ends with one man saying “me” twice. The cross is wide enough for the world and narrow enough to have a single name written on it, and this is the same Paul who had been dragging women out of houses to prison (Acts 8:3). Luther urged his readers to read the words “me” and “for me” with great vehemence, and to take them as spoken of themselves.

He did not send help. The Son of God loved this particular man, with this particular record, while that record was still being written. And he did not send help; he gave himself, the only gift that costs the giver everything. He had the Father’s glory and set it down. He had legions and did not call them. He went to a public execution for people who were his enemies at the time, and he would not be talked out of it (Ephesians 5:2; 1 John 3:16). Eternity will not be long enough to get to the end of a love like that.

What “crucified with Christ” does not mean. It is not a special experience that advanced Christians reach, nor a feeling to be worked up, nor a command (“crucify yourself!”). It is true of every believer by union with Christ (Romans 6:3–6). It does not mean Paul no longer struggles with sin (5:17). It means Christ has replaced self as the centre, the source of his life, and the object of his trust.

How do I live by faith on an ordinary day? By turning, again and again, from yourself to Christ. In the morning, before the list, remember who you are in him: crucified, raised and loved. When temptation comes, say no on the strength of the fact that the old self who loved that sin was put to death. When you fail, go straight back to the one who loved you and gave himself for you, without waiting to feel better first. When you have to do something hard, ask him for the strength, and expect him to give it, because he lives in you. None of this needs a feeling. It needs only the habit of looking at him.

Why would the God of the galaxies notice me? We feel this more than Paul’s first readers could, because we know the scale. Carl Sagan, looking at a photograph of the earth taken from the edge of the solar system, called our planet “a mote of dust suspended in a sunbeam”. On that scale a single human life can look like a rounding error, and the claim that its Maker loves me personally can sound like vanity. But that assumes worth is measured by size, and nobody lives as if it were: no one values a child less than a mountain. The psalmist felt the same vertigo under the night sky: “what is man that you are mindful of him, and the son of man that you care for him?” (Psalm 8:4). Paul gives the answer the psalmist could only wait for. The God who made the galaxies did not show his greatness by being too large to notice us. He showed it by becoming small: a body, a name, a cross outside one city on one small planet. And there, Paul says, he was thinking of me.

Can I say “for me” if I am not sure I am chosen? Yes. You do not need to look into God’s secret decree before you come to Christ; no one can. The gospel invites every sinner to trust Christ, and promises that whoever comes to him will never be cast out (John 6:37). Reformed Christians believe in definite or particular atonement: that Christ died for his people in particular, and that the cross was aimed at saving them and actually accomplished it (John 10:11, 15; Ephesians 5:25). But you discover that you are one of them not by peering into heaven but by coming to him. Many faithful Christians believe instead that Christ died for all in the same way; both gladly offer him to everyone, and neither asks you to settle the question before you come. If you trust Christ, you may say without presumption that the Son of God loved me and gave himself for me. Paul’s “me” is the word of every believer.

verseByVerse.quote: I do not nullify the grace of God, for if righteousness were through the law, then Christ died for no purpose.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul will not set aside God’s grace, because if anyone could be made right with God by keeping the law, Christ’s death would have been pointless.

I do not nullify the grace of God. “Nullify” (atheteō) means to set aside or cancel: the term for treating a legal instrument as void. Paul is probably throwing a charge back: accused of treating God’s law as nothing, he answers that it is his accusers who are annulling something, and it is grace. The verse closes the defence that began in 1:11. Chapter 2 ends at the cross and chapter 3 begins there (3:1), because the cross is the one thing a gospel of law-keeping has no real need of.

If righteousness were through the law. Suppose any route to being right with God runs through human obedience, even a small one, even as a supplement to grace. Then God had a way of saving people that did not require the death of his Son, and Calvary was not a rescue but an appalling waste: a Father watching his Son die in the dark for something that could have been managed another way.

For no purpose. For nothing, in vain (dōrean): the same word Paul uses elsewhere for freely, as a gift (Romans 3:24), and the play is bitter. Either righteousness is given freely, or Christ died freely, for nothing.

Why Paul’s anger is not excessive. The Judaizers thought they were adding a little rigour to a message that had gone soft. But you cannot say Christ plus my performance without saying, underneath it, that his performance was insufficient, and the cross does not survive being called a supplement. Every addition to grace is an insult to the cross.

Had there been another way. Had there been another way, the Son of God would have taken it; he asked in the garden, three times, and his sweat became like great drops of blood falling down to the ground (Matthew 26:39–44; Luke 22:44, a verse missing from some early manuscripts). There was not. He did not die for no purpose. He died for sinners, and it is finished, and there is nothing to add to it (Hebrews 10:11–14).

What if I keep feeling I must earn God’s favour? Most Christians do. Treat the feeling as a temptation, not a revelation. When it comes, answer it with this verse: if I could earn it, Christ died for nothing, and he did not die for nothing. Thank God out loud for what Christ has already done. Then go and obey, not to earn, but because you are loved; and when the obedience goes badly, do not let that reopen the question. The question was closed at the cross.

Does this mean sincere, good people of other religions are lost? Paul’s logic answers it. If righteousness could come through the law of Moses, given by God himself, then Christ died for nothing; how much more if it could come through any other path. The cross was necessary because there is no other way to God, and so salvation is through conscious faith in Christ alone (John 14:6; Acts 4:12). That is not arrogance; we are saved the same way, as beggars. Some Christians hope that God may save people through Christ without their ever knowing his name; Scripture gives no such promise to rest on, which is why the church sends missionaries, and every soul is safe in the hands of a Judge who will do what is right (Genesis 18:25). It is a reason for urgency and compassion. The people you love who trust in their own goodness need to hear about the one who died because their goodness could never be enough.

2.text: <sup>1</sup>Then after fourteen years I went up again to Jerusalem with Barnabas, taking Titus along with me.<sup>2</sup>I went up because of a revelation and set before them (though privately before those who seemed influential) the gospel that I proclaim among the Gentiles, in order to make sure I was not running or had not run in vain.<sup>3</sup>But even Titus, who was with me, was not forced to be circumcised, though he was a Greek.<sup>4</sup>Yet because of false brothers secretly brought in—who slipped in to spy out our freedom that we have in Christ Jesus, so that they might bring us into slavery—<sup>5</sup>to them we did not yield in submission even for a moment, so that the truth of the gospel might be preserved for you.<sup>6</sup>And from those who seemed to be influential (what they were makes no difference to me; God shows no partiality)—those, I say, who seemed influential added nothing to me.<sup>7</sup>On the contrary, when they saw that I had been entrusted with the gospel to the uncircumcised, just as Peter had been entrusted with the gospel to the circumcised<sup>8</sup>(for he who worked through Peter for his apostolic ministry to the circumcised worked also through me for mine to the Gentiles),<sup>9</sup>and when James and Cephas and John, who seemed to be pillars, perceived the grace that was given to me, they gave the right hand of fellowship to Barnabas and me, that we should go to the Gentiles and they to the circumcised.<sup>10</sup>Only, they asked us to remember the poor, the very thing I was eager to do.<sup>11</sup>But when Cephas came to Antioch, I opposed him to his face, because he stood condemned.<sup>12</sup>For before certain men came from James, he was eating with the Gentiles; but when they came he drew back and separated himself, fearing the circumcision party.<sup>13</sup>And the rest of the Jews acted hypocritically along with him, so that even Barnabas was led astray by their hypocrisy.<sup>14</sup>But when I saw that their conduct was not in step with the truth of the gospel, I said to Cephas before them all, “If you, though a Jew, live like a Gentile and not like a Jew, how can you force the Gentiles to live like Jews?”<sup>15</sup>We ourselves are Jews by birth and not Gentile sinners;<sup>16</sup>yet we know that a person is not justified by works of the law but through faith in Jesus Christ, so we also have believed in Christ Jesus, in order to be justified by faith in Christ and not by works of the law, because by works of the law no one will be justified.<sup>17</sup>But if, in our endeavor to be justified in Christ, we too were found to be sinners, is Christ then a servant of sin? Certainly not!<sup>18</sup>For if I rebuild what I tore down, I prove myself to be a transgressor.<sup>19</sup>For through the law I died to the law, so that I might live to God.<sup>20</sup>I have been crucified with Christ. It is no longer I who live, but Christ who lives in me. And the life I now live in the flesh I live by faith in the Son of God, who loved me and gave himself for me.<sup>21</sup>I do not nullify the grace of God, for if righteousness were through the law, then Christ died for no purpose.

keyVerse.quote: yet we know that a person is not justified by works of the law but through faith in Jesus Christ, so we also have believed in Christ Jesus, in order to be justified by faith in Christ and not by works of the law, because by works of the law no one will be justified.
keyVerse.note: This is the truth the whole chapter defends: it is why Titus was not circumcised and why Paul opposed Peter at Antioch, and the rest of the letter unfolds it. Paul says it three times in one verse so that no one can miss it. The way to be right with God is not doing but believing, and what faith receives is Christ himself.

2.reflection:
Paul took the uncircumcised Titus to Jerusalem and would not let circumcision be added as a requirement (vv. 3–5). What things, good in themselves, are Christians tempted to make necessary for full acceptance today? How can you tell when something has moved from free to necessary?

Peter knew the truth, but changed his seat when the wrong people walked in, and others followed him (vv. 11–13). Where does fear of what others think most shape what you do? Who might a church like ours quietly leave at a separate table?

Paul says a person is justified through faith in Christ, not by works of the law (v. 16). How would you explain the difference between being declared righteous and being made righteous, and why does it matter on a day when you have failed badly?

“I have been crucified with Christ… who loved me and gave himself for me” (v. 20). What difference does it make to read that “me” as spoken of yourself? What would living by faith in the Son of God look like in your ordinary week?

3.title: The Promise and the Law: Abraham, Faith, and the Curse
3.overview:
Where we are. Paul has told his own story in chapters 1–2 and ended on its centre: a person is justified through faith in Christ, for “if righteousness were through the law, then Christ died for no purpose” (2:21). Chapter 3 is the heart of the argument of chapters 3–4, which proves that truth from the Galatians’ own experience and from Scripture.

The message. God has always put people right with himself, and given them his Spirit, through faith in his promise, never through keeping the law; and that promise has one heir, Christ. So everyone who belongs to Christ, Jew or Gentile, slave or free, man or woman, is a full son of God and heir of all that God swore to Abraham. To add the law as a condition is not to complete the promise but to cancel it.

Why it was said. The teachers troubling Galatia (see the introduction) appealed to Abraham, who was circumcised, and to Moses, whose law came from God. Surely, they said, Gentile believers must take on the law to belong fully to Abraham’s family. Paul answers both appeals from the very Scriptures his opponents were using.

How the chapter makes its case. He begins with what happened to the Galatians: they received the Spirit by hearing with faith, not by works of the law, and God is still at work among them on those terms (vv. 1–5). Abraham was counted righteous the same way, so believers are his sons, blessed along with him (vv. 6–9). The law, by contrast, curses all who rely on it, because no one keeps all of it; but Christ redeemed us from that curse by becoming a curse for us (vv. 10–14). The promise was ratified centuries before the law came, and a later law cannot amend it (vv. 15–18). Why then the law? To expose sin, and for a time, as a guardian keeping God’s people until Christ came (vv. 19–25). Now all who believe are sons of God, clothed with Christ, one in him and heirs (vv. 26–29).

Where it leads. Everything in the chapter meets in Christ. He is the one offspring to whom the promise was made (v. 16), the one man who did all that the law required, and the one who hung on the tree under the curse that was ours (v. 13). The blessing God promised a childless man under the stars reaches the nations because God’s own Son took the curse and handed us the blessing.

For us. Few of us are tempted by circumcision, but all of us drift towards finishing by our own effort what the Spirit began, and standing on our record instead of Christ’s. This chapter calls us back to the empty hands with which we began, and tells every believer, however weak, that nothing is missing: in Christ you are a son, and an heir.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Faith, not law, is how God gives his Spirit and his righteousness, as both the Galatians’ own experience and Abraham’s story show. Paul asks what happened when they first believed: Christ crucified had been set before their eyes (v. 1), and they received the Spirit by hearing with faith, not by works of the law (v. 2), so to try to finish by the flesh is folly (vv. 3–4). God still works among them on the same terms, just as Abraham believed and was counted righteous (vv. 5–6). So those of faith are Abraham’s sons, and the gospel announced to him in advance blesses believing Gentiles along with him (vv. 7–9).
verseByVerse.theology:
The Spirit Is Received by Faith

Paul’s appeal in vv. 2 and 5 is not to religious feeling but to a fact: how God gave them his Spirit. The Spirit unites us to Christ, and that union is received by faith alone; here Paul argues it from their own experience. If the Spirit came through hearing the gospel and not through works of the law, then law-keeping was never the channel, and no later addition can make it one.

Verse 3 shows that the Christian life does not have two stages, beginning by grace and advancing by performance. The same Spirit, received in the same way, is at work from first to last. And vv. 6–9 show that this is not new: justification by faith is how God has always dealt with sinners (on Abraham, counted righteous before he was circumcised, see the note on vv. 5–6).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The Judaizers were not asking the Galatians to abandon Christ. They were offering completion: take the mark, keep the calendar, and become full sons of Abraham. Paul makes them look at their own conversion, when they had nothing in their hands and God gave them his Spirit, and then he takes Abraham, the Judaizers’ own best example, and shows that he too was justified by faith.

Now: Few believers decide to be justified by works; the drift of v. 3 is quieter (see the note on vv. 3–4). The cure is in vv. 6–9: there is one way in, by faith in God’s promise, and the newest believer stands in it beside Abraham himself.

verseByVerse.quote: O foolish Galatians! Who has bewitched you? It was before your eyes that Jesus Christ was publicly portrayed as crucified.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Galatians had seen Christ crucified set before them as plainly as a public notice, and they have let something charm their eyes away from him. Paul’s rebuke is the shock of love at people who have stopped thinking about what they already know.

O foolish Galatians! The letter has already left out the usual thanksgiving; now it drops the courtesy altogether. Anoētoi means not stupid but without understanding: people with perfectly good minds who have stopped using them on the one subject where everything is at stake.

Who has bewitched you? The word (baskainō) belongs to the world of the evil eye, the malign look thought to wither a crop or sicken a child, an idea Paul’s readers in superstitious Galatia knew well. Paul does not believe in the evil eye or say that a spell was cast. He uses the only picture that fits: they have not been out-reasoned but charmed. Something has looked at them and done them harm, yet what was set before their eyes was Jesus Christ crucified: two sights competing for one congregation, and whichever you keep looking at will shape you.

Publicly portrayed as crucified. Posted up, placarded (prographō): written large in a public place, like a governor’s ruling in the marketplace. That is Paul’s picture of his own preaching. He had not offered them a religious option but put up a public notice, and it said: the Son of God was executed, and it was for you. None of them had been at Golgotha, nor had Paul, but preaching that does its work sets the cross before people until a listener in a Galatian market town could shut his eyes and see a man on a Roman beam dying in his place. The word “crucified” picks up 2:21: if righteousness came through the law, Christ died for nothing, and these people had seen him die.

The placard was his own Son. God did not leave the Galatians to guess what he is like: the notice in their town was his own Son, dying for enemies. Every spell that dazzles us away from it is a cheap light beside a crucified Lord, and the God who painted that picture before our eyes is still the one who opens them to see it.

How do I keep Christ crucified before my eyes? Put yourself, deliberately and often, where the cross is set before you. Sit under preaching full of Christ and his cross, not only of advice. Come to the Lord’s Supper as the moment the Lord himself places his death in front of you (1 Corinthians 11:26). Read the Gospel accounts of the crucifixion slowly, more than once a year, and sing hymns that dwell on it. When your conscience accuses you, answer it by looking there first, not at your week. The cross never changes; it fades from view only because we stop looking.

Textual note. Some later manuscripts, followed by the King James Version, add “that ye should not obey the truth” after “bewitched you”, and “among you” after “crucified”. The earliest manuscripts lack both, and modern translations leave them out. The meaning is unchanged.
verseByVerse.note: “Bewitched” pictures someone under a spell or the evil eye. “Publicly portrayed” uses the word for a public notice posted for all to read.

verseByVerse.quote: Let me ask you only this: Did you receive the Spirit by works of the law or by hearing with faith?
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Galatians’ own experience settles the matter: God gave them his Spirit when they heard the gospel and believed it, not when they kept the law. And anyone who has the Spirit already belongs to God.

Let me ask you only this. Paul has a whole letter of arguments ready, but first he asks one question, which, answered honestly, brings down the programme of the Judaizers, the teachers who insisted that Gentile believers be circumcised and keep the law of Moses.

Did you receive the Spirit by works of the law or by hearing with faith? The question is about their biography, not their theology. What they believe now is exactly what is in dispute, renegotiated weekly by men with impressive credentials. What happened to them then is a matter of record, and every one of them was there. And the Spirit is the decisive mark of belonging to God: “Anyone who does not have the Spirit of Christ does not belong to him” (Romans 8:9). If they have the Spirit, they already belong.

What had happened. A travel-worn stranger had announced a crucified and risen Jew as Lord of the world. Some believed, and God gave them himself: sins forgiven, a new hunger for God, love for people they had despised, and in some cases open displays of his power. Most were uncircumcised pagans who had never kept a Sabbath. When God gave them his greatest gift, what was in their hands? Nothing. That is what God is like: he gives the best first, and he gives it to the empty-handed.

A gift poured out by the risen Son. Why should hearing be enough? Because the Spirit was not a reward for listening well but the gift Christ had won. Christ became a curse for us so that we might receive the promised Spirit through faith (vv. 13–14), and the exalted Jesus received from the Father the promised Holy Spirit and poured him out (Acts 2:33). When the Galatians believed, the crucified and risen Lord was sharing with the empty-handed what he had bought with his own blood.

What it does not mean. Not that the Spirit is received in a second experience after faith. They received him when they believed. There is no Christian without the Spirit, and no later stage at which a believer is given him for the first time.

How do I know I have received the Spirit? Not mainly by an unusual experience, though God may give one, but by what he does. He makes you trust Christ and call God Father (4:6; Romans 8:15–16). He makes Christ precious and the Bible alive to you, gives you a new hatred of your sin and a desire to please God, grows love, joy, peace and the rest of his fruit, slowly and often unnoticed (5:22–23), and draws you to other believers. If you believe in Jesus and want to follow him, however weakly, the Spirit is already at work in you, for no one can say Jesus is Lord except by the Holy Spirit (1 Corinthians 12:3).

Uncertain wording. “Hearing with faith” (akoē pisteōs) is a compressed phrase. It can mean a hearing that believes, or the message heard that produces faith (compare Romans 10:17). Paul may well intend both: a message announced, and a heart that stops arguing and takes it. Either way the contrast with “works of the law” stands: receiving, not achieving.

verseByVerse.quote: Are you so foolish? Having begun by the Spirit, are you now being perfected by the flesh? Did you suffer so many things in vain—if indeed it was in vain?
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Christian life is finished the way it began, by the Spirit received through faith; to try to complete it by human effort and religious marks is folly.

Begun and perfected. Paul asks a second time, “Are you so foolish?”, and now names the folly in the sentence of this letter that ordinary Christians perhaps most need to hear. Begun (enarxamenoi) and perfected (epiteleō, to complete) are a matched pair that could be used of a sacrifice, begun and then brought to completion. Nobody in Galatia proposed to abandon the Spirit; the false teachers said that faith is the start, but circumcision and law-keeping complete you. Paul answers: you began with the Spirit of God himself at work in you, and you now propose to finish with a knife and a calendar.

What “flesh” means here. Not first lust or temper. Circumcision is a cut in literal flesh; the whole programme of the Judaizers lands on the body. So “the flesh” here is what a human being can do, mark, keep and show by his own effort: religious achievement that is visible, measurable, and yours.

Did you suffer so many things in vain? The verb paschō can mean suffer or simply experience. These people had paid for their faith. If these churches included the towns of Acts 13–14, as this commentary holds (see the introduction), they had watched Paul stoned at Lystra and dragged out of the city for dead, taken their own share of it, and been told that “through many tribulations we must enter the kingdom of God” (Acts 14:19–22). Or Paul may mean the many blessings they had experienced. Either way, was all of it for nothing?

If indeed it was in vain. And then he cannot finish the sentence. The fierce debater breaks off and will not pronounce them lost. He raises the possibility so that they feel the danger, then refuses to say it has happened. He is furious with them and cannot bear to lose them, and the two belong together (2 Corinthians 2:4; Galatians 4:19).

Perfected by a single offering. The Galatians were being offered completion. But “by a single offering he has perfected for all time those who are being sanctified” (Hebrews 10:14). The finishing the false teachers were selling had already been done on a cross, and the Spirit’s work is to make us, day by day, more like the one in whom we are already complete (Colossians 2:10). We did not begin ourselves, and we will not finish ourselves, and that is not our humiliation. It is our rest.

How it happens to us. This verse finds the reader who is doing nothing obviously wrong. Almost no Christian decides to be justified by works. You come to Christ with empty hands; then, over a few years, the hands slowly fill: a devotional habit, a serving rota, a reputation for reliability. None of it is bad; all of it may be the Spirit’s own fruit. But somewhere the ground of your confidence migrates from the finished work of Christ to the evidence of your progress, and you never notice the day it moved. Test it with your worst week, when you prayed nothing and snapped at everyone. Was God as pleased with you in Christ that Sunday as on your best? The gospel says yes, because on both Sundays you stood in Christ, not in your week. If something in you flinches, the way back is the way you began: empty hands, and Christ.

Then what do I actually do to grow? Christians do make effort; Paul worked harder than anyone, yet said it was not he, but the grace of God that was with him (1 Corinthians 15:10). So use the means God has given, as a needy child, not as a contractor. Read and hear his word, through which the Spirit grows faith. Pray, confessing that you cannot do it alone. Come to the Lord’s Supper and the fellowship of the church. Obey in the thing in front of you, asking for strength as you do it. Put sin to death by the Spirit (Romans 8:13): name it, flee it, cut off what feeds it. The difference between Spirit and flesh is not whether you make an effort, but what you lean on while you make it, and who gets the credit when it works.

Where Christians differ: sanctification by effort? Justification is the Judge’s verdict, given once and never revised; sanctification is the slow, real change by which the Spirit makes the justified person holy in practice. Some think that justification is by faith but sanctification by our own effort and rule-keeping. This commentary’s view: sanctification, like justification, is a work of the Spirit received by faith. It involves real effort and obedience (Philippians 2:12–13), but effort that depends on the Spirit, not on the flesh. Christians grow not by adding laws but by walking in the Spirit (5:16, 25).

verseByVerse.quote: Does he who supplies the Spirit to you and works miracles among you do so by works of the law, or by hearing with faith— just as Abraham “believed God, and it was counted to him as righteousness”?
verseByVerse.commentary:
God is still giving the Spirit and working miracles among them for the same reason he counted Abraham righteous: they believed, not that they kept the law. The sentence runs straight on to make Abraham the answer to Paul’s question.

He who supplies the Spirit. The last question moves from their past into their present: epichorēgōn means going on supplying, and “works miracles among you” is present too (Acts 14:3, 8–10).
