Whatever was being said about their deficient standing, the evidence was in the room while the argument went on. The verb began in the theatre: the chorēgos was the wealthy citizen who paid, at his own expense, for a chorus at the civic festival. By Paul’s day it meant to supply generously, and the picture still suits: God is not paying wages but underwriting the whole thing, because he chose to.

Just as Abraham believed God. The quotation is Genesis 15:6, and Paul chose his ground with care. The false teachers appealed to Abraham, who was circumcised (Genesis 17). Paul appeals to him too: before he was circumcised, he was counted righteous by faith (Romans 4:9–11). Galatia and Abraham are the same transaction: God spoke, a man believed him, and God credited it to him as righteousness.

Counted. A bookkeeping term (logizomai): to credit, to post an entry to an account. A childless old man under a sky full of stars took God at his word, and God wrote “righteous” in the ledger against his name: in full, that night, before circumcision, and long before he offered Isaac on Moriah. Theologians call this imputation.

Written for us also. The words “it was counted to him” were written for our sake also, who believe in him who raised Jesus from the dead (Romans 4:23–25). And the entry is no fiction. God can write righteous against a sinner’s name without falsifying the books because the debt was posted to Christ: for our sake God made him to be sin who knew no sin, so that in him we might become the righteousness of God (2 Corinthians 5:21).

What it does not mean. Not that Abraham’s faith was so admirable that God accepted it in place of the righteousness he lacked; that would put the ground of acceptance back inside the man. Faith is the empty hand that receives a righteousness belonging to another (Romans 4:3–5; Philippians 3:9).

Do Paul and James disagree about Abraham? James quotes the same verse and says Abraham was justified by works when he offered up Isaac (James 2:21–23). Genesis 15 gives the verdict; Genesis 22, many years later, shows the faith was real. James speaks of faith shown to be real, Paul of faith counted before God. The faith that received God’s verdict under the stars was the same faith that climbed Moriah.

Is my faith strong enough to be counted? It is not the strength of your faith that saves you, but the strength of the one you trust. Abraham’s faith was real but not flawless: between Genesis 15 and 22 he lied about his wife and tried to force the promise through Hagar. A drowning man who grabs a rope with a trembling hand is pulled out as surely as one with a firm grip: the rope does the saving. If you are trusting Christ, even with doubts and fears, God counts his righteousness to you in full. Ask him to strengthen your faith, like the father who said, “I believe; help my unbelief” (Mark 9:24).

Where Christians differ: do miracles continue? They were the signs that accompanied the first preaching of the gospel in Galatia; at Iconium, Luke says, the Lord bore witness to the word of his grace, granting signs and wonders to be done by their hands (Acts 14:3). Paul’s point is not that miracles are normal, but that God gave the Spirit and his powers to people who believed, not to people who kept the law. Continuationists, who believe all the gifts of the apostolic age continue today, take the present tense here as evidence that such works go on in every church, and many of them are careful, faithful readers of Scripture. This commentary’s view: the more likely reading is that these signs belonged to the apostolic founding of the churches, the signs of a true apostle (2 Corinthians 12:12; Hebrews 2:3–4), and have ceased in that form; the Spirit himself, received by faith, remains, and God still answers prayer, heals and acts in his providence as he pleases. Brothers who see it differently are to be loved as brothers.

parallels.desc: he believed the LORD, and he counted it to him as righteousness

verseByVerse.quote: Know then that it is those of faith who are the sons of Abraham. And the Scripture, foreseeing that God would justify the Gentiles by faith, preached the gospel beforehand to Abraham, saying, “In you shall all the nations be blessed.” So then, those who are of faith are blessed along with Abraham, the man of faith.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Abraham’s true children are those who believe as he did, and God planned from the start to bless the Gentiles through him by faith. So a believing Gentile shares Abraham’s blessing on the same footing as Abraham himself.

Those of faith are the sons of Abraham. In a first-century synagogue this was a bombshell: to be a son of Abraham was a legal identity, traced by blood and marked in the body, and a Gentile could enter only by becoming, in effect, a Jew. That was the Judaizers’ offer, and from the inside it looked generous. Paul cuts the ground from under it: Abraham’s true children are those who share his faith (Romans 4:11–12, 16). Jesus said the same to men who boasted of their descent: “If you were Abraham’s children, you would be doing the works Abraham did” (John 8:39). Descent alone never made a man Abraham’s son, or Ishmael and Esau would have been in.

The Scripture, foreseeing. Scripture foresaw and Scripture preached: what Scripture says, God says. God planned from the start to justify Gentiles who simply believed him, on the ground of what his Son would do (Romans 3:24–26). Whoever opens his Bible is not reading about a God who once spoke, but being spoken to.

Preached the gospel beforehand to Abraham. One Greek word (proeuangelizomai): to announce the gospel in advance. When God told a childless man from Mesopotamia, “in you all the families of the earth shall be blessed” (Genesis 12:3; 18:18), the gospel Paul preaches was already being announced, in its earliest form. The gospel is the fulfilment of God’s oldest promise. So the Judaizers had the story inside out. They treated Gentile inclusion as a late concession, granted only on Jewish terms; it was the point from the beginning, for the family existed so that the blessing could reach everyone else.

The blessing has a name. How would a blessing reach every family on earth through one old man from Ur? Through his offspring. Peter quoted the same promise in the temple and told his hearers what it meant: “God, having raised up his servant, sent him to you first, to bless you by turning every one of you from your wickedness” (Acts 3:25–26). The blessing of Abraham is Jesus, crucified and raised, turning sinners back to God.

Blessed along with Abraham. Not after him, at a lower grade. An Anatolian farmer who believed a travelling preacher stands in the same blessing as the patriarch. Abraham has been a believer for four thousand years and is blessed by faith. You believed last March and are blessed by faith. There is one queue, and everybody in it got in the same way. At its head stands the God who looked at a childless man under the stars and already saw the farmers of Galatia and the city-dwellers of every continent, and promised to bless them all through one Seed. He has kept that promise ever since, one believer at a time, and will not stop until every nation has come in.

Has the church then replaced Israel? Not in the usual sense. Paul does not say the Jewish people have no future, but that Abraham’s true family has always been defined by faith, not blood. Gentiles who believe are added to that family; Jews who believe are its natural members; and unbelieving Jews can be grafted back in (Romans 11:23). The family was never replaced. It was enlarged to its intended size.

Do Jewish people today need to believe in Jesus? Yes, and to say so is not hostility but love. Paul, a Jew, grieved over his own people and prayed that they would be saved (Romans 9:1–3; 10:1). Since Abraham’s true children are those of faith, and the promise was always to his offspring, Christ, there is no way to Abraham’s blessing that bypasses Abraham’s Seed. So Christians should love Jewish people, reject every form of antisemitism as a sin against the people from whom Christ came, and share the gospel with them gladly, humbly, and first (Romans 1:16).

Where Christians differ: Israel and the church. Dispensationalists, who read the Bible as a series of distinct eras, distinguish sharply between Israel and the church as two peoples with separate promises; many of them are devoted students of Scripture and warm friends of the Jewish people. This commentary’s view: Paul teaches that all who have faith, Jew or Gentile, are Abraham’s children and heirs of the promise (v. 29). There is one people of God across history, united by faith in the promised offspring, Christ. This is covenant theology’s insight: the one covenant of grace, administered in different ways, runs from Abraham to the church (the Westminster Confession 7.5–6). God has not cast off the Jewish people (Romans 11:1–2, 23), but they are saved within the one people, not alongside it.

parallels.desc: in you all the families of the earth shall be blessed

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 10–14 — The Righteous Shall Live by Faith
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The law cannot bring the blessing, because it curses everyone who relies on it; Christ brings it by bearing that curse himself. Those who rely on works of the law stand under the curse on all who do not keep everything written (v. 10). Scripture says the righteous live by faith (Habakkuk 2:4), while the law’s principle is doing (Leviticus 18:5), and no sinner can meet its terms (vv. 11–12). Then the summit of the chapter: Christ redeemed us by becoming a curse for us on the tree (v. 13), so that Abraham’s blessing might reach the Gentiles and we might receive the promised Spirit through faith, which brings the argument back to the question of v. 2 (v. 14).
verseByVerse.theology:
Penal Substitution: The Curse Exchanged

Verse 13 says plainly that Christ bore in our place the penalty due to sinners, the law’s curse. The curse of vv. 10–12 fell on him, so that the blessing of v. 14 could come to those who had no claim to it. He did not only suffer with us; he suffered instead of us, bearing what was ours.

This does not mean the Father stopped loving the Son (see the note on v. 13).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The Judaizers offered the law as a supplement to faith. Verses 10–12 show that the law cannot be a supplement: as a way to God it accepts only perfect obedience, and no one has given it. Verse 13 names the one way out, and v. 14 explains how a Gentile with no covenant and no ancestry ends up with the Spirit of God.

Now: Some readers come to v. 10 already afraid that God is disappointed with them; that fear is answered in the note on v. 10.

verseByVerse.quote: For all who rely on works of the law are under a curse; for it is written, “Cursed be everyone who does not abide by all things written in the Book of the Law, and do them.”
verseByVerse.commentary:
Anyone who stakes his standing with God on keeping the law stands under its curse, because the law demands complete obedience and no one gives it.

All who rely on works of the law. Now Paul argues from the law itself. He does not say that those who break the law are under a curse, but those who rely on it: the serious, observant ones, whose standing with God rests on their law-keeping. The people who thought the law was their shelter are standing under the one thing it guarantees for sinners. In Scripture a curse is not a spell or a run of bad luck but the opposite of God’s blessing: his sentence of judgment on the sinner, shutting him out from his favour (Deuteronomy 28:15; Matthew 25:41).

For it is written. The proof comes from the law’s own closing ceremony. In Deuteronomy 27 Israel is drawn up on two mountains, Ebal and Gerizim, with the covenant read aloud between them, and the last of twelve curses is the one Paul takes (Deuteronomy 27:26). After every curse the whole nation answered Amen, ratifying the terms themselves.

Four words. Everyone: no exemptions. All things: the whole code, not a representative selection. Abide by: continuously, not in a good season. Do them: performance, not agreement; you can admire a command all your life without once obeying it. The step Paul leaves unsaid every reader knows: no one does all things.

A seamless garment. The law is not an exam with a pass mark but a garment woven in one piece: tear it anywhere and it is torn. “Whoever keeps the whole law but fails in one point has become guilty of all of it” (James 2:10), because the law is the expression of one Person’s will, and to break any of it is to say no to him. So the choice is not between an easier and a harder road to God, but between a road and a cliff. Whoever stands on law-keeping has entered a system with only two verdicts, flawless obedience and curse, and has already failed, which is why the law-keeper’s religion is so often anxious under its composure.

An altar on the mountain of curse. Moses told Israel to build an altar and offer burnt offerings on Mount Ebal, the very mountain where the tribes stood for the curse (Deuteronomy 27:4–7, 13). The sacrifice stood where the curse fell. On the day Israel said Amen to its own condemnation, God was already pointing to an offering made in their place. It came when the one man who kept all things, who could say “I always do the things that are pleasing to him” (John 8:29), went outside the city wall to take the law’s curse on himself. God did not pretend the terms were softer than they were. The God who is too holy to cancel his own law loves sinners too much to leave them under it, and at the cross both are seen at once: his justice satisfied to the last letter, and his mercy flowing out through the very place where it was satisfied.

In everyday life. Most of us stand on our record more often than we think: when we feel we deserve an answer to prayer because we have been faithful, or that God owes us a smoother life for our service. Such small reliances on works breed anxiety or resentment. You do not have to stand on your own record. Christ kept all things written for you and took the curse you earned, so his obedience is counted as yours (Romans 5:19), and your imperfect service is accepted for his sake, not weighed as wages.

Is God disappointed with me? Some readers come to this verse with their stomach tight, unable to shake the sense that God is disappointed with them, and it looks like proof. Look at exactly what Paul says. Not that people who sin are cursed with no way out, or there would be no hope for anyone, but that people who rely on law-keeping are cursed, because they have chosen a standard that will certainly convict them. The curse is aimed less at your failure than at the thing you were trying to use to cover it. And it did not stay where it was aimed: Christ redeemed us from it by becoming a curse for us (v. 13).

Were the Israelites of the Old Testament all under this curse? Not those who trusted God. They were saved as Abraham was, by faith in God’s promise, looking forward to the Redeemer. The law itself provided sacrifices pointing to Christ, and the psalms are full of people who knew they could not stand on their own record and cast themselves on God’s mercy (Psalm 32:1–2; 130:3–4). Paul condemns relying on the law as the ground of acceptance, which the faithful in Israel never did. David, Isaiah and Daniel were not law-climbers but forgiven sinners, who loved God’s law because they had first received his mercy.

parallels.desc: cursed be anyone who does not confirm the words of this law

verseByVerse.quote: Now it is evident that no one is justified before God by the law, for “The righteous shall live by faith.” But the law is not of faith, rather “The one who does them shall live by them.”
verseByVerse.commentary:
Scripture itself shows that no one is put right with God by the law: the righteous live by trusting God, while the law offers life only to those who do all it commands.

“The righteous shall live by faith.” Evident (dēlon) means plain, already established, and two Old Testament quotations settle how anyone has ever been right with God. The first is Habakkuk 2:4 (also Romans 1:17; Hebrews 10:38). Habakkuk had been watching the Babylonians come, and he was given not an explanation but a way to survive: the righteous man will live by faith, keeping his footing when everything he can see is against him. By his own account it was this verse, as Paul quotes it in Romans 1:17, that opened the gospel to Martin Luther.

The one who does them shall live by them. The second is Leviticus 18:5. As a way to righteousness, the law says: do and live. Faith says: believe and live. One puts the weight on the one who does, the other on the one who is trusted: two answers to the question who is responsible for my standing before God, and the second cancels the first.

How can Paul set Moses against Habakkuk? He is not pitting one Old Testament verse against another. In Leviticus 18:5 God speaks to a people he has already redeemed from Egypt: keep my laws and you will enjoy life with me in the land. For them obedience was the grateful way of life of the redeemed, with sacrifices provided for their failures. But the false teachers were using the law as a ladder to climb up to God. Paul takes them at their word: make the law the ground of your acceptance, and Leviticus 18:5 states the terms. You must do them, all of them (v. 10), and no sinner can. Habakkuk 2:4 states the only way open to sinners.

A sound contract offered to a bankrupt. The law really does promise life to whoever keeps it, and nothing is wrong with it: it is “holy and righteous and good” (Romans 7:12). The defect is in the material it has to work with. The law was “weakened by the flesh” (Romans 8:3), our sinful nature, like a perfectly sound contract offered to a bankrupt.

The coming one. The prophet was told to wait for the vision: “it will surely come” (Habakkuk 2:3). Hebrews reads that waiting as waiting for Christ: “Yet a little while, and the coming one will come and will not delay; but my righteous one shall live by faith” (Hebrews 10:37–38). Faith was never faith in faith, but trust in a person. The righteous live by faith because the Righteous One has come.

He earned the life. Leviticus 18:5 was never revoked. Someone had to do the things and live by them, and someone did (4:4–5; Romans 10:4–5): exactly one man on this earth could stand under the law’s own terms and claim its promise honestly. He earned the life. Then he went to a place where the law had nothing but a curse to give, and he took the curse instead, and left the life to us.

What does living by faith look like when life is hard? It looks like Habakkuk. He got no explanation of why the Babylonians were coming, only a promise and a God to trust. By the end of his book the fig tree has not blossomed, the fields have failed and the stalls are empty, and he says he will still rejoice in the LORD and take joy in the God of his salvation (Habakkuk 3:17–18). Living by faith does not mean pretending things are fine, but telling God honestly that they are not, and then trusting what he has said about himself over what your circumstances are saying. The righteous do not live by understanding. They live by faith.

parallels.desc: the righteous shall live by his faith
by doing them a person shall live

verseByVerse.quote: Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us—for it is written, “Cursed is everyone who is hanged on a tree”—
verseByVerse.commentary:
Christ set us free from the curse the law pronounces on sinners by taking that curse on himself, in our place, on the cross. Everything in the chapter has been climbing to this sentence.

Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law. Redeemed is exagorazō, a market-place word: to buy out, as a slave could be bought out of slavery, with a real price paid for a real release. And it is not from the law as God’s good will that he redeemed us, but from its curse, the penalty it pronounces on lawbreakers: death and God’s wrath.

By becoming a curse for us. How he did it is deliberately shocking. He did not redeem us merely by pitying us or showing how much God cares; he himself came under the curse. “For us” is hyper hēmōn, on our behalf, in our place. This is penal substitution: Christ bore in our place the penalty God’s law pronounces on our sin, so that it will never be laid on us (Isaiah 53:5–6; 2 Corinthians 5:21; 1 Peter 2:24).

Who is the “us”? How could Gentiles, who never lived under the law of Moses, be redeemed from its curse? Paul, a Jew, speaks first of Israel, who stood under the law and its curse (v. 10). But Gentiles are not outside the verdict: they have the work of the law written on their hearts and are condemned by it just as surely (Romans 2:14–15; 3:19). And v. 14 shows the order of the rescue: Christ redeemed Israel from the curse so that Abraham’s blessing might flow out from Israel to the nations.

Hanged on a tree. No Jew could hear this text without flinching (Deuteronomy 21:23). In Deuteronomy 21 hanging is not the method of execution. A man is put to death, and then his body is hung on a tree as a public sign of what he was, and taken down by nightfall, because a hanged man is cursed by God. The tree announced the verdict of heaven to everyone walking past.

Saul before a cross. For a Pharisee this text was the closing argument against Jesus of Nazareth: God had published his verdict on a beam outside the city wall, and a crucified Messiah was a stumbling block to Jews (1 Corinthians 1:23). On the Damascus road it was turned round. Saul had been right that the tree published a curse, and wrong about only one thing: whose curse it was. It was ours. “For us”: those two small words are the whole gospel. He was cursed, and not for anything he had done. The Son of God walked into the courtroom, took the sentence before it reached us, and carried it out of the city on his own back. The tree designed to publish the curse of God has become the place where the curse of God was spent in full.

What it does not mean. Not that Christ was personally guilty, or that God stopped loving his Son. Jesus said the opposite: “For this reason the Father loves me, because I lay down my life” (John 10:17). The Son was never more precious to the Father than in the hour he bore our sentence, and the sentence was real: both are true at once.

In everyday life. When your past sins come back to accuse you, do not answer by listing your recent improvements. Name the sin, and then say: that curse fell on him, outside the city wall, and it will not fall on me.

Why did it have to be a cross? Because God meant the manner of Christ’s death to say what it was. Only a death on a tree could show, in the law’s own language, that he died under the curse. The authorities may well have wanted him crucified to show that God had rejected him, and the Romans to shame him; God used both to publish what they did not intend, that the curse of God was falling on this man for sinners. The shame was not a side effect of his saving death but part of the price, and Jesus despised it for the joy set before him (Hebrews 12:2).

Is it fair that an innocent man should be punished for the guilty? It would be unjust if a judge seized an unwilling bystander, but that is not what happened. The Son came willingly, one with the Father in purpose. He is himself the Judge who was wronged, choosing to bear the penalty of those who wronged him. And he is our representative, united to us as our head, as Adam was, so that what he did counts for those who are his. God is not punishing a third party; in his Son he is taking the cost of our sin on himself. That is the highest justice joined to the deepest love (Romans 3:25–26).
verseByVerse.note: Under the law, the body of an executed criminal hung on a tree was under God’s curse.

parallels.desc: a hanged man is cursed by God

verseByVerse.quote: so that in Christ Jesus the blessing of Abraham might come to the Gentiles, so that we might receive the promised Spirit through faith.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Christ bore the curse so that the blessing promised to Abraham might reach the Gentiles, and so that all who believe might receive the promised Spirit. He rescued us not only from something but for something.

The blessing of Abraham. The purpose comes twice: “so that”, “so that”. First, the blessing promised to Abraham, justification and life, now flows to the nations (v. 8). Travelling since Genesis 12, the promise arrives, in a Galatian town, in the hands of people whose grandparents worshipped Zeus.

The promised Spirit. Second, the Spirit, and the circle closes. Paul began by asking how they received the Spirit (v. 2); now he says the cross is why they received him, through faith. The Spirit is not a bonus for advanced believers but the promise itself: God coming to live in Gentile bodies, as Ezekiel (Ezekiel 36:27) and Joel (Joel 2:28) foretold. The Galatians had him, and they were being told they lacked something.

In Christ Jesus. Not because God relaxed the terms. The Judaizers wanted Gentiles brought in through the door marked become a Jew; God brought them in through a door marked be in Christ, the only door there has ever been. Nothing was cheapened to let the nations in. The full weight of the law’s sentence fell, and it fell on his Son, so that a man in Iconium with no covenant, no ancestry and no merit could be given the Spirit of the living God.

Am I missing a deeper blessing? A common Christian discouragement is the settled suspicion that you have received a lesser version of the faith than others: that there is a deeper blessing, a level of God’s favour others reached and you did not. Verse 14 rules that out. The blessing of Abraham and the promised Spirit are not prizes handed out at different levels of attainment. They are one gift, purchased at one cross, received by one faith, and if you are in Christ you have them. You may grow in enjoying what you have; you will never be given more of a standing than you already possess.

How do I depend on the Spirit day by day? Begin each day by acknowledging him: you live in me, and I need you today. Before you read Scripture, ask him to open it. Before a hard conversation, ask for the right words and a gentle heart. When temptation comes, ask for strength, then act, trusting that he is giving it. When you fail, do not grieve him further by hiding; confess and return. Depending on the Spirit is not a feeling you wait for but a posture of asking, trusting and obeying, all day long.

parallels.desc: I will pour my Spirit upon your offspring

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God’s promise to Abraham stands untouched by the law that came later, because it was a sworn and free gift. Calling the Galatians brothers again, Paul takes an everyday example: once a will or covenant is ratified, no one adds a clause (v. 15), and the Judaizers’ demand was exactly such an amendment. The promise was made to Abraham’s offspring, singular, who is Christ (v. 16). The law came 430 years later and cannot cancel it (v. 17), and an inheritance cannot come both by law and by promise: God gave it to Abraham freely, and it stands given (v. 18).
verseByVerse.theology:
The Promise Comes First and Cannot Fail

God’s unconditional oath to bless all nations through Abraham’s offspring came before the law of Moses and does not depend on it. The covenant of grace, God’s one plan to save sinners by grace through faith in the promised Christ, runs through the whole Bible, and the law given at Sinai served it for a season without changing its terms.

Verse 16 shows why the promise cannot fail: it was made to the one heir who would not break it (see the note on vv. 15–16), and v. 18 says it stands given (see the note on vv. 17–18). A promise that rests on the character of the one who swore it is a different kind of possession from anything that depends on the one who receives it.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The Judaizers argued, in effect, that the law of Moses changed the conditions of the earlier promise to Abraham. Verses 15 and 17 show that this is impossible, and v. 18 shows what it would cost: not an improved promise but no promise at all.

Now: Because the inheritance rests on God’s promise and not on our performance, a believer who fails can run to his Father instead of hiding from him (see the note on vv. 17–18).

verseByVerse.quote: To give a human example, brothers: even with a man-made covenant, no one annuls it or adds to it once it has been ratified. Now the promises were made to Abraham and to his offspring. It does not say, “And to offsprings,” referring to many, but referring to one, “And to your offspring,” who is Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
As no one can add a clause to a will once it is ratified, nothing that came later can amend God’s sworn promise to Abraham, a promise made to his one offspring, Christ.

To give a human example, brothers. He has just been at Golgotha; now he takes them to a lawyer’s office. And he calls them brothers, the anger letting a warm word through, as at 1:11. An opponent might reply: granted that Abraham was justified by faith, did God not give the law later, at Sinai, so that the later word sets the terms now? Verses 15–18 answer him; v. 19 takes the next question.

A man-made covenant. The word (diathēkē) covers both a covenant and a last will and testament. Once a will is legally confirmed, nobody can come along later and insert a clause. How much more an agreement God has sworn to! The Judaizers were not proposing to tear up the promise to Abraham, only to amend it: the promise, plus a condition. Anyone attempting that is not adding to God’s covenant but writing a different one.

Who is Christ. God’s promises to Abraham are repeated again and again (Genesis 12:7; 13:15; 17:8; 22:18). Paul observes that God said “to your offspring”, singular, and concludes that the promise was made to one person, Christ. To a modern reader that looks like a trick, since offspring (literally seed) is a collective noun, and Genesis 15:5 promised descendants as numerous as the stars. But in v. 29 Paul himself uses the word collectively, of a whole church. A man does not build an argument on a word’s singularity and then use it of a crowd unless he knows exactly what the word does.

The promise always narrowed. That is the argument. Ishmael was a son of Abraham and not the line of promise: “through Isaac shall your offspring be named” (Genesis 21:12). Esau was passed over. The line runs to Judah, then to David’s house, narrowing at every fork. The singular lets Paul say what the history was always saying: this promise had one destination, and it was a person (Genesis 22:17–18). God made his covenant with one man who would not break it, and everyone else gets in by being in him. Paul is reading the Old Testament as the risen Christ taught his disciples to read it on the Emmaus road (Luke 24:27).

In everyday life. If the promise was made to Christ, it cannot fail, because its heir cannot fail. When you doubt whether God will keep his word to you, stop looking at your own reliability and look at his Son’s. The promise rests on the one to whom it was made, and you are in him.

Do all the promises of the Old Testament apply to me? All God’s covenant promises find their yes in Christ (2 Corinthians 1:20), and if you are in Christ you share in them: forgiveness, God as your God, his presence, his Spirit, his faithfulness, an everlasting inheritance. But read each promise in its setting. Some were given to particular people in particular situations, such as a king or the exiles in Babylon; they show God’s character rather than guaranteeing you the same outcome. Ask what the promise shows about God and how it is fulfilled in Christ, and you can claim it through him without twisting it.
verseByVerse.note: “Offspring” (literally “seed”) is a singular noun that can refer to one descendant or many.

parallels.desc: in your offspring shall all the nations be blessed

verseByVerse.quote: This is what I mean: the law, which came 430 years afterward, does not annul a covenant previously ratified by God, so as to make the promise void. For if the inheritance comes by the law, it no longer comes by promise; but God gave it to Abraham by a promise.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The promise came first and was given freely, so the law, arriving four centuries later, cannot cancel it or turn the inheritance into a wage.

The law, which came 430 years afterward. Now Paul puts a date on it. The promise is the older document by four centuries, and in any court the later paper cannot cancel the earlier. Exodus 12:40 says Israel lived in Egypt 430 years, but the Greek Old Testament that Paul’s readers used, and the Samaritan text, read “in Egypt and in Canaan”, which makes the 430 years run from the patriarchs to the exodus; Paul uses the text his churches had in their hands. Nothing depends on the exact figure: the promise came first.

If the inheritance comes by the law. Verse 18 is the cleanest either-or in the letter. An inheritance is given; a wage is earned. A promise is something one party swears and the other receives; a law is something one party demands and the other performs. Make my performance a condition and you have not enriched the promise; you have dissolved it.

Gave it by a promise. To give freely (charizomai), from the same root as grace, in a tense that describes a finished act whose result remains: God has given, and it stands given. The deed was signed before Sinai, by one who does not go back on his word (Romans 4:13–16; Hebrews 6:17–18). Through Egypt and the wilderness, judges, kings and exile, through every generation that failed to keep the law, the promise stood untouched, because it had never rested on them.

A will that needed a death. Diathēkē also means a will, and a will takes effect only at death. So Christ is the mediator of a new covenant, that those who are called may receive the promised eternal inheritance, since a death has occurred (Hebrews 9:15–17). The inheritance promised to Abraham comes to us through the death of the Son, and we are fellow heirs with him (Romans 8:17).

The father and the tidy room. A father tells his son that the house will be his; it is written, signed, witnessed. Later he says: and keep your room tidy. If tidiness is how a son who has been given a house behaves in it, nothing has changed. But if tidiness is now the condition of inheriting, the son has a contract, and he will spend the rest of his life measuring the floor, never once sure. That is the difference between a Christian who obeys God and one who is trying to secure God. The behaviour can look identical until something goes wrong: one fails and runs to his Father; the other fails and hides, because the failure has just put his inheritance in doubt.

Can I lose my inheritance? Not if it rests on God’s promise, and that is exactly Paul’s point. An inheritance that depended on your performance could be forfeited any day. One given by promise depends on the faithfulness of the one who promised, and God does not break his word. So Scripture speaks of an inheritance imperishable, undefiled and unfading, kept in heaven for you, by God’s power guarding you through faith (1 Peter 1:4–5). True believers persevere not because they hold on so tightly, but because they are held. If you fear you have lost it, the fear itself shows you care; bring it to Christ, and rest on what he has promised.
verseByVerse.note: Exodus gives 430 years for Israel’s stay in Egypt; Paul uses the figure for the long gap between the promise and the law.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 19–25 — The Purpose of the Law
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The law was never meant to give life: God gave it to expose sin and to keep his people in custody, for a time, until Christ came. It was added because of transgressions, until the offspring should come, and came at one remove, through angels and Moses (v. 19), while the promise rests on God alone (v. 20). So the law does not oppose the promise; it simply cannot give life, and by shutting everyone up under sin it leaves faith in Christ as the only way out (vv. 21–22). It was a guardian until Christ came, and now that faith has come, believers are no longer under it (vv. 23–25).
verseByVerse.theology:
The Law as Guardian: Real, Strict, Temporary

The covenant of grace is one across both Testaments, and the law of Moses had a distinct job within it. Verses 19 and 24 show that the law was truly from God, truly binding in its time, and truly serving the promise, but it was given for a stage and not for the end. Its ending as the framework of God’s people is not God changing his mind; it is God completing his plan.

God’s moral will has not been repealed (5:14). And v. 22 shows that the law’s severity was a mercy (see the note on vv. 21–22).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The Judaizers wanted the guardian brought back after the child had come of age. Paul answers that the guardian was appointed for a term that has ended (vv. 19, 25), and that the promise never depended on two signatures (v. 20).

Now: Many believers are adults in Christ and still live as if under supervision (see the note on vv. 23–25).

verseByVerse.quote: Why then the law? It was added because of transgressions, until the offspring should come to whom the promise had been made, and it was put in place through angels by an intermediary.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God gave the law to expose sin, for a limited time until Christ came, and at one remove, through angels and Moses, unlike the promise he gave Abraham directly. Each phrase puts the law in its place without insulting it.

It was added because of transgressions. If the law cannot justify, give life or amend the promise, why did God give it at all? Was Sinai a mistake? Added is the first demotion: an addition is not the foundation. Sin was in the world before Sinai, but a transgression is a stepping over, the deliberate breaking of God’s known law, and you cannot step over a line that has not been drawn. The law drew the line. It turned the vague human sense that something is wrong with us into specific counts, written on stone by the finger of God (Exodus 31:18). Paul would not have known what it is to covet if the law had not said, “You shall not covet” (Romans 7:7; 5:20). The law makes sin visible, restrains it, and shows our need of a Saviour.

The diagnosis, not the medicine. That is one of the kindest things God could have done. A man who feels vaguely unwell will put off the appointment for years; handed a diagnosis with a name on it, he goes that afternoon. The law neither causes the disease nor cures it, and anyone who mistakes the chart for the medicine will die holding it. But without it we would have gone on managing our symptoms and calling ourselves basically decent people. The diagnosis was given so that the cure would be wanted, and the cure is the Lord himself.

Until the offspring should come. The second demotion. The law, as the governing covenant, came with an end written into it: not a failure but a term, which ran until the Offspring arrived, Christ (v. 16). Everything in the law was waiting for him: its sacrifices for the Lamb of God, its priesthood for a priest who lives for ever, its tabernacle for the Word who became flesh and dwelt among us (John 1:14, 29; Hebrews 7:24–25). “Christ is the end of the law for righteousness to everyone who believes” (Romans 10:4): he is its goal, and so the end of its term.

Through angels by an intermediary. The third demotion, and the sharpest. Scripture describes Sinai as attended by angelic hosts (Deuteronomy 33:2), and both Stephen and Hebrews take it for granted that the law was delivered by angels (Acts 7:53; Hebrews 2:2). Then Moses stood between the LORD and the people, because they were afraid (Deuteronomy 5:5; Exodus 20:19), and rightly: sinners cannot stand near a holy God without someone between. Count the links: God, angels, Moses, Israel. Now count the links in the promise: God, Abraham. The law came down a staircase; the promise was handed over directly. And when the Offspring arrived, God himself had come down the whole staircase to stand among us.

In everyday life. Read one of the Ten Commandments slowly this week, as Jesus read them in the Sermon on the Mount: not only the deed but the desire. Let it show you where you stand. Then go to Christ with what it has shown you, and thank him that he kept it all.

Why would God give a law he knew no one could keep? It was never meant to be the road by which we earn our way to him. It was given to a people already redeemed, as the shape of a holy life, with sacrifices built in for their failures, and to show all of us what we are and what we need. A law sinners could keep perfectly would have flattered us and left us without Christ. A law we cannot keep strips away every excuse and sends us to the one who kept it for us. God was not setting a trap but drawing a map, and every road on it ends at the cross.

Where Christians differ: the uses of the law. Some say the law has no role for Christians at all; others make it the centre of the Christian life. This commentary’s view: the Reformers identified three uses of the law. First, it shows sin and drives sinners to Christ (the use Paul focuses on here). Second, it restrains evil in society. Third, it guides believers in how to please God (often called the third use of the law), as the moral law summarised in the Ten Commandments (Romans 13:8–10). The ceremonial and civil laws of Israel (its sacrifices and purity rules, and its national laws) were fulfilled and ended in Christ, but the moral law remains the rule of life: not as a covenant of works, a way of earning life by obedience, but as the will of our Father (the Westminster Confession 19.5–6; the 1689 London Baptist Confession 19.5–6).
verseByVerse.note: Jewish tradition held that angels were present at the giving of the law; Moses was the intermediary.

parallels.desc: I stood between the LORD and you

verseByVerse.quote: Now an intermediary implies more than one, but God is one.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The law came through a go-between, in a covenant with two parties, but the promise rests on God alone, and so it cannot fail.

Now an intermediary implies more than one. A mediator stands between parties, each with obligations. So the very presence of Moses shows what kind of arrangement Sinai was: a two-sided covenant with conditions, with a man in the middle holding the terms. Everything depended on both parties keeping their word, and the people had barely promised before there was a golden calf at the foot of the mountain (Exodus 19:8; 32:1–6).

But God is one. When God came to Abraham there was no second party and no man in the middle. Abraham did not negotiate; he was asleep. God put him into a deep sleep and then passed alone between the pieces of the sacrifice: a smoking fire pot and a flaming torch walking the aisle of blood by themselves (Genesis 15:12, 17). In such a ceremony both parties walked between the pieces, invoking the animals’ fate on whoever broke faith (Jeremiah 34:18–20). God walked it alone, binding only himself, while Abraham lay there as a witness, not a partner to the oath. An agreement with two signatures can fail; a promise with one cannot, when the one who signed it is God, who does not have a bad year.

He walked between the pieces alone. God swore the whole covenant by himself, knowing every century of unfaithfulness to come, and what it would cost him to keep his oath when the other side had broken theirs. He walked between the pieces alone under the night sky, and when the time came his Son walked out to a hill alone, and kept it. “If we are faithless, he remains faithful, for he cannot deny himself” (2 Timothy 2:13).

What it does not mean. Not that Christ is not a mediator. He is the one mediator between God and men (1 Timothy 2:5), and is himself God. Moses stood between two parties as a third man; Christ stands between God and us as both God and man, so that in him the promise rests on God alone and is brought to us by one of us.

Why do I need a mediator? Because there is a real distance between a holy God and sinners, not of miles but of guilt. Moses could carry God’s words to the people, but he could not take away their sin; he once offered to be blotted out for them, and God would not accept it (Exodus 32:32–33). Christ is the mediator Moses could not be. He does not only carry messages; he offers himself, and he always lives to intercede for those who draw near to God through him (Hebrews 7:25). You need no other go-between, no priest, saint or ritual. You come to the Father through the Son.

Uncertain wording. This is famously one of Paul’s most compressed sentences, explained in a great many ways. What is clear: a mediator implies more than one party, and “God is one” echoes Israel’s confession (Deuteronomy 6:4). Less certain is how Paul links the two. The most likely sense is the one taken above: the law involved two parties with Moses between them, while the promise rests on God alone. Some take “God is one” instead as in Romans 3:29–30, the one God of Jew and Gentile alike, whose promise creates one family. Either way the direction of the thought is not in doubt: the promise stands above the law.

verseByVerse.quote: Is the law then contrary to the promises of God? Certainly not! For if a law had been given that could give life, then righteousness would indeed be by the law. But the Scripture imprisoned everything under sin, so that the promise by faith in Jesus Christ might be given to those who believe.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The law does not oppose God’s promises; it simply cannot give life, and by shutting everyone up under sin Scripture leaves faith in Christ as the only way out.

Certainly not! Having demoted the law three times, Paul asks the question his opponents would shout. The answer is mē genoito, the strongest negative he owns, kept for conclusions he finds unthinkable. Law and promise came from the same God and serve one plan. They are not rivals but a diagnosis and a cure, and only a fool sets those against each other.

A law that could give life. If any legal code could make a dead man live, God would have used it. The law can command, but it cannot give the power to obey (Romans 8:3). A speed limit has never once made a reckless man careful; it tells him what careful looks like and records that he is not. That is the true measure of our condition. If we were merely misinformed, instruction would be enough; if merely weak, encouragement. But we were dead in trespasses and sins (Ephesians 2:1), and nothing you say to a corpse improves it. We needed resurrection.

Imprisoned everything under sin. Shut up together, locked in with no other door (synkleiō): the word Luke uses for a shoal of fish enclosed in a net (Luke 5:6). And the object is not only everyone but everything (Romans 3:9–20; 11:32). To be under sin is more than to have sinned now and then: it is to live under sin’s guilt, which condemns us, and its power, which rules us. And it is Scripture that did the locking, so there is no higher court to appeal to against the verdict.

What the law could not do. What the law could not do, God did by sending his own Son. The law could describe life; Christ is the life (John 14:6). A Person has raised the dead, and he speaks to the dead still: “the dead will hear the voice of the Son of God, and those who hear will live” (John 5:25).

So that the promise. The imprisonment is a mercy. While a man believes there is another way out, he will keep trying doors: being respectable, useful, sincere, spiritual. God locked every one of them so that we would finally turn round and see the one door that stands open, with a person’s name on it. The jailer and the deliverer are the same God, and he never meant the prison to be the end of the story: he himself became the door (John 10:9), and he holds it open still to everyone who believes. If the harder you try, the more failures you count, do not read that as God’s absence. It may well be his kindness, closing the exits so that you will turn round to Christ.

Does “everything under sin” include the good people I know? Yes, and it includes you and me. Some people are kinder and more honest than others, and God is pleased with real kindness wherever it is found. But no one has loved God with all his heart or kept the law, and a good life lived for oneself is still a life lived apart from God. The verse does not say everyone is as bad as he could be, but that everyone is shut in the same prison, respectable and disreputable alike, and needs the same way out. That is humbling, and it is also the great leveller: the nicest and the worst person you know are invited to Christ on exactly the same terms.

verseByVerse.quote: Now before faith came, we were held captive under the law, imprisoned until the coming faith would be revealed. So then, the law was our guardian until Christ came, in order that we might be justified by faith. But now that faith has come, we are no longer under a guardian,
verseByVerse.commentary:
The law was a temporary guardian, keeping God’s people in custody until Christ came; now that he has come, and faith in him is the open way, believers are no longer under it.

Before faith came. Abraham had faith, and so did Habakkuk. Paul means the era of faith, opened when Christ came, when faith in him became the open, announced way in. The Old Testament believer was looking down a corridor at a door he could not yet see. We are standing in the room. Paul says “we were held captive”, speaking as a Jew; in v. 26 he turns to “you”, Jew and Gentile together.

Held captive. To guard, as a garrison guards a city (phroureō). Israel was guarded by the law, but only for a time: custody, not a life sentence. This finishes Paul’s answer to “Why then the law?” (v. 19): it had a time limit.

Our guardian. The law was our paidagōgos. Older versions said schoolmaster, which misleads. A paidagōgos was a household slave, often stern, who had charge of a boy from about six until he came of age. He walked him to school and home, kept him off the wrong streets, checked his manners, and had a stick. He was not there to educate the boy, but to get him to the one who would. Three things about him answer the Judaizers. He was genuinely appointed: the boy who resented him was resenting his father’s arrangement. He was genuinely strict. And he was genuinely temporary: nobody was under a paidagōgos at thirty, and even his strictness was aimed at the moment he would hand the boy over. Paul takes up the picture again at 4:1–7.

Walked to the door of Christ. Where was the guardian taking the boy? To a Person. Moses wrote of him (John 5:46; Luke 24:44). The lamb at Passover, the blood on the mercy seat, the priests who died and had to be replaced, the curse on the one who failed: all were walking the boy toward Christ. And the one he is handed over to is no harsher guardian with longer lists. It is the Son himself: Come to me, all who labour and are heavy laden, and learn from me, for I am gentle and lowly in heart (Matthew 11:28–29).

No longer under a guardian. The son has come of age, and the Judaizers were telling the grown man that if he really wanted to please his father, he should send for the old slave again and ask to be walked to school. Everything strict and narrow in the old arrangement was the Father’s care for children too young for the house; everything open and free in the new is the same Father’s joy in sons come of age. He has never been anything but a father.

What it does not mean. Not that believers may live as they please. God’s moral will has not been repealed; Paul will spend two chapters telling these people how to live (5:14). What has ended is the law as the framework of the relationship, the guardianship, with its ceremonies, under which God’s people lived as minors. Christians are under the law of Christ (1 Corinthians 9:21). Nor were Old Testament believers second-class: they were children in the same family, in the care their age required.

How do I stop living like a child under supervision? Many believers still live as if under the guardian: measuring the day’s performance, expecting the stick, surprised by kindness. Believe what your Father has said: you are his son or daughter, not his employee or his ward on probation. Talk to him as a child talks to a loving father, plainly and often. Obey because you want to please him, not to keep him from punishing you. When you fail, go to him, not away. And let the Spirit’s cry of Abba, Father (4:6) become your own. It takes time to unlearn the guardian, but the guardian has been dismissed.
verseByVerse.note: The “guardian” (paidagogos) was a household slave who supervised a child, took him to school and kept him in line until he came of age.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Through faith every believer is a full son and heir in God’s family, because each one is in Christ. Sons through faith, they have been baptised into Christ and clothed with him (vv. 26–27). So the divisions that ruled the ancient world, Jew and Greek, slave and free, male and female, no longer decide anyone’s standing before God, for all are one in Christ (v. 28). And all who belong to Christ, Abraham’s one offspring, are Abraham’s offspring too, heirs of everything God promised (v. 29).
verseByVerse.theology:
Union with Christ, and the Unity It Creates

Verses 26–27 give the ground of everything Paul has argued: the believer’s standing is not a quality in himself but a place. He is in Christ, clothed with Christ, and so shares the standing of the Son.

Verse 28 shows that the gospel does not only change individuals; it makes a community in which race, class and sex no longer decide anyone’s worth or access to God. Christians who honour Scripture differ on what the verse means for roles in church and home (see the box “Where Christians differ: does this verse abolish gender roles?” at the end of the note on v. 28).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Verse 28 says that the three walls of the ancient world (described in the note on v. 28) do not run through the church, because everyone in it is wearing the same garment (v. 27), and v. 29 tells Gentile believers that they are full heirs, not associate members.

Now: Every congregation has people who have quietly concluded that they are second rank; v. 28 is for them (see the note on v. 28).

verseByVerse.quote: for in Christ Jesus you are all sons of God, through faith. For as many of you as were baptized into Christ have put on Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Every believer, Jew or Gentile, is a full son and heir in God’s family through faith, joined to Christ and clothed with him. The boy under the guardian has become not a graduate but a son.

In Christ Jesus you are all sons of God, through faith. Every word counts. You: the uncircumcised, told they were not yet full members. All: no tiers. Sons: adult sons with full rights of inheritance (4:5–7). Through faith: not through the knife. And governing everything, in Christ Jesus: the sonship is ours because we are in the Son.

Sons, not only children. Paul writes huioi, sons, deliberately, because in that world sons inherited and daughters generally did not. The word is about legal status, the standing of the heir. So a woman reading v. 26 is told that she holds the inheritance rights of a son in the household of God. Far from excluding her, it is the most generous word in the sentence.

Baptized into Christ. In the New Testament faith and baptism belonged together: people believed and were baptised at once (Acts 8:12; 16:31–33), so Paul can speak of baptism as the moment they were joined to Christ (Romans 6:3–4). What actually unites a person to Christ is the Spirit, received through faith (v. 14; 1 Corinthians 12:13); baptism is the outward picture and public confession of it, as we might say “she gave her hand in marriage” and mean the whole covenant of marriage.

Have put on Christ. “Put on” is the ordinary word for dressing (endyō). In the Roman world a boy who came of age laid aside the child’s toga with its purple border and put on the plain white toga virilis, the garment of a man. Paul has just dismissed the guardian; now he hands out the adult garment, and the garment is Christ himself, his righteousness covering us (Romans 13:14; Isaiah 61:10).

He hung there stripped. The eternal Son put on our flesh so that we could put on him, and at the cross the soldiers cast lots for his tunic (John 19:23–24). He hung there stripped, so that sinners could stand before the Father dressed. No one in the great multitude before his throne will be wearing anything they made: they have washed their robes and made them white in the blood of the Lamb (Revelation 7:14).

What the Father sees. When the Father looks at a believer, he sees first not a person making progress but his Son’s own righteousness worn as clothing, covering everything the man is ashamed of. That is why assurance is possible for people who know themselves well: the clothing does not fluctuate with the wearer. We spend much of life dressing to be approved; the one garment that makes us acceptable to God has already been put on us. There is no better-dressed Christian in your congregation than you. The most disciplined believer you know is wearing exactly what you are wearing, and neither of you made it or paid for it.

I was baptised as an infant. Should I be baptised now? On the view this commentary holds, baptism is for those who have believed, so a believer baptised only as an infant has not yet received believer’s baptism and should ask for it, gladly, as an act of obedience and public confession. It is not a rejection of your parents’ love or prayers, which were real gifts. Talk it through with your pastor, and read the New Testament passages on baptism yourself. And hold your view with charity towards the many faithful Christians who baptise infants (see below): you are clothed with the same Christ.

Where Christians differ: does baptism save? Roman Catholic, Lutheran and some other Christians take this verse to mean that water baptism itself unites a person to Christ and regenerates them. This commentary’s view: Paul has just said we are sons through faith (v. 26), and the whole chapter insists that everything comes through faith (vv. 2, 14, 26), nothing by an outward rite performed on the body. Baptism is the sign of union with Christ, which is received by faith; it is not the cause of union. Those baptised with faith truly put on Christ; baptism without faith does not save (1 Peter 3:21; the 1689 London Baptist Confession 29.1; the Westminster Confession 28.5). This commentary holds believer’s baptism: the sign follows the faith it signifies, which is the order of these verses, sons through faith (v. 26), then baptised into Christ (v. 27). Christians who baptise infants see baptism as the sign of the covenant given, like circumcision, to believers’ children (Colossians 2:11–12); they are our brothers, and both sides confess what this verse indisputably says: what clothes a sinner before God is Christ, received by faith.

verseByVerse.quote: There is neither Jew nor Greek, there is neither slave nor free, there is no male and female, for you are all one in Christ Jesus.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In Christ the great divisions of race, class and sex no longer decide anyone’s standing before God: every believer holds the same whole Christ.

Neither Jew nor Greek. Those three pairs were the load-bearing walls of the ancient world. Jew and Greek was the great religious and ethnic divide; slave and free the great social one, and a large part of the people of a city like Corinth were slaves, owned as property; male and female decided whose testimony counted in court. A Jewish morning prayer recorded in later rabbinic sources thanked God for not making the man praying a Gentile, a slave, or a woman. Paul says that in Christ those walls do not run through the room.

No male and female. The first two pairs are “neither … nor”. The third changes to “no male and female”, the wording of Genesis 1:27 in the Greek Old Testament. Paul has reached back to creation: even the deepest distinction God made in humanity does not determine your standing in Christ.

All one in Christ Jesus. One is heis, one person: not identical, but one body. What is being levelled? Paul has not changed the subject: who is a son of Abraham, who is justified, who inherits. On that ground the walls are gone entirely. One Christ, one righteousness, one inheritance, and every believer holds all of it. Christ has no larger portion for anyone in the building than the one he has already given you. At the foot of the cross there is no hierarchy of worth, and in the inheritance no smaller share.

Difference remains; difference as worth has gone. Paul goes on being a Jew; Onesimus goes on being a slave in Roman law while Paul works on Philemon to receive him as a brother; men and women go on being men and women. What has gone is difference as a measure of worth and as a condition of access to God.

Why equality keeps building new walls. Almost everyone today agrees with this verse about human worth (where that conviction came from is the subject of the note on Acts 17:26), yet our societies are as tribal as ever. Some try to heal division by saying difference does not matter; others make it everything: you are your group, and groups are ranked, innocent or guilty, as a whole. Either way the walls go back up, sometimes with the old order turned upside down. The psychologist Jonathan Haidt, in The Righteous Mind, has argued that our moral convictions bind us into teams and then blind us to everyone outside them. Paul saw why. People who must justify themselves need someone to be better than, and the old prayer of thanks for not being a Gentile, a slave or a woman has secular versions too. The gospel removes the need. Nobody at the foot of the cross earned his place, so nobody needs a lesser person to stand on. Equality is safest with people who know they were equally lost and equally rescued.

In everyday life. Every congregation contains people who have quietly concluded that they are the second rank: the woman talked past in every church she has attended, the man whose accent or prison record marks him out. Seek one of them out this Sunday, as Christ sought you, and listen.

Does this verse condemn racism and snobbery in the church? Yes, plainly. If Christ has given the same standing to every believer, then a church that treats some believers as lesser because of their race, nationality, class, education or sex is denying in practice what this verse says. That was Peter’s sin at Antioch (2:11–14). It can look like congregations divided by colour with no language reason, leaders always from one social group, a cool welcome for the poor or the foreigner, jokes at someone’s background. Repent of it where you see it in yourself, and gently challenge it where you see it in your church. The one table of the Lord is meant to look like the one family he has made.

Where Christians differ: does this verse abolish gender roles? Egalitarians use this verse to argue that all distinctions of role between men and women in the church and home are abolished in Christ; they see the verse as the principle and the restrictions elsewhere as temporary concessions to Paul’s culture. This commentary’s view: the context is about who is justified and who is an heir of Abraham: all believers equally, regardless of race, class or sex. It is about status before God, not roles in the church. The distinctions themselves are not abolished: Jews remain Jews, men remain men. Paul elsewhere teaches distinct roles for men and women in the home and church (1 Corinthians 11:3; Ephesians 5:22–33; 1 Timothy 2:12), grounded in creation, not culture. Slavery is no parallel: Paul gave instructions to slaves while sowing the seeds of their freedom, urging slaves to take freedom when they could and condemning slave-traders (1 Corinthians 7:21; 1 Timothy 1:10; Philemon 16), but he never grounded slavery in creation. Equal in worth, distinct in calling: the complementarian view. And headship in Scripture is the self-giving love of Christ for his church, never domination; any abuse of a wife or of any person is a grave sin that the church must never tolerate or cover. Many faithful Christians read this verse the egalitarian way out of a real concern for the dignity of women, a concern the verse itself shares; this commentary honours them as brothers and sisters while holding the view above.

verseByVerse.quote: And if you are Christ’s, then you are Abraham’s offspring, heirs according to promise.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Everyone who belongs to Christ is Abraham’s offspring and an heir of everything God promised him.

If you are Christ’s. The chapter comes to rest here. The promise was made to the Offspring, and the Offspring is Christ (v. 16). So everything depends on one question: are you his? Now Paul uses offspring in its collective sense: in Christ, all believers are Abraham’s seed.

Heirs according to promise. An heir has been given a standing, and the estate follows from it. He does not earn it, or receive it for being useful, but because of who he is in the family (Romans 8:16–17; Ephesians 1:11).

Not by lowering the requirements. Paul does not say you have qualified, or that God has been generous with the entry requirements. Every one of them was met by one man, and you are in him. God narrowed the promise through Isaac and Jacob and Judah and David until it came down to one, and that one carried the curse of the broken law out of the city on his own back so that the promise could be paid to everyone who had no claim on it. Nothing was waived, and nothing failed.

What is actually inherited? Scripture is not vague, and the vagueness of much Christian talk about the future is a loss, not a virtue. Everything God promised Abraham: righteousness, the Spirit, the world to come (Romans 4:13). God himself as your portion, the substance of every promise (Genesis 15:1). A body that does not fail, raised imperishable (1 Corinthians 15:42–44). A world put right and handed over, the meek inheriting the earth (Matthew 5:5; Romans 8:17–21). The sight of God’s face, which Moses asked for and was not given (1 John 3:2; Revelation 22:4). And real service in a real kingdom (Luke 19:17). That stands to the account of every Galatian who believed Paul, and to yours.

If I am an heir, why does my life feel so poor? Because you are an heir before the reading of the will. Paul will say in the next chapter that an heir, while he is a child, may look no different from a slave (4:1). The estate is real but mostly unseen, in a world that contradicts it: illness, loss, loneliness, a body wearing out. That is the normal Christian condition, not a sign you have missed out. The inheritance is kept for you, not yet handed over (1 Peter 1:4). Meanwhile you have the down payment, the Spirit himself, the guarantee of what is to come (Ephesians 1:14). Live on the deposit, and look forward to the estate.

Where Christians differ: the land and Israel’s future. Are the promises of land and nation to Israel now void? Some Christians hold that they remain for ethnic Israel, with a future earthly fulfilment. This commentary’s view: with many Reformed Christians, that the promise was always larger than a strip of land: Abraham would be heir of the world (Romans 4:13), the renewed creation. Since all who are Christ’s are Abraham’s heirs, the promises are fulfilled in Christ and shared by everyone in him, Jew and Gentile alike, which is not a rejection of the Jewish people (Romans 11:1). (See the note on Israel and the church at 3:7–9.)

3.text: <sup>1</sup>O foolish Galatians! Who has bewitched you? It was before your eyes that Jesus Christ was publicly portrayed as crucified.<sup>2</sup>Let me ask you only this: Did you receive the Spirit by works of the law or by hearing with faith?<sup>3</sup>Are you so foolish? Having begun by the Spirit, are you now being perfected by the flesh?<sup>4</sup>Did you suffer so many things in vain—if indeed it was in vain?<sup>5</sup>Does he who supplies the Spirit to you and works miracles among you do so by works of the law, or by hearing with faith—<sup>6</sup>just as Abraham “believed God, and it was counted to him as righteousness”?<sup>7</sup>Know then that it is those of faith who are the sons of Abraham.<sup>8</sup>And the Scripture, foreseeing that God would justify the Gentiles by faith, preached the gospel beforehand to Abraham, saying, “In you shall all the nations be blessed.”<sup>9</sup>So then, those who are of faith are blessed along with Abraham, the man of faith.<sup>10</sup>For all who rely on works of the law are under a curse; for it is written, “Cursed be everyone who does not abide by all things written in the Book of the Law, and do them.”<sup>11</sup>Now it is evident that no one is justified before God by the law, for “The righteous shall live by faith.”<sup>12</sup>But the law is not of faith, rather “The one who does them shall live by them.”<sup>13</sup>Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us—for it is written, “Cursed is everyone who is hanged on a tree”—<sup>14</sup>so that in Christ Jesus the blessing of Abraham might come to the Gentiles, so that we might receive the promised Spirit through faith.<sup>15</sup>To give a human example, brothers: even with a man-made covenant, no one annuls it or adds to it once it has been ratified.<sup>16</sup>Now the promises were made to Abraham and to his offspring. It does not say, “And to offsprings,” referring to many, but referring to one, “And to your offspring,” who is Christ.<sup>17</sup>This is what I mean: the law, which came 430 years afterward, does not annul a covenant previously ratified by God, so as to make the promise void.<sup>18</sup>For if the inheritance comes by the law, it no longer comes by promise; but God gave it to Abraham by a promise.<sup>19</sup>Why then the law? It was added because of transgressions, until the offspring should come to whom the promise had been made, and it was put in place through angels by an intermediary.<sup>20</sup>Now an intermediary implies more than one, but God is one.<sup>21</sup>Is the law then contrary to the promises of God? Certainly not! For if a law had been given that could give life, then righteousness would indeed be by the law.<sup>22</sup>But the Scripture imprisoned everything under sin, so that the promise by faith in Jesus Christ might be given to those who believe.<sup>23</sup>Now before faith came, we were held captive under the law, imprisoned until the coming faith would be revealed.<sup>24</sup>So then, the law was our guardian until Christ came, in order that we might be justified by faith.<sup>25</sup>But now that faith has come, we are no longer under a guardian,<sup>26</sup>for in Christ Jesus you are all sons of God, through faith.<sup>27</sup>For as many of you as were baptized into Christ have put on Christ.<sup>28</sup>There is neither Jew nor Greek, there is neither slave nor free, there is no male and female, for you are all one in Christ Jesus.<sup>29</sup>And if you are Christ’s, then you are Abraham’s offspring, heirs according to promise.

keyVerse.quote: Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us
keyVerse.note: This is the summit the whole chapter climbs to. The law could only curse those who relied on it, and Christ did not set the curse aside but took it on himself, in our place. Everything else in the chapter flows from here: the blessing of Abraham reaching the Gentiles, the Spirit received by faith, and believers made sons and heirs.

3.reflection:
Paul asks the Galatians to remember how they first received the Spirit (vv. 2–5). What did you bring to God when he welcomed you? Where are you tempted to finish by your own effort what the Spirit began?

Verse 10 says that all who rely on keeping the law are under a curse, and verse 13 that Christ became a curse for us. How does the cross answer the feeling that God is disappointed with you?

Paul calls the law a guardian until Christ came (vv. 19–25). What good does the law do, and what goes wrong when Christians treat God’s commands as a way to secure his favour rather than as their Father’s will for his sons?

“You are all one in Christ Jesus” (v. 28). Who might feel second-rank in a church like ours, and what would it look like to treat them as full heirs alongside us?

4.title: Sons and Heirs: From Slavery to Sonship
4.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 4 completes the argument begun at 3:1, that the Galatians are God’s sons through faith in Christ, not through the law, then turns it into a personal plea that leads into the call to stand firm in freedom (5:1).

The message. In Christ you are no longer a slave but a son. God sent his Son to buy you out of slavery and adopt you, and sent the Spirit of his Son into your heart to cry “Abba! Father!” So do not go back to living like a slave, earning a place in a house where you already belong as an heir.

Why it was said. Teachers from Judea were telling these mostly Gentile churches that faith in Christ was not enough without circumcision and the law, and they had begun keeping the Jewish calendar (v. 10; see the introduction). They thought they were going on to maturity; Paul shows them they were going back to the nursery.

How the chapter makes its case. First a picture (vv. 1–7): an heir under age lives like a slave until the date his father has set; at God’s set time he sent his Son to redeem and adopt, and his Spirit into their hearts. Then a plea (vv. 8–20): known now by God, how can they turn back to slavery? Paul recalls their welcome when he came to them sick, unmasks the rivals’ flattery, and labours again until Christ is formed in them. Last, an argument from the law itself (vv. 21–31): Abraham’s two sons, by the slave Hagar and the free Sarah, stand for two covenants, slavery and freedom, and Scripture says the slave woman and her son must be cast out.

Where it leads. At the centre stands one sending: God’s own Son, born of a woman and under the law, came into our slavery to buy us out and give us his own place in the family (vv. 4–5). His Spirit puts his own word, Abba, in our mouths, so that an adopted child’s poorest prayer reaches the Father in the voice of the eternal Son. And the true Son was cast out in our place, so that no child he brings into the house will ever be sent away.

For us. Many Christians believe in grace and still live like hired servants, anxious whether they have done enough. This chapter calls us to stop earning a place already given, to keep our habits of devotion as children, not slaves, to long for Christ to be formed in us and others, and to rest as children of the free woman.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God has made believers his sons and heirs, no longer slaves under guardians. An heir who is still a child lives no better than a slave until the date his father has set (vv. 1–2), and so did Jew and Gentile alike, enslaved to the elementary principles of the world (v. 3). Then, at the time God had set, he sent his Son, born under the law, to buy out those under the law and adopt them as sons (vv. 4–5), and he sent the Spirit of his Son into their hearts, crying “Abba! Father!” (v. 6). So each believer is no longer a slave but a son, and an heir through God (v. 7).
verseByVerse.theology:
Adoption, and the Sending of the Son and the Spirit

In vv. 4–6 the Father sends the Son, and the Father sends the Spirit of the Son. The two sendings are distinct and belong together: the Son wins redemption and adoption for us, outside us, as a settled legal fact, and the Spirit brings them home within, so that the adopted child knows the Father and calls on him.

Adoption (huiothesia) is stated more clearly in this chapter than almost anywhere, and it goes beyond forgiveness. What changes is not the son’s conduct but his family. Verse 7 sums it up: no longer a slave but a son, and an heir, through God. J. I. Packer called adoption the highest privilege the gospel offers.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The Galatians already had everything vv. 4–7 describe: the Spirit, the cry of Abba, the inheritance. The Judaizers were offering them a route to a standing they already held, and vv. 1–3 show what they would be going back to: the nursery, the guardians and a calendar.

Now: Verse 6 answers the believer who does not feel like a son (see the note on vv. 6–7).

verseByVerse.quote: I mean that the heir, as long as he is a child, is no different from a slave, though he is the owner of everything, but he is under guardians and managers until the date set by his father.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Before Christ came, God’s people were like a young heir: the estate was already theirs, but they lived under guardians until the day their Father had set.

I mean that the heir, as long as he is a child. Chapter 3 ended with the guardian dismissed; now Paul runs the same picture from inside the household. The child is nēpios, a minor, a son not yet of legal age.

No different from a slave. In law he is the owner: the deeds are in his name. In practice it makes no difference, because he is seven. He cannot sell a field or give an order anyone has to obey. Watch him through the day and you could not tell him from the boy who carries the water.

But he is under guardians and managers. The epitropoi had authority over the boy’s person; the oikonomoi ran the property. Both were servants, both had more practical power over the estate than its owner did, and both held it only for a time.

Until the date set by his father. The arrangements varied in the ancient world (see Inheritance and the Firstborn), but in every version neither the boy nor the guardians chose the day. The father named it. God set the time for his people’s coming of age, and the date he wrote in the will was the coming of Christ (v. 4). He is no landlord letting rooms on good behaviour, but a Father who drew up the will, set the day, kept the estate through centuries of guardians, and never forgot the name on the deeds.

Ownership and enjoyment. Believers before Christ were truly saved, by faith in the Christ to come; but ownership and enjoyment are different things. Abraham was promised that he would be heir of the world (Romans 4:13), and died having bought only a burial plot for his wife (Genesis 23). He owned everything and held almost nothing, and was content to wait for “the city that has foundations, whose designer and builder is God” (Hebrews 11:10).

The Owner in the form of a slave. The picture of an owner of everything who looks no different from a slave has one perfect instance: the Son. He was in the form of God, the appointed heir of all things, and he took the form of a servant (Philippians 2:6–7; Hebrews 1:2), so ordinary to his neighbours that they asked, “Is not this the carpenter’s son?” (Matthew 13:55). The Lord of the estate entered the condition of the minors so that minors could come of age in him (vv. 4–5).

In everyday life. Much Christian frustration is about timing: the prayer unanswered for eleven years, the season that will not lift. Verse 2 does not promise that the date is soon. It says there is one, and that a Father fixed it, not the guardians who seem to be running your life.

Is God unkind to keep anyone in that position? No more than a father is unkind to his seven-year-old.
