The guardians were a protection, not a punishment: the law fenced and taught Israel and kept the line of promise intact until the Christ was born. The heir’s position was restricted, but his inheritance was secure, and every rule that hemmed him in was a sign that something very large had been reserved for him.

What does living as a son who has come of age actually look like? Freedom of access rather than a rulebook for every step. A minor needs a rule for everything because he does not yet know his father’s mind; a grown son has his father’s Spirit and word, and obeys from the inside. So you pray boldly, without first proving you deserve a hearing; confess sin quickly, because a son does not hide from his father; read God’s commands as the family’s way of life, not an entrance exam; and stop treating other believers’ consciences as your guardians, for you answer to the Father himself.

verseByVerse.quote: In the same way we also, when we were children, were enslaved to the elementary principles of the world.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Before Christ came, Jew and Gentile alike were minors in bondage, enslaved to the elementary principles of the world. Law-keeping Jew and idol-worshipping pagan both needed to be set free.

In the same way we also, when we were children. Paul puts the whole human race inside the picture. That we includes the Pharisee in the same sentence as men who grew up sacrificing to Cybele.

The elementary principles of the world. Ta stoicheia tou kosmou. Whatever the exact sense (see the box below), two things are certain: the Gentiles were under the stoicheia before they knew God (vv. 8–9), and the Judaizers’ programme would put the Galatians back under them. Paul has just put the law of Moses and the pagan festival calendar in the same class.

Not according to Christ. In Colossians Paul sets the same phrase against one name: “according to the elemental spirits of the world, and not according to Christ” (Colossians 2:8). Christ is their conqueror: at the cross he disarmed the rulers and authorities and put them to open shame (Colossians 2:15). The Galatians were choosing between masters Christ has already defeated and the Christ who defeated them. None of those masters ever set a slave free; only one Master has come into the market to buy his slaves out of it, the one by whom the world and all its elements were made.

Disappointment or dread. The danger lies in good practices, not bad ones. Imagine dropping the most valued religious habit in your life for a fortnight, not through rebellion but through illness. Is what rises in you disappointment, or dread? Disappointment is a son who has missed his father’s company. Dread is a slave who has missed a quota. The habit is identical; the relationship is not.

What it does not mean. Not that the law of Moses and paganism are the same; the law is holy, and the commandment holy and righteous and good (Romans 7:12). But as ways of approaching God apart from Christ, both enslave. Make any good, God-given thing, the Sabbath, the sacraments, a doctrinal system, a discipline of prayer, the thing that secures your standing with God, and it will do what an idol does: demand, never say enough, and make you its servant.

So should I drop my routines if they have become a burden? No. The answer to a habit that has become a quota is to change its ground, not to abandon it. Bible, prayer and church are the ordinary means by which God feeds his children; what has to go is the idea that they hold up your acceptance. Before you open your Bible tomorrow, tell God plainly that you are already accepted in Christ and have come to hear your Father, not to earn his attention. On the day you miss it, do not punish yourself with extra; come back the next morning as a son comes back to the table. The routine stays; the slavery goes.

Uncertain wording. “Elementary principles” translates stoicheia, one of the genuinely disputed words in Paul. It means things in a row: the ABCs, the basic building blocks of anything. Some take it that way here: the rudiments of religion, rules and rituals, so that going back to them is like an adult sounding out letters. Others hear something darker, since Paul says enslaved: the spiritual powers thought to stand behind the elements, the heavenly bodies and their calendars (Colossians 2:8, 20). Most readers today combine the two, and Paul’s argument does not depend on the choice.
verseByVerse.note: The “elementary principles” may mean the basic rules of religion, or the spiritual powers people believed ruled the world.

verseByVerse.quote: But when the fullness of time had come, God sent forth his Son, born of woman, born under the law, to redeem those who were under the law, so that we might receive adoption as sons.
verseByVerse.commentary:
At the moment he had chosen, God sent his own Son into our condition, to buy us out of slavery and make us his sons.

But when the fullness of time had come. Everything before has been minority, guardians, waiting; then God moves. The phrase is to plērōma tou chronou: the vessel full to the brim, not a minute early and not a minute late, the moment God had set (v. 2; Mark 1:15; Ephesians 1:10).

Why then? Some of the answer is visible: Roman roads and a Roman peace to walk them; one language a Galatian, a Roman and an Alexandrian could all read; synagogues in every city, the Scriptures in Greek, and Gentile God-fearers ready to hear; and among many a worn-out trust in the old gods. But the deeper answer is in the sentence itself: it was “the date set by his father” (v. 2). History was not waiting for conditions to be right. It was waiting for a Father to say now, and the conditions were his preparations.

God sent forth his Son. God sent out (exapostellō) one who was already his Son, from the Father’s side; he did not begin at Bethlehem. The Son of God became the son of Mary so that the sons of Adam could become the sons of God.

Born of woman. A Hebrew way of saying human, mortal, of our stock: “Man who is born of a woman is few of days and full of trouble” (Job 14:1). Truly human, with every weakness of our flesh except its sin.

Born under the law. He entered the jurisdiction that condemned us: circumcised on the eighth day, presented in the temple with the poor family’s offering of two birds (Luke 2:21–24, 41–42). He kept every clause of the code that was killing us, for us.

To redeem. The purpose comes in two halves. The first is exagorasē, the slave-market word of 3:13: to buy out. The price was himself.

Adoption as sons. The second half is more than release. Huiothesia, placing as a son, is a Roman legal term. A man without a suitable heir would take a young man, often an adult, into his family by a formal act before witnesses; from that day he bore his new father’s name, inherited like a natural son, and in some forms his old debts were cancelled. God’s adoption goes further: Roman law allowed a father later to release a son; God never does (John 10:28–29).

Adoption, new birth and justification. The new birth makes a person a child of God by an inward act: a heart made alive, so that he begins to want what he never wanted (John 1:12–13). Adoption is an outward, legal act: a standing conferred, a name given, an inheritance settled. And beyond justification, we are not only declared righteous in the court but welcomed into the family. On a day when the inward evidence is hard to find, the outward act stands exactly where it stood, because it was never yours to perform.

More than a rescue. Redemption alone would have set the slave free at the gate. God did not stop at the gate: he gave him his name and walked him into the house as a son. That is not a rescue. That is a family.

In everyday life. The day the adoption court signs, the child’s name is changed and no one can take it back. When you are tempted to think your standing with God rises and falls with your week, remember that your adoption was settled by the Son’s blood, not by your behaviour, and receive your Father’s correction without fearing that it means rejection (Hebrews 12:5–11).

Why did Jesus need to keep the law, if he was going to die for us anyway? Because we needed two things, not one: our guilt taken away, and a righteousness we did not have. His death bore the curse we had earned (3:13); his life of perfect obedience supplied the record we had failed to produce. Theologians call these his passive and active obedience. God does not merely wipe your slate clean and leave it blank; he writes his Son’s life on it, some thirty years of perfect love for God and neighbour (Romans 5:19; 2 Corinthians 5:21). Every year of the hidden life at Nazareth was for you as much as the cross.

Does sons leave out daughters? No. Paul says sons because in the ancient world it was sons who inherited, and he wants every believer to know they have the heir’s full standing. He has just said “there is no male and female, for you are all one in Christ Jesus” (3:28). So a Christian woman is a son in exactly this sense: not lesser, not dependent on someone else’s portion, but an heir in her own right. Elsewhere the Lord says it outright: “you shall be sons and daughters to me” (2 Corinthians 6:18).

Did Paul know of the virgin birth? Some argue from “born of woman” that he did not. That is more weight than the phrase will carry: Paul is writing not about how Jesus was conceived but about how fully he shared our condition, and his wording is at least consistent with the virgin birth: a mother, and no human father named. And Luke, who travelled with Paul, records the annunciation in detail (Luke 1:26–38).

verseByVerse.quote: And because you are sons, God has sent the Spirit of his Son into our hearts, crying, “Abba! Father!” So you are no longer a slave, but a son, and if a son, then an heir through God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Because God has made you his sons, he has given you the Spirit of his Son, who teaches your heart to call him Father.

Because you are sons. The order of the first four words settles many anxious questions. Not: cry Abba hard enough and you will become a son. The sonship comes first (v. 5), and the Spirit is sent because of it. The felt experience is the consequence of the status, never the cause.

Two sendings. God sent his Son (v. 4); God has sent the Spirit of his Son (v. 6): the same verb twice. The Son was sent into the world to do something for us; the Spirit into our hearts to do something in us. Salvation is the whole Godhead, Father, Son and Spirit, bringing a family home.

The Spirit of his Son. He is named as the Son’s own Spirit, because what he brings into the believer’s heart is the Son’s relationship to the Father. You are brought inside the Son’s relationship, not given a separate one, and come to God as Jesus did, as a child who expects to be heard. He taught his disciples to begin with his own word, Father (Luke 11:2), and the Spirit makes it true in your mouth.

Crying, “Abba! Father!” Abba is not baby-talk; grown men used it of their fathers all their lives. It is the Aramaic word for father used within the family: warm, domestic, not the formal, roundabout titles for God used in the synagogue, but the word a son would use turning round in the doorway. And the verb, krazō, is not a whisper but a loud, heartfelt cry, the cry of a child who knows he will be heard.

Who is doing the crying? Here Paul says the Spirit cries; in Romans he says we cry, the Spirit himself bearing witness with our spirit that we are children of God (Romans 8:15–16). Both are true, and together they are an enormous comfort: the prayer of a Christian is the Spirit of God praying in him. The man who gets three words in and dries up, ashamed of how thin it sounds, is describing only how his prayer sounds from the outside. The cry that reaches the Father is the cry of the Son’s Spirit, and it is not thin.

No longer a slave. In verse 7 you becomes singular: each believer is to hear it personally. “No longer”: slavery is your past, not your present. “Son”: a status given to you. “Heir”: believers are heirs of God and fellow heirs with Christ (Romans 8:17), and through God, not by the law.

In the flow. Verse 7 completes the argument begun at 3:1, where Paul asked how they received the Spirit (3:2); from here argument turns to appeal (vv. 8–9).

In the accent of the Son. The Son who could say Abba by right, from all eternity, shares that word with people who had no right to it at all, and the Spirit puts it in their mouths, so that their poorest prayers arrive at the throne in the accent of the Son.

In everyday life. Begin your praying with the words Abba, Father, and stay on them for a moment before you ask for anything. And when you are tempted to slink back to God like a hired servant, rehearsing why he should let you in, remember the prodigal: he had his speech ready, and his father never let him finish it (Luke 15:18–24).

What it does not mean. Not that God is our Father in the same way he is Christ’s. Christ is the eternal Son by nature; we are sons by adoption and grace. Jesus kept the distinction carefully: “I am ascending to my Father and your Father” (John 20:17), not “our Father”, as though the two were the same. But in Christ we share his place, and the Father loves us with the love with which he has loved him (John 17:23).

So should I call God Daddy? You may speak to him with the warmth and directness of a child, and you should. But Abba is no licence for casualness. Jesus said Abba in the garden (Mark 14:36), in the hour when, Luke tells us, his sweat became like great drops of blood (Luke 22:44, a verse missing from some early manuscripts), and in the same breath he said, “not what I will, but what you will.” The word holds intimacy and reverence together. So come close, come often, come without rehearsing, and remember whom you are calling Father: the nearness is astonishing because he is so great.

What exactly do I inherit? First and greatest, God himself: “The LORD is my portion” (Lamentations 3:24), and eternal life is to know him (John 17:3). Then everything that is Christ’s, as his fellow heir: the new earth the meek will inherit (Matthew 5:5), an inheritance imperishable, undefiled and unfading (1 Peter 1:4). You have a share of it now in the Spirit, the guarantee of the rest (Ephesians 1:14). And it cannot be lost, because it is not kept by you. It is kept for you, and you are kept for it.

What if I do not feel any of this? Then you are in the company of many of God’s dearest children. In illness, depression, grief or plain tiredness the feeling may be absent for long stretches, and nothing has happened to the sonship: a son asleep in his bed is as much his father’s son as a son laughing at his table. The Spirit’s witness is often quieter than warmth: you cannot stop coming back to Christ; you hate your sin and want to be holy; when you are in trouble, the word that rises to your lips is still Father. Those are the Spirit’s work. Feelings come and go; your adoption does not. Keep praying the word Father when it feels dry, and let the feeling follow when God gives it.
verseByVerse.note: “Abba” is the Aramaic word for “father,” used within the family.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Those whom God has brought out of slavery into his family must not walk back into bondage. Paul argues first: once enslaved to beings that are not gods, and now known by the true God, the Galatians are taking up the calendar as if it could complete their standing, and his labour is at risk (vv. 8–11). Then he pleads: he reminds them how they welcomed him when he came to them sick (vv. 12–15), asks whether telling the truth has made him their enemy (v. 16), exposes the rivals who court them for their own ends (vv. 17–18), and tells them he is in labour again until Christ is formed in them (vv. 19–20).
verseByVerse.theology:
Two Kinds of Bondage, and the Goal of Ministry

When Paul sets the Judaizers’ calendar beside the pagan one the Galatians had left (vv. 8–10), he is speaking of what it does, not saying the two are morally the same (see the note on v. 3). Moralism, the attempt to be accepted by God through being good, is not a minor error but a rival gospel, and it produces its own bondage.

Verse 9 contains one of Paul’s plainest statements of election, given in passing as a pastoral correction (see the note on vv. 8–9). And v. 19 gives the goal of all ministry: Christ formed in his people (see the note on vv. 19–20).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The Galatians had loved Paul extravagantly (vv. 14–15) and had cooled by v. 16, and vv. 17–18 explain why: the Judaizers courted them and flattered them, then held the door a few inches short of open. Paul wanted not their loyalty to him but Christ formed in them (vv. 19–20).

Now: Verse 10 raises the question of Christmas, Easter and Sunday (see the note on vv. 10–11, with its box “Where Christians differ: holy days”). Verses 17–18 describe spiritual manipulation with uncomfortable accuracy, and v. 13 belongs to the reader whose plans have been rerouted by illness.

verseByVerse.quote: Formerly, when you did not know God, you were enslaved to those that by nature are not gods. But now that you have come to know God, or rather to be known by God, how can you turn back again to the weak and worthless elementary principles of the world, whose slaves you want to be once more?
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Galatians were rescued from false gods by the true God, who knew them before they knew him, so to go back into slavery now, under any system, makes no sense.

By nature are not gods. Galatia was crowded with religion: the mother goddess with her ecstatic priests, the imperial cult, the household shrines. The Galatians had been intensely religious and enslaved at the same time, to beings who did not exist as gods (1 Corinthians 8:4–5). A career, a reputation, a body, a bank balance, the approval of a parent: each can be served with the same anxious devotion, demanding more and never saying enough, and each of them too is by nature not a god.

Or rather to be known by God. Paul corrects himself mid-sentence. They do know God now, the sweetest thing about them, but the decisive act was not their discovery; the verb belongs to God. They were known: sought, chosen and drawn before they had turned a single thought toward him.

Known means loved. In Scripture, for God to know a person is for God to set his love on him and claim him: “Before I formed you in the womb I knew you” (Jeremiah 1:5); “You only have I known of all the families of the earth” (Amos 3:2); “if anyone loves God, he is known by God” (1 Corinthians 8:3). Some read it as God merely foreseeing their faith, but that turns Paul’s correction upside down: they came to know God because God first knew them. This is election, God’s free choice to set his love on his people before they chose him (Ephesians 1:4), brought in not as a subject for debate but in passing, to correct and steady them.

Weak and worthless. Weak (asthenēs): they cannot deliver what they demand. Worthless (ptōchos): literally beggarly, with nothing in the account. Going back to the law as a system of righteousness is as much slavery as going back to idols, and both leave a man begging from a pauper.

Whose slaves you want to be once more? Paul will not let them call this mere pressure: somewhere in them, they wanted it. Israel, not long out of Egypt, was already remembering the cucumbers and the melons and forgetting the whips (Numbers 11:5).

He knew us first. “I know my own and my own know me,” Jesus said, and “I lay down my life for the sheep” (John 10:14–15). To be known by God is to be one of those for whom the Shepherd died, the opposite of the most terrible sentence he will ever speak: “I never knew you” (Matthew 7:23). While the Galatians were still carrying offerings to statues that could not see them, the living God had set his love on them and was sending a sick missionary up the road to find them. He has written their names where no beggarly power can erase them.

Where the doctrine earns its keep. If your Christian life began with God knowing you, what holds it up is not your grip on him but his on you. So ask the assurance question the right way round: not, do I know God well enough, but, does God know me? And the evidence that he does is that you are asking at all.

The secular age has not escaped the law. Leaving religion behind does not mean leaving rule-keeping behind. Our culture has its clean and unclean foods, its sacred numbers counted on the wrist, its rituals of self-improvement, its forbidden words, and a public square where one sentence from ten years ago can get a person cast out with no way back. In The Fall the unbelieving Albert Camus has his narrator remark that God is not needed to make us guilty or to punish us: other people, helped by ourselves, are quite enough, and the last judgment happens every day. The old slavery in modern dress: the codes are weak, for none can forgive, and beggarly, for none will ever say you have done enough. The gospel is the one court where the verdict is given before the performance, because the sentence has already been served by someone else.

Why would anyone want to go back? Because slavery feels safe and freedom feels exposed. Under a list you know where you stand; under grace you have nothing to bring and nothing to boast about, which is hard for proud hearts, and the only place where rest is real. A longing for a system that would tell you precisely how good you are is not seriousness but the old slave in you reaching for his chains.

Are idols nothing, or demons? Both, in different senses. The gods the idols represent do not exist as gods; they are by nature not gods. But Paul says elsewhere that what pagans sacrifice they offer to demons and not to God (1 Corinthians 10:20). Behind the empty idol stand real spiritual powers who use the worship of nothing to enslave people (compare v. 3). An idol is a lie with a liar behind it.

parallels.desc: no gods, but the work of men’s hands

verseByVerse.quote: You observe days and months and seasons and years! I am afraid I may have labored over you in vain.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Galatians had begun keeping the Old Testament calendar as something needed to stand right with God, and Paul fears his labour among them is being undone.

You observe days! A Jew raised on that calendar watches Gentile converts take it up, and can hardly speak. The verb, paratēreō, means to observe with anxious care.

The whole year. The four terms most likely map onto the Jewish year: Sabbaths, new moons, the festivals, and the sabbatical years (Colossians 2:16). Not a stray superstition, but the God-given calendar of the Old Testament, taken up as a requirement for righteousness.

The ground, not the observance. Paul attacks not the observance but its ground: the Galatians were taking on the calendar to complete their standing with God. The same act can be worship or slavery, depending on what it is asked to do. Writing to Rome, Paul allows both practices in the same congregation, each fully convinced in his own mind and neither despising the other (Romans 14:5–6), provided neither is made a way of earning standing with God.

Watching the clock after the hour has struck. The whole calendar of Israel had been counting toward the fullness of time (v. 4). To go back to it now is to keep staring at the clock after the guest you were waiting for is sitting at your table.

I am afraid I may have labored over you in vain. Then the mood drops. The man who issued anathemas admits he is frightened, though he does not say they are lost. He has given these towns a great deal, if they are the churches of Acts 14: the stoning at Lystra and the long roads walked twice over (Acts 14:19–23).

The shadows bow to him. All the days and seasons of the old calendar were sketches of one Person: the Sabbath of the rest he gives, the Passover of the Lamb he is, the Day of Atonement of the blood he shed once for all. When the substance has come, the shadows bow to him, and his people gather on the morning of his rising to celebrate that the work is finished, and that the One who rested in the tomb on the Sabbath rose on the first day to make all things new.

Everybody has a calendar. Sunday attendance, the daily reading, the fast in Lent: each can be kept as a son or as a slave (see the note on v. 3), and the cure for the slave is not to try harder but to hear again that Christ has done it all.

So should I keep Sunday differently from other days? Yes, gladly, but as a gift, not a test. The Lord’s Day is the day Christ rose, and his people have gathered on it since the first Easter. Make it the day you meet with the church, hear the word, share the Lord’s Supper, and rest from ordinary work as far as your calling allows. But do not make your way of keeping it the measure of other Christians, or imagine that it puts God in your debt. It is a feast with your Father, not a payment to him.

Does Paul fear that the Galatians are lost? He fears for them; he does not pronounce on them. Some may never have been truly converted, but he writes to them as his little children (v. 19), and his fear is a father’s anguish. Warnings like this are a means God uses to keep his people (compare 5:4): the true child hears and runs back, showing that God’s hold on him was real. Those whom God has truly known he will keep (John 10:28–29), and he keeps them partly by letters like this one.

Where Christians differ: holy days. Some say this verse forbids keeping any special days, Sunday, Christmas or Easter included. Others insist on keeping the Jewish seventh-day Sabbath. Many Reformed Christians, following the Westminster Confession and the 1689 London Baptist Confession, hold that the fourth commandment still binds as the Christian Sabbath, now kept on the Lord’s Day, so that Paul here condemns only the Jewish ceremonial days (Westminster 21.7–8; 1689 22.7–8); they are serious, godly brothers, and their reading deserves respect. This commentary’s view: Paul condemns observing days as a requirement for being right with God, as part of the old covenant law. The Old Testament Sabbath was a shadow fulfilled in Christ (Colossians 2:16–17), who is himself our rest (Matthew 11:28; Hebrews 4:9–10). Gathering on the Lord’s Day, the day of resurrection, is a privilege of the new covenant, not a return to the law (Acts 20:7; Revelation 1:10): Christians gladly set it apart for worship, fellowship and rest, out of joy and wisdom rather than as a binding law with rules about work, and no one may bind another’s conscience about it (Romans 14:5). Christians may also remember Christ’s birth and resurrection, so long as this is not made a means of righteousness or bound on others.

verseByVerse.quote: Brothers, I entreat you, become as I am, for I also have become as you are. You did me no wrong.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul begs them to stand where he stands, on Christ alone, since he gave up all the law had given him in order to stand where they stood.

Brothers, I entreat you. The tone changes: brothers, family. Entreat (deomai) is the verb for begging, the word of a man who has run out of arguments and is simply asking.

Become as I am. More specific than a general appeal to imitate Paul. He was a Jew of impeccable pedigree, circumcised the eighth day, a Pharisee (Philippians 3:5). He had by birth every marker the Judaizers were selling, and he had laid them down, living among Gentiles as a Gentile (1 Corinthians 9:21). So the appeal is: I gave up my law-keeping to stand where you stand, on Christ alone. Do not walk into the room I walked out of.

What it cost him. Writing to Philippi, Paul listed everything he had laid down and said he counted it all as loss, as rubbish, because of the surpassing worth of knowing Christ (Philippians 3:7–8). The word means what you throw out. He wanted only to be found in Christ, not having a righteousness of his own (Philippians 3:9).

You did me no wrong. They treated him well. Anyone saying a hard thing to someone they love is tempted to let personal hurt do the work, because a wound wins arguments. Paul clears his own grievance away, so that they have nothing to react to but the truth.

He became as we are. Paul became as the Galatians were, but he was only following his Lord a long way behind. The Son of God set aside the glory of heaven and became as we are, flesh and blood, under the law, numbered with the transgressors, so that we might become as he is: sons, free, beloved, heirs. Christ did us no wrong, and we did him every wrong, and he still came down to stand where we stood.

What are you holding on to? Some believers are simply spared giving anything up for Christ. But most of us carry something we have never considered laying down: a family standing, a competence we are known for, a record of respectability, a theological rigour that has become an identity. None is wrong to have; every one is fatal to hold on to as what makes you acceptable. Ask what you would lose if it were gone: only the thing itself, or your sense of being acceptable?

How do I raise a hard truth without making it about me? Ask honestly whether you are hurt, and if you are, deal with that before God first, so that it does not leak into the conversation. Then speak about the thing itself in plain words, say that you are not nursing a grievance, and mean it, and make clear that you want their good. And if they are hurt by what you say, do not reach for your own hurt to win the exchange. Let the truth carry its own weight.

verseByVerse.quote: You know it was because of a bodily ailment that I preached the gospel to you at first, and though my condition was a trial to you, you did not scorn or despise me, but received me as an angel of God, as Christ Jesus.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul first came to them ill, and though his condition was hard to look at, they welcomed him as God’s messenger, even as Christ Jesus.

A bodily ailment. The gospel came to Galatia because Paul was ill. It seems something stopped or diverted him, and in that condition he preached, and churches were born. What the illness was, no one knows (see the box below).

Not the obstacle but the mechanism. The illness brought the mission about. Joseph in the pit, Jeremiah in the cistern, John on Patmos, Paul in chains writing the prison letters: God’s habit of building his church out of interrupted plans is nearly the rule.

And though my condition was a trial to you. It was hard to look at. Some saw illness as a sign of demonic attack or divine displeasure, so a visibly sick preacher of God’s favour seemed to contradict his message.

You did not scorn or despise me. The second verb means literally you did not spit out (ekptyō): people spat at the sight of the visibly diseased, to ward off contagion and the evil eye. Hold that beside 3:1: they once refused to treat a sick preacher as cursed, and now someone has looked at them and they are enchanted.

As an angel of God. They treated a sick, unimpressive stranger as God’s messenger, even as Christ Jesus, and in the only sense that matters, he was. “Whoever receives you receives me,” Jesus said (Matthew 10:40).

The world spat on him. The gospel arrived in Galatia carried by a sick man, and it arrived in the world carried by a crucified one: a man of sorrows and acquainted with grief, one from whom men hide their faces (Isaiah 53:3). The world spat on him, literally, and he bore it. Our God has always loved to put his treasure in jars of clay, so that the surpassing power belongs to him and not to us (2 Corinthians 4:7).

Does God really use sickness for good, or is that just something people say? He really does, though never by making the sickness itself good. Illness is part of the curse that Christ came to undo, but God bends even the curse to serve his children (Romans 8:28). Here the evidence is a province of churches; in your case it may be a nurse who watches you trust God, a friendship that would never have happened, or a deepening of faith nothing else could have worked. You may pray for healing, and you should, and seeking good medical care is no failure of faith. And the months you thought were wasted are not.

How should I treat a sick or weak Christian, or a weak preacher? As the Galatians first treated Paul. Do not measure a messenger by his health, polish or charm. Visit the sick, sit with the disabled, listen to the preacher who stammers, and receive Christ’s word through them. God most often works through the weak (1 Corinthians 1:27; 12:22).

Uncertain wording. We do not know what the “bodily ailment” was. Some have suggested malaria caught in the coastal lowlands, which would drive a man up onto the Anatolian plateau where these towns are. Some suggest a disease of the eyes, on the strength of the gouged-out eyes in verse 15 and the large letters of 6:11. Others have thought of the thorn in the flesh of 2 Corinthians 12. Paul does not say, and sick Christians have been the richer for his silence: no one can be told that their affliction is not the kind God uses.
verseByVerse.note: We do not know what the illness was; some think it affected his eyes.

verseByVerse.quote: What then has become of your blessedness? For I testify to you that, if possible, you would have gouged out your eyes and given them to me. Have I then become your enemy by telling you the truth?
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Galatians’ first joy in the gospel has drained away, and the friend who told them the truth is now treated as their enemy.

What then has become of your blessedness? The word (makarismos), from the same root as the Beatitudes’ blessed, is the happiness of people who know they have been given everything. Paul asks not where their doctrine went but where their joy went.

The blessing David spoke of. In Romans Paul writes that David speaks of the blessing of the one to whom God counts righteousness apart from works: “Blessed are those whose lawless deeds are forgiven” (Romans 4:6–7). That was the Galatians’ blessedness, the joy of being forgiven, and it lasts exactly as long as Christ’s work is the ground you stand on. Add law to Christ and forgiveness feels conditional again.

Legalism changes the atmosphere first. The doctrine is still broadly right and the meetings still happen, but the gladness has gone out of the room, replaced by an anxious carefulness everyone mistakes for seriousness. If you want to know whether a church has drifted, do not start with its confession. Start with whether anyone in it looks relieved.

Have I then become your enemy by telling you the truth? A lonely sentence. The word for telling the truth is alētheuōn: truthing, dealing truthfully, the word Paul uses when he tells the church to speak the truth in love (Ephesians 4:15). He has not changed; what has changed is what they are willing to hear, and so the man who loves them most is counted their enemy.

Two things held together. Being treated as the enemy is not proof that you were wrong: Paul is right and unwelcome at the same time. Nor is it proof that you were right: some are treated as enemies because they told the truth, and some because they enjoyed telling it. The test is what Paul does next: he does not withdraw or harden, and within three verses he is calling them “my little children”. Truth-telling that has stopped hurting the one who does it has usually stopped being love (2 Corinthians 2:4).

The truest Friend. Christ told the truth and was made an enemy for it: “He came to his own, and his own people did not receive him” (John 1:11). He did not withdraw, and he did not harden. He prayed for them from the cross, loved us while we counted him our enemy, and made us his friends.

I have lost my joy. Does that mean I have drifted into legalism? Not necessarily. Joy can be dimmed by grief, illness, depression, exhaustion or long trials, and those are not sins; if low mood lingers, talk to a pastor or biblical counsellor, and see your doctor too. But ask one honest question: has my confidence before God become tied to my performance? If you feel accepted only on good weeks, that is very often where the joy has leaked away. Go back to the gospel itself. Read 2:20 and Romans 8:1 slowly and believe them about yourself. Joy grows where grace is believed, not where it is merely agreed with.

What if someone treats me as an enemy for telling them the truth? Check yourself first: were you right, and were you loving? If you were harsh, apologise for the harshness without withdrawing the truth. Then keep loving them, praying for them and keeping the door open. Paul did not stop writing to the Galatians; he wrote them this letter.

Uncertain wording. “You would have gouged out your eyes and given them to me” may be a proverb for giving away what you value most, or a hint that Paul’s ailment affected his eyes (compare 6:11). Either way the point is plain: there was nothing they would not have given him.

verseByVerse.quote: They make much of you, but for no good purpose. They want to shut you out, that you may make much of them. It is always good to be made much of for a good purpose, and not only when I am present with you,
verseByVerse.commentary:
The rival teachers are flattering the Galatians to make them dependent, but true zeal seeks a person’s good and does not fade when the teacher is away.

They make much of you, but for no good purpose. Paul names a technique that has never gone out of use. The verb is zēloō: to court, to pay ardent attention to, as a suitor might. The Judaizers were not bullying the Galatians but flattering them, making them feel worth a long journey.

They want to shut you out. The second move is the point of the first: to exclude the Galatians from Paul and the true fellowship (see the box below), so that they would depend on the teachers and court them in return. The courting is the bait; the shutting out is the hook: a belonging that is always nearly yours and never quite. It works because every heart is hungry to be noticed and approved, and the only safe place for that hunger is the approval that cannot be withdrawn: God’s, given in Christ (3:26).

Two marks of healthy zeal. Verse 18 does not condemn all such attention. The first mark is purpose: what do they want you for? A teacher who wants Christ formed in you will be delighted when you grow past needing him. A teacher who wants you to make much of him will find your independence threatening, and will say so in spiritual language. The second is that it lasts: “not only when I am present with you”. Paul’s own zeal passes that test as he writes: absent, unpopular, and still labouring over them.

Courting for another. Paul uses the suitor’s language of himself too: “I betrothed you to one husband, to present you as a pure virgin to Christ” (2 Corinthians 11:2). The false teachers courted the Galatians for themselves; Paul courts them for Christ, as the friend of the bridegroom, not the bridegroom (John 3:29). And Christ’s zeal for us never switches off when we are out of the room. He does not want us to need him less as we grow, but more, for his is the only love that grows by being leaned on.

The anatomy of manipulation. Spiritual manipulation needs no heretic; it happens wherever a leader’s significance depends on being needed, and it can be sincere. The signs: unusual attention early; a suggestion that you have been seen more clearly here than anywhere else; a group with an inner circle; a standard you are always approaching; a gentle discouragement from friendships or teaching outside the group; and a quiet impression that leaving would be a betrayal.

In everyday life. You need no one’s inner circle, because the Father has already made you his child (3:26). So look at your own zeal: is there someone you have been warm to only while they were useful to you? Send them a message this week that asks nothing back.

What it does not mean. Not that warm attention is always manipulative, or that a church that welcomes newcomers eagerly is suspect. Watch where the attention is leading: toward Christ and the wider body of his people, or toward one leader and one group.

I think I may be in a group like this. What should I do? Test it against Scripture and wise believers outside it. Am I free to hear other faithful teachers and have Christian friends elsewhere? Is my standing with God tied, openly or quietly, to my loyalty here? Would leaving be treated as sin? If the answers worry you, talk to a trusted pastor or mature Christian from another church. You do not owe a group your conscience; you owe that to Christ. And if there is abuse, spiritual or otherwise, it must never be tolerated or covered: seek help, and if a crime has been committed, report it.

How do I make sure I am not the one doing this? Are you glad when the people you help grow, find other teachers and need you less? Do you speak well of other faithful churches, and keep loving those who disagree or move on? If you lead, invite others to examine your influence. The aim of all ministry is that people make much of Christ, not of us (John 3:30).

Uncertain wording. Paul does not say what the teachers want to shut the Galatians out from. Most take it as shutting them out from Paul and from the fellowship of those who hold his gospel; others think of being shut out from Christ and his grace (compare 5:4), or from the circle of those the teachers counted fully obedient, until they conformed. The likely sense joins the first and the last: cut off from their true teacher, they would be left outside a door only the new teachers could open. Verse 18 is compressed too, but its point is clear: good zeal does not depend on Paul being in the room.

verseByVerse.quote: my little children, for whom I am again in the anguish of childbirth until Christ is formed in you! I wish I could be present with you now and change my tone, for I am perplexed about you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul is in anguish over them like a mother in labour, and he will not rest until Christ himself takes shape in their lives.

My little children. The anger drops out of the letter, and what is left is a parent. The tender address comes at the point where he has the least reason to be tender (see the textual note below).

In the anguish of childbirth. Elsewhere he is their father (1 Corinthians 4:15); here he is their mother in labour: ōdinō, the word for birth pangs. He went through it once to bring them to birth, and now a second time.

Until Christ is formed in you! Not until they see he was right. The verb is morphoō, to take shape, from the same root as “conformed to the image of his Son” (Romans 8:29): something taking its proper shape from the inside, like a child in the womb. The aim is not that they look like Paul, or keep the law, but that they look like Christ (2 Corinthians 3:18).

Change my tone. He knows how the letter sounds. He is not withdrawing the anathemas, but he would give a great deal to be in the room, because a voice can soften and a letter cannot.

For I am perplexed about you. At a loss, without a way through (aporoumai). The apostle who has just settled the doctrine of justification does not know what to do about these people: a mercy to anyone praying for someone who has drifted, for certainty about the truth and bewilderment about a person can go together.

He does not abandon them in the womb. Out of the anguish of his soul the Servant shall see and be satisfied (Isaiah 53:11): Christ laboured on the cross to bring a people to birth, and he does not abandon them in the womb. By his Spirit he is being formed in us now, slowly, through every trial and every Sunday, and when he appears we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is (1 John 3:2).

The metric of ministry. A church can be strong in attendance, giving and doctrine while Christ is no more formed in it than a decade ago. Paul’s measure is brutal in its simplicity: do these people look more like Jesus than they did? A ministry that produces admirers, partisans or well-informed critics of other churches has produced something, but not this.

What it does not mean. Not that they needed to be born again a second time; the new birth happens once (John 3:3–8; 1 Peter 1:23). Paul’s labour now is for their growth.

What does Christ formed in me actually look like? It looks like the fruit Paul names in the next chapter: love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness, self-control (5:22–23). It looks like humility that does not need to be noticed, readiness to forgive, love for the unlovely, and delight in the Father. It does not come by willpower. The Spirit forms Christ in us through the word, prayer, the Lord’s Supper, the fellowship of the church and the daily trials God sends. It is usually slow, often invisible to the person himself, and very often seen first by others.

I am praying for someone who has drifted, and I do not know what to do. Then you are where Paul was. Pray specifically that Christ would be formed in them, not merely that they would return to church or agree with you. Keep the relationship warm. Say the truth when there is an opportunity, in person rather than in a long message if you can. And leave the outcome with God. Paul was at a loss, and God still had the Galatians in hand.

Textual note. Many early manuscripts read teknia, little children, which would be the only time Paul uses that tender word; others read tekna, children, the reading most modern editions print. Either way the tenderness is unmistakable.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 21–31 — Hagar and Sarah: Two Covenants
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Scripture itself shows that the heirs are the children of promise, not the children of human effort, and that believers are those free children. Abraham had two sons: Ishmael by the slave Hagar, born by human arrangement, and Isaac by the free Sarah, born through promise (vv. 21–23). The two mothers stand for two covenants: Sinai and the present Jerusalem, in slavery; and the Jerusalem above, free, whose barren house God fills with children (vv. 24–27). Believers are Isaac’s kind, and should expect Isaac’s kind of opposition (vv. 28–29). Law-keeping and grace cannot share the inheritance: the slave woman must go, and we are children of the free woman (vv. 30–31).
verseByVerse.theology:
Typology, and Why the Two Covenants Cannot Share a House

Verse 24 is not allegory of the kind that dissolves history but typology: reading real events as God-given patterns that point to Christ (see the note on vv. 24–25).

Verses 24–25 give the test for the whole section: what a covenant produces shows what kind of covenant it is, when it is used as a way of salvation. And v. 30 shows why grace and merit cannot be mixed, and that Paul casts out a system, not persons (see the note on vv. 30–31).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The Judaizers presented themselves as Abraham’s true heirs. Verse 22 shows that physical descent was never the mark, and v. 29 explains why religious men were persecuting a Gentile church (see the note on vv. 28–29).

Now: Verse 23 touches most of us (see “Hagar’s tent” in the note on vv. 21–23), and v. 29 warns us about what rises in us when someone else is blessed (see the note on vv. 28–29).

verseByVerse.quote: Tell me, you who desire to be under the law, do you not listen to the law? For it is written that Abraham had two sons, one by a slave woman and one by a free woman. But the son of the slave was born according to the flesh, while the son of the free woman was born through promise.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The law the Galatians want to live under tells a story against them: Abraham had two sons, one produced by human effort and one given by God’s promise.

Tell me, you who desire to be under the law, do you not listen to the law? You want the law? Then let us read it, and see that the Judaizers have been quoting a book they have not understood. The second “law” means the Torah, the five books of Moses as a whole, not the commandments as a code: Paul is going to Genesis.

In the flow. Verse 21 begins the last doctrinal argument of the letter, gathering every thread: Abraham and his true children (3:6–9, 29), promise against law (3:15–18), the slave and the son (4:1–7), flesh against Spirit (3:3). It leads straight into 5:1: Christ has set us free for freedom.

For it is written that Abraham had two sons. Ishmael by the slave woman Hagar, Isaac by his free wife Sarah (Genesis 16; 21). Physical descent from Abraham cannot be the qualification, because Ishmael had it: he was Abraham’s son, circumcised by Abraham’s own hand (Genesis 17:23–25), and outside the covenant line. Descent by blood never made an heir, and the family tree proves it before you have left Genesis.

One by a slave woman and one by a free woman. A child born to a slave was a slave (see Slavery in the Ancient World); a child born to the free wife was the heir.

Born according to the flesh. Verse 23 gives the real distinction: how each son came to exist. Ishmael was produced by a plan. God had promised Abraham a son; ten years passed (Genesis 16:3); Sarah did the arithmetic on her own body, concluded that God needed help, and offered her slave (Genesis 16:1–4). It was legal, customary, and it worked. “According to the flesh” here means not immorality but competence: human ability acting on God’s behalf, because waiting had become unbearable.

Born through promise. Isaac was produced by nothing at all. Sarah was ninety and past every natural possibility, and she had laughed at the announcement (Genesis 18:10–14). There was a promise, and then, at the time God had said, there was a baby (Genesis 21:1–2). “Is anything too hard for the LORD?” God asked. That is the question of the whole letter.

Children of promise in the Son of promise. Through Isaac shall your offspring be named (Genesis 21:12), and that offspring is Christ (3:16). So believers are children of promise like Isaac (4:28) because they are Christ’s (3:29). And the question asked at the tent door was answered again at Nazareth: “nothing will be impossible with God” (Luke 1:37).

A child who should have been impossible. Nobody arranged your new birth; nobody could have. The God who gave a son to a woman of ninety gave life to your dead heart, so that no one could mistake whose child you are. He gives life to the dead and calls into existence the things that do not exist (Romans 4:17), and every Christian is, like Isaac, a child who should have been impossible, and a cause of laughter and joy.

Hagar’s tent. Everyone believes God can save; the question is whether he needs our help. The Galatians were not abandoning Christ but proposing to assist him. The instinct is universal, and it usually looks like responsibility: the outcome you are engineering, by means you would rather not examine, because God is taking too long. That is Hagar’s tent. It is usually not wickedness but Sarah with a calendar, right about the arithmetic and wrong about God.

So is it wrong to plan, or to work hard? No. Abraham’s fault was not that he acted, but that he acted to secure by his own means what God had promised to give in his own way, and by a means God had not approved. Christians are to work, plan, save, seek medical help and use every lawful means, in faith, as God’s gifts, not in place of faith. A good test is whether the plan requires you to bend God’s commands. Sarah’s plan did, and it filled the tent with grief for a generation (Genesis 16:4–6; 21:9–11).
verseByVerse.note: Abraham’s son by the slave woman Hagar was Ishmael; his son by the free woman Sarah was Isaac, born by promise.

verseByVerse.quote: Now this may be interpreted allegorically: these women are two covenants. One is from Mount Sinai, bearing children for slavery; she is Hagar. Now Hagar is Mount Sinai in Arabia; she corresponds to the present Jerusalem, for she is in slavery with her children.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Hagar and Sarah stand for two covenants, and Hagar stands for Sinai: the law, used as a way to be accepted by God, can bear only slaves.

Now this may be interpreted allegorically. The verb is allēgoreō: to speak another way, figuratively. In Paul’s century, Alexandrian interpreters, Philo above all, read the Old Testament in a way that dissolved the history: Abraham became the soul, Sarah virtue. If Paul is doing that, any text can mean anything.

The history is his premise. But it is not what he is doing. He has just insisted that it is written that Abraham had two sons, and he treats the mothers and the manner of each birth as facts. It happened, and God so arranged it that it carries a meaning the coming of Christ has now made visible, as the risen Christ interpreted in all the Scriptures the things concerning himself (Luke 24:27). If God governs history, the pattern in a true story is not something a reader imposes; it is something the Author put there.

These women are two covenants. Two arrangements by which people seek to stand before God, and the two families they produce: at Sinai, a law to be kept; with Abraham, a promise to be believed (Genesis 15:18; Exodus 24:7–8). To a first-century Jew it was shocking: Hagar, the Egyptian slave who was sent away, is Sinai.

Now Hagar is Mount Sinai in Arabia. However the link is made (see the boxes below), the heart of it is the pattern: a slave mother, a covenant leading to slavery, children born into it.

The present Jerusalem. The city and temple, the visible centre of the religion the Judaizers were selling, which had rejected Christ and clung to the law. In four clauses Paul puts the Jerusalem establishment on Hagar’s side of the family, and the Galatians on Sarah’s. A system that demands performance, used as a way of salvation, can only produce people in bondage, however holy the mountain it came from.

The Son who climbed it for us. Sinai thundered, and the people trembled and could not draw near. But Christ went up a different hill, outside the present Jerusalem, and bore the curse that Sinai pronounced. A covenant that bears children for slavery cannot set them free. Their freedom comes from the Son, “born under the law, to redeem those who were under the law” (vv. 4–5): he kept the law and bore its curse, so that whoever trusts him, Jew or Gentile, is a son. The law shows us the mountain we cannot climb; the gospel shows us the Son who climbed it for us.

What it does not mean. Not that Jewish people are rejected by God. The present Jerusalem means the system of law-keeping the false teachers offered, not the Jewish people as a race. Paul grieved for his own people with great sorrow and unceasing anguish (Romans 9:1–3). Any reading of this verse that feeds contempt for Jewish people has turned Paul’s own heart upside down.

Was the covenant at Sinai a bad thing, then? No. God gave it, and it was holy and good (Romans 7:12). It began with grace: “I am the LORD your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of slavery” (Exodus 20:2). Its sacrifices pointed to Christ, and believers like David were justified by faith under it (Romans 4:6–8). But it was for a time of childhood (vv. 1–3), keeping Israel under strict rules until Christ came (3:23–24). It could command but could not give the Spirit or a new heart (3:21; Jeremiah 31:31–33). Hagar stands for Sinai clung to after Christ has come, as the way to be accepted by God: the law cut off from the promise it was meant to serve.

How can I tell whether my church is a Hagar church or a Sarah church? Not by the strictness of its morals, for the free children of God love his law, but by what people are trusting. Is the gospel of Christ’s finished work preached clearly and often, so that sinners leave knowing they are forgiven? Do people confess sins honestly, or only hide them? Are newcomers with messy pasts welcomed as fully as long-standing members? Is obedience urged as the fruit of grace, or as the price of acceptance? A free church is serious about holiness but not anxious about standing.

Where Christians differ: allegory in interpretation. Some use this passage to justify reading allegories into all of Scripture, finding hidden meanings unrelated to the plain sense. This commentary’s view: Paul’s method here is closer to typology, reading real people and events as patterns God built in to point forward to Christ, than to free allegory. He does not deny the history; he sees in it what God designed it to show (1 Corinthians 10:6, 11). Interpreters should first grasp the plain meaning of a text, and find further meanings only where Scripture itself warrants them. Paul, writing under inspiration, had that warrant; later interpreters must stay within what Scripture teaches.

Uncertain wording. “Hagar is Mount Sinai in Arabia” is one of the most compressed sentences in the letter, and exactly how Paul joins the two is not certain. Hagar’s descendants through Ishmael settled in Arabia (Genesis 25:12–18), where Sinai lies, so the slave mother and the mountain of the law belong to the same region, outside the land of promise. Some have suggested a play on an Arabic word for rock that sounds like Hagar’s name, but that is a guess. The likely meaning is the plainer one: Hagar and Sinai belong together, by place and above all by pattern.

Textual note. Some manuscripts read “For Sinai is a mountain in Arabia”, without Hagar’s name. The point of the passage is the same either way.

verseByVerse.quote: But the Jerusalem above is free, and she is our mother. For it is written, “Rejoice, O barren one who does not bear; break forth and cry aloud, you who are not in labor! For the children of the desolate one will be more than those of the one who has a husband.”
verseByVerse.commentary:
Believers belong to the free Jerusalem above, their true mother, and God is keeping his promise to the barren woman by filling her house with children.

But the Jerusalem above is free. The Galatians had been made to feel provincial, their membership depending on a committee far away. Their mother lives elsewhere: the heavenly Jerusalem. Believers have already come to it (Hebrews 12:22); John sees her coming down out of heaven, prepared as a bride (Revelation 21:2). Our citizenship is already registered there (Philippians 3:20).

And she is our mother. This is why the early church could call the church a mother: not because she gives grace of herself, but because God brings his children to birth within her through the word and Spirit, and feeds and raises them there.

Rejoice, O barren one. The quotation is Isaiah 54:1. In its own setting the barren one is Zion in exile, emptied of her children, and God tells her to start singing before there is anything visible to sing about, because the children are coming. The verse comes immediately after Isaiah 53, where the suffering servant, whom the New Testament names as Jesus (Acts 8:32–35), makes many to be accounted righteous: the barren woman is told to sing because of what the servant has just done.

The children of the desolate one. Paul sees this fulfilled first in Sarah, decades with an empty tent while Hagar had a son; and then in the church, a small, mostly Gentile movement that would out-populate the establishment that despised it. It has, in thousands of languages.

The God of barren women. Sarah, Rebekah, Rachel, Hannah, Elizabeth: the line of promise runs straight through barren women, so that when the child finally comes nobody can mistake where he came from. “The barren has borne seven,” sang Hannah (1 Samuel 2:5). God waits until there is nothing left to explain it, and then he fills the tent.

Bought by his suffering. The barren woman’s children were bought by the Servant’s suffering. He was crushed, and the empty tent filled, and is filling still, with children from every tribe and tongue and people and nation.

In everyday life. When you feel small or excluded from the people who seem to matter, remember your address, and live as a citizen of the free city above: unafraid of committees, generous, glad.

A word for a particular reader. Some woman reading this is barren, has been told to rejoice by people who meant well, and it landed like a stone. The text does not ask her to pretend. Isaiah’s command is addressed to a woman whose grief is real and whose situation has not changed, and it rests not on optimism but on God’s promise. Scripture never asks anyone to feel that a loss is not a loss. It does say that the emptiness God leaves in a life for a while is not his verdict on that life.

What it does not mean. Not that the church replaces Israel entirely. Jewish believers are part of the Jerusalem above too, from Peter and Paul to the present day. Christians differ on God’s purposes for the Jewish people as a nation (Romans 11:25–29), but agree that there is one family of Abraham, and that no one enters it except through Christ.

Does this promise that God will give me children? Not as a guarantee of a pregnancy. Isaiah 54 is a promise to God’s people as a whole, fulfilled in the gathering of the church. It is right to pray for children, and God sometimes gives them after long barrenness; but many faithful believers never have children, and they are not less blessed or less fruitful. In Christ the childless are given spiritual sons and daughters, a name better than sons and daughters (Isaiah 56:4–5), and a family in the church. Your fruitfulness in God’s kingdom does not depend on your womb.

parallels.desc: sing, O barren one, who did not bear

verseByVerse.quote: Now you, brothers, like Isaac, are children of promise. But just as at that time he who was born according to the flesh persecuted him who was born according to the Spirit, so also it is now.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Believers are children of promise, like Isaac, and like him they should expect hostility from those who rely on what they can produce.

Like Isaac. First, the assurance: not candidates, not probationers, but Isaac, the miracle child nobody could have produced.

Just as at that time. The reference is Genesis 21:9. On the day Isaac was weaned Abraham threw a feast, and Sarah saw Ishmael laughing, a play on Isaac’s own name, Yitzchaq, he laughs. Ishmael was most likely mocking the child at the party held in his honour. Paul calls it persecution: the older brother, produced by human arrangement, could not bear the child who was pure gift. “Born according to the Spirit” means that Isaac was born by God’s power, as every believer is born again.

So also it is now. The people persecuting the Galatian churches were not pagans. They were religious men with a claim to Abraham, and what they could not tolerate was a family they had not qualified for.

Why grace provokes rage. Free grace writes off a lifetime’s investment: if the Gentile who believed last month is as accepted as the Pharisee who has kept the calendar for forty years, the forty years bought nothing. Nobody hears that calmly. The elder brother in the parable is furious at exactly this, and he never once says an untrue thing about himself (Luke 15:29–30).

Mocked at his own feast. The child of promise was mocked at his own feast, and centuries later the true Son of promise was mocked at his: they clothed him in purple, bowed to him in jest, spat on him and laughed. The flesh has always hated the gift, but it cannot stop the inheritance passing to the heir. Paul knew this from the inside: he had been violently persecuting the church of God (1:13), until the risen Christ asked, “Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?” (Acts 9:4). The hostility of self-made religion toward the children of the Spirit is aimed, in the end, at Christ himself (John 15:18, 20), and he counts every blow as struck at him.

A comfort and a warning. A comfort: hostility from religious people is not evidence that you have gone wrong; it begins at a child’s birthday party in Genesis. And a warning, the more useful one. Watch what rises in you when someone is blessed without earning it: the radiant convert with the disgraceful history, the newcomer given what you waited years for. That flicker of resentment is the Ishmael in us, recognising the child of promise and resenting him for it.

How do I know which son I am? Both sons were Abraham’s, both lived in the same tent, both were circumcised, and nobody watching could have told which line the promise was attached to. The difference was not sincerity or effort but where each son came from. So ask what you are actually resting on; the answer surfaces fastest at the extremes. After a good stretch, does your confidence before God quietly rise, and after a bad one, fall? Then, whatever you believe on paper, that confidence is Hagar’s, produced by you. If yours moves a little, as most do, the answer is not despair but to rest again on Christ.

You are being told your name. The test is not, have I enough faith? That sends a man inside himself to weigh a quality he never can. Isaac did not qualify by being a better baby. If you are resting on what Christ has done, you are not being told to work up assurance. You are being told your name.

What does persecution from religious people look like today? Rarely violence in the West, though elsewhere it can be; more often mockery, suspicion and exclusion: being called careless about holiness because you preach free grace; being treated as second-class because you do not keep a group’s extra rules; being shut out of fellowship for questioning a leader. Do not exaggerate ordinary disagreement into persecution, and do not assume every critic is an Ishmael; sometimes your critics are right. But when you are opposed for trusting Christ alone, recognise the old pattern and take heart.

verseByVerse.quote: But what does the Scripture say? “Cast out the slave woman and her son, for the son of the slave woman shall not inherit with the son of the free woman.” So, brothers, we are not children of the slave but of the free woman.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Grace and law-keeping cannot share the inheritance, so the system of earning must go, and believers are the free children of promise.

But what does the Scripture say? Paul stops arguing and lets the text pronounce, and he chooses the hardest sentence in the chapter.

Cast out the slave woman. It is Genesis 21:10, and in Genesis it is Sarah who says it, apparently in anger, and the thing is very displeasing to Abraham (Genesis 21:11). What makes it Scripture rather than a domestic quarrel is verse 12, where God tells Abraham to do as Sarah says: “through Isaac shall your offspring be named.” The line of promise must not be confused with the line of human arrangement.

What is to be cast out? Paul applies the verse not to persons but to the two covenants he has been contrasting. What cannot stay is the system: law-keeping as the ground of acceptance, sitting alongside the gospel as a supplementary option. The Galatians were trying to keep both mothers in the house. That is impossible, not because grace is intolerant, but because the two produce different children, and only one inherits. So the Galatians should cast out the false teachers’ message, and refuse its teachers the authority to shape the church.

Not a mixture but a failure. Add merit to grace and you do not get a moderate position; you get merit, because the moment my performance is part of the ground, the whole weight has shifted onto it. Otherwise grace would no longer be grace (Romans 11:6). A little law as the basis of standing is like a little water in petrol. It is not a mixture. It is a failure.

Not children of the slave. The chapter lands on an identity, not a warning, and the pronoun is we: Paul puts himself in the sentence. Chapter 5 is built on it: “For freedom Christ has set us free” (5:1).

The son remains for ever. Jesus laid down the same household law: the slave does not remain in the house for ever; the son remains for ever, so if the Son sets you free, you will be free indeed (John 8:34–36). The only Son who ever had that standing by right laid it down, was counted with the slaves, and was cast out to suffer outside the gate (Hebrews 13:12), so that the children of the slave woman could be brought in as heirs. Isaac kept the inheritance because Ishmael was sent away; we keep ours because the true Son was sent away in our place. Scripture says of the slave’s son, “Cast out”; the Son says of everyone the Father gives him, “whoever comes to me I will never cast out” (John 6:37). The door of the Father’s house has closed behind us, not in front of us.

What it does not mean. Not cruelty to people. Paul casts out a doctrine; he spends the surrounding verses in labour pains for the people who hold it. To quote verse 30 to justify hardness with a person is to read the sentence and miss the chapter. Genesis itself handles Ishmael tenderly: God hears the boy crying in the desert and is with him as he grows (Genesis 21:17–20). Scripture is more tender than our use of it.

How do I cast out the slave woman in my own heart? By refusing, every day, to let your performance become the ground of your standing with God. When you have a good day, do not let it make you feel more accepted; thank God for the grace that helped you. When you have a bad day, do not let it make you feel less accepted; confess it, and rest again on Christ. Throw out the inner ledger. Then obey, gladly, because the free son loves his Father’s house and his Father’s ways.

Does this mean my church should expel people who hold wrong views? Not on the strength of this verse alone. Paul’s target is a false gospel that adds works to Christ for justification, which he has already called accursed (1:8–9). A church must not let it be taught from its pulpit, nor give authority to teachers who persist in it after patient correction (Titus 3:10). But most disagreements among Christians are not about the ground of salvation, and they are to be borne with in love. And even those who are put out of fellowship are to be prayed for and pursued, with the aim of their restoration (2 Thessalonians 3:14–15).

parallels.desc: cast out this slave woman with her son
