keyVerse.quote: But when the fullness of time had come, God sent forth his Son, born of woman, born under the law, to redeem those who were under the law, so that we might receive adoption as sons.
keyVerse.note: These verses are the hinge of the chapter: everything before them is waiting under guardians, and everything after them is sonship. God sent his own Son into our condition, under the very law that held us, to buy us out and bring us into his family. The Spirit (v. 6) and the inheritance (v. 7) both flow from this one sending.

4.reflection:
Paul says believers were once like heirs under age, owners of everything yet living like slaves (vv. 1–7). In what ways do you still relate to God more like a hired servant than a son or daughter? What difference would it make to begin your prayers, as the Spirit teaches, with “Father”?

The Galatians were taking up good, God-given practices as a way to stand right with God (vv. 9–10). Which good habits in your life could turn from a gift into a quota? How would you be able to tell?

The Galatians came to treat Paul as their enemy for telling them the truth (v. 16), while flattering teachers won them over (v. 17). How can we tell loving truth from flattery, and how should we respond when a friend tells us something hard?

Paul longs for Christ to be formed in the Galatians (v. 19) and reminds them that they are children of promise, like Isaac (v. 28). Where are you tempted, like Sarah, to arrange by your own effort what God has promised to give? What would it look like to wait on him instead?

5.title: For Freedom Christ Has Set Us Free: The Spirit and the Flesh
5.overview:
Where we are. Chapters 1–4 have argued that a sinner is right with God through faith in Christ alone. Chapter 5 draws the conclusion and turns argument into life, leading into the church’s life together in chapter 6.

The message. Christ has set you free, so do not go back into slavery by adding anything to him; and do not turn your freedom into licence either, but use it to serve one another in love. The Spirit, not the law, is God’s answer to the flesh: freedom produces not moral chaos but something better than law-keeping ever could, a life that fulfils the law from the inside.

Why it was said. The Galatians were on the point of accepting circumcision, offered to them as a fuller belonging (see the introduction). Behind it lay a fear: without the law, would grace not let people do as they liked? Meanwhile the congregations were biting and devouring one another over how to be holy (v. 15).

How the chapter makes its case. First, stand firm (vv. 1–12): to add circumcision to Christ is to lose Christ and grace, for what counts is faith working through love (vv. 2–6), and Paul will not take the offence out of the cross (vv. 7–12). Then, what freedom is for (vv. 13–15): serving one another in love, the goal the whole law was aiming at. Last, how such a life is possible (vv. 16–26): walk by the Spirit, who is at war with the flesh. The flesh produces many works that tear a community apart; the Spirit grows one fruit, a single character, which no law forbids (vv. 19–23). Those who belong to Christ have crucified the flesh and keep in step with the Spirit (vv. 24–26).

Where it leads. Every part of the chapter rests on Christ: the Liberator who carried the law’s yoke and bore its curse, so that it would never be laid on us; the stumbling stone whose cross leaves nothing for us to add; the one man who loved his neighbour as himself, and then more than himself. And the nine words of the Spirit’s fruit, read slowly, make up his face: the Spirit is making ordinary believers like the Son.

For us. Ask what you add after “Christ, and…” when you wonder where you stand with God, and cross it out. Then spend your freedom on someone else, do not be surprised by the fight within, and let the Spirit grow, slowly, what you could never manufacture.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Christ has set you free, so do not trade that freedom for a yoke by adding anything to him. Verse 1 sums up four chapters. Verses 2–6 show the cost of accepting circumcision as what completes your standing: Christ is of no advantage, the whole law is owed, and grace is abandoned; but believers wait by faith, through the Spirit, for the hope of righteousness, and what counts is faith working through love. Then Paul appeals (vv. 7–12): someone cut in on their race, this teaching is not from the God who calls them, and a little of it changes the whole. Yet he is confident in the Lord about them, leaves the troubler to God, and will not remove the offence of the cross.
verseByVerse.theology:
Freedom as the Goal of Redemption, and What Falling from Grace Means

Gospel freedom is freedom from performance-based religion, the liberty to live as sons rather than as slaves calculating wages. It is not lawlessness: the law’s moral demands are fulfilled from within by those who walk by the Spirit, rather than imposed from outside on those who must earn their standing.

Verse 4 describes a change of position, not of conduct, and is best read beside v. 10 (see the note on v. 4).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Circumcision was offered to the Galatians as an upgrade, a fuller belonging. Verses 2–3 show it was an exchange: Christ given up for the whole law. Verse 12 would have struck hard locally (see the note on vv. 10–12).

Now: Standing firm (v. 1) is mostly a matter of how you answer one question (see “What standing firm looks like” in the note on v. 1), and v. 8 gives a test for any new teaching (see the note on vv. 7–9).

verseByVerse.quote: For freedom Christ has set us free; stand firm therefore, and do not submit again to a yoke of slavery.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Christ set us free so that we would live free, so hold your ground and let no one put the yoke back on. Four chapters of argument are compressed here into the line the letter is remembered by.

For freedom Christ has set us free. Why say freedom twice? Because freedom is what Christ’s rescue is for: not a stage on the way to something else, nor a probationary liberty, nor a transfer to a stricter and more mature religion. He released his people because he wanted them free.

Free from what, and free for what? Free from the law as a way of righteousness, from its curse (3:13), from the guardians and the elementary principles (4:1–9), from sin’s slavery, and from the endless anxious question of whether you have done enough. And free for God: to call him Father, to obey him from the heart, to love your neighbour without calculating. Many Christians treat grace as the doorway and law as the corridor beyond it: saved by grace, they say, and then describe a daily life in which everything depends on their performance. Paul says the door and the corridor are made of the same thing: “As you received Christ Jesus the Lord, so walk in him” (Colossians 2:6).

Stand firm therefore. Stand fast, as a soldier holds his position. Left alone, a free man drifts back toward slavery, because slavery is restful in a way that liberty is not: a slave is told what to do and knows exactly where he stands. Freedom asks you to live without a scoreboard, and that can feel harder than obedience.

Again. Do not submit: the verb is passive, do not let yourselves be subjected. Nobody was going to force the Galatians; they were going to agree, for reasons that felt like devotion. And again is the sharpest word in the sentence, because these Gentiles had never been under Moses in their lives. A return to law-keeping would land them back where their paganism had them: performing, appeasing, never sure.

A yoke of slavery. A yoke was the wooden frame laid across the shoulders of working animals, a picture of burden and servitude. The rabbis called the law’s yoke a glad discipline; Peter, at the Jerusalem council, called it a yoke “that neither our fathers nor we have been able to bear” (Acts 15:10). Jesus also offers a yoke: “Take my yoke upon you, and learn from me, for I am gentle and lowly in heart… For my yoke is easy, and my burden is light” (Matthew 11:29–30). So the question is never whether a man will wear a yoke, but whose.

The yoke he carried. The Son of God took the yoke of the law on his own shoulders, carried it the whole way without stumbling, and then bore its curse on a cross, so that the beam would never be laid on ours again. The only yoke he lays on us now is his own, shaped by the hands of a carpenter who is gentle and lowly in heart.

What standing firm looks like. On a Wednesday, it mostly means refusing to answer one question the way your instincts want to: “Where do I stand with God today?” The instinctive answer reaches for the last few days: how you prayed, how you spoke to your wife, whether you did the thing you promised yourself you would stop doing. The week matters a great deal, but it is not the ground you stand on, and the day you let it become the ground, the yoke is back on your shoulders and nobody had to put it there.

Is it legalism to keep personal rules, like not drinking or fasting on Fridays? Not in itself. A Christian may freely adopt a rule for wisdom’s sake: to avoid a temptation, to discipline the body, to serve a weaker brother (Romans 14:21; 1 Corinthians 9:27). It becomes a yoke of slavery when you think keeping it makes you more acceptable to God, or bind it on other Christians as though God had commanded it. Hold it loosely, and never use it to measure the brother who does not keep it.
verseByVerse.note: A yoke was the wooden frame joining working animals — a picture of burdensome obligation.

verseByVerse.quote: Look: I, Paul, say to you that if you accept circumcision, Christ will be of no advantage to you. I testify again to every man who accepts circumcision that he is obligated to keep the whole law.
verseByVerse.commentary:
To accept circumcision as what completes your standing with God is to give up Christ and take on the whole law instead.

Look: I, Paul, say to you. Paul puts his name, and the whole weight of his apostleship (chapters 1–2), on what comes next.

Of no advantage. Not less advantage. None. Yet circumcision is a small thing, a rite God himself commanded, which counts for nothing either way (v. 6). The issue is what it is being asked to do. A man who accepts it as the thing that completes his standing with God has not added a little security to Christ; he has changed systems. And in that system Christ is not an asset, because it does not deal in gifts but in obligations. You cannot have Christ as a partial Saviour.

Obligated to keep the whole law. Verse 3 closes the escape route. The Judaizers were selling one item, and Paul says there is no such thing: take hold of a corner of the law and you have taken hold of all of it (James 2:10), for life, without a single failure. Nobody mentioned that in the sales pitch, and no one has ever kept it, except the one man who kept it for those who could not (4:4–5).

But Paul circumcised Timothy. A fair objection, and his opponents were evidently raising it (v. 11). Paul circumcised Timothy (Acts 16:3) yet refused to let Titus be circumcised (2:3), because the cases are opposite in everything that matters. In Jerusalem the demand for Titus was made as a condition, to prove that a Gentile could not be fully accepted otherwise, and Paul did not yield for a moment. Timothy’s mother was Jewish, so to the synagogues he would have counted as a Jew left uncircumcised, and every door Paul wanted to preach behind would have shut. That was about gaining a hearing, not gaining standing. One question governed Paul: is anyone claiming this is necessary? When nobody is, he is flexible to the point of inconvenience; the moment somebody says “you must”, he will not move an inch. The same principle governs many secondary practices in church life.

What would circumcision be today? Anything added to Christ as a condition of being right with God: a particular experience, a style of worship, a political position, a level of Bible knowledge, a list of things good Christians do not do, a baptism in the right church, a feeling of being sorry enough. Any of these can be good, or a matter of conviction. The moment it becomes Christ and something, it becomes Christ of no advantage. Ask of any teaching: does it leave Christ standing alone as my whole righteousness?

In everyday life. Finish this sentence honestly: “I am right with God because Christ died and rose for me, and because I ...” If anything comes after the “and”, cross it out. Then live today out of the first half alone, and do your good works as a thank you, not as a down payment.

May Christians circumcise their sons today, for health or family reasons? Yes. Neither circumcision nor uncircumcision counts for anything (v. 6); what is forbidden is circumcision as a requirement for being accepted by God. A Jewish Christian parent may circumcise his son as a mark of his heritage; no one may make it a condition of salvation.

verseByVerse.quote: You are severed from Christ, you who would be justified by the law; you have fallen away from grace.
verseByVerse.commentary:
To seek to be right with God by the law is to step off the ground of grace, where alone Christ saves. Paul is describing a change of position, not a moral fall.

Severed from Christ. This verse frightens people, and the reader most likely to be holding it is not a Judaizer but a Christian who has had a bad year. So look at what it says. In ordinary speech, to fall from grace is to disgrace yourself. But these people have not fallen into sin; they have become more religious, keeping a calendar and considering a rite in order to please God more thoroughly. Paul cannot mean a moral collapse.

Two changes of position. Both halves of the sentence describe where a person stands, not how he behaves. Severed (katargeō) means cut off, so that Christ’s work no longer benefits you, and it applies to “you who would be justified by the law”. Justification is acquittal: guilt removed and the believer counted right with God, though not made sinless on the spot (Romans 4:5). Its only ground is Christ, received by faith. Fallen away means falling out of grace as out of a place, off the ground where Christ does his work and onto the ground of law.

The lifeboat. Think of a man in a lifeboat who decides to swim alongside it, still holding the rope. He has not stopped believing in the boat; he has stopped being in it. Paul is not saying God has thrown the Galatians out, but that standing on the law does not add to Christ’s work; it replaces it.

Hold it beside verse 10. Six verses later, to the same people, Paul says: “I have confidence in the Lord that you will take no other view.” So verse 4 is not a verdict passed on the Galatians but the warning that will keep them from the thing described, and it works by being heard.

Grace has a name. Grace is not a policy in heaven but Christ himself, given for us. Severed from Christ and fallen away from grace are one loss: “the grace of God has appeared, bringing salvation” (Titus 2:11), and it appeared in a person. The boat in the picture is the Son of God, “who loved me and gave himself for me” (2:20), and his is the righteousness Paul wanted, not his own but that which comes through faith in Christ (Philippians 3:9). So the way back is not more effort but less: stop asking whether you have done enough, look at what he has done, and stand there.

What it does not mean. It does not mean that sinning makes you fall from grace. Grace is for sinners: where sin increased, grace abounded all the more (Romans 5:20). Grace is not a ledge we cling to by our fingernails but a country, and its King is the one who holds us there.

I am afraid this describes me. Does it? The verse describes a person seeking to be justified by his own law-keeping and at peace with that arrangement. If you are afraid because you know your record will not carry you, that is the exact opposite. Nobody standing on his own performance is troubled by the news that performance will not do. A warning against a cliff is not a report that you have gone over it, and those who read it most anxiously are almost always furthest from the edge.

How would I know if I were trying to be justified by the law? Watch where your confidence goes when you think of standing before God. If you find yourself listing what you have done, how long you have been a Christian, what you give and what you avoid, you are reaching for the rope instead of the boat. If you find yourself saying, nothing in my hands I bring, simply to the cross I cling, you are in grace. Most Christians drift between the two in a single week. The remedy is not to examine yourself harder but to look at Christ longer.

Where Christians differ: can a believer fall from grace? Arminian Christians take this verse to mean that true believers can lose their salvation: the Galatians were real believers who could forfeit it by trusting in the law. They are right that the warning is real and must not be blunted. This commentary’s view: Paul is describing the meaning and consequence of seeking justification by law: it is a rejection of grace and of Christ. Those who persist in it show they never truly rested on Christ (1 John 2:19). True believers may be confused and tempted, as the Galatians were, but God keeps his own (Philippians 1:6; John 10:28–29), and warnings like this are among his means of keeping them. Those whom he justified he also glorified (Romans 8:30). Falling from grace here means abandoning the principle of grace, not a true believer being lost. That is why Paul can write verse 4 and verse 10 in the same breath.

verseByVerse.quote: For through the Spirit, by faith, we ourselves eagerly wait for the hope of righteousness. For in Christ Jesus neither circumcision nor uncircumcision counts for anything, but only faith working through love.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Believers wait for God’s final verdict by faith, through the Spirit, not by law; and in Christ no religious mark counts, only faith that goes to work in love.

For through the Spirit, by faith, we ourselves. Paul has just said you to those seeking justification by law; now an emphatic we ourselves draws a line down the middle of the room and invites the Galatians back over it.

The hope of righteousness. To eagerly wait (apekdechometha) is to wait for something certainly coming and not yet here: a striking word for righteousness, when Paul has spent three chapters insisting the believer is justified already. The hope is that same verdict declared publicly at the last judgment, and the day when we are finally and actually like him. Both are true: believers are already justified (Romans 5:1), with nothing outstanding, and they wait for the day it is made public and their lives match it, when the man you want to be and the man you are have become the same man. The discomfort of living in that gap is not a sign that anything has gone wrong.

The hope has a face. The righteousness we wait for is a person. Christ Jesus became to us righteousness (1 Corinthians 1:30), and the day the verdict is published is the day he appears: “When Christ who is your life appears, then you also will appear with him in glory” (Colossians 3:4). So the waiting is eager, not anxious. The believer is not waiting to find out whether his record will pass, but for the one who has already passed it for him, and “when he appears we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is” (1 John 3:2).

The legalist cannot wait. Waiting requires that the outcome be secure without you. A man whose standing depends on his own progress has to be getting somewhere, visibly, or the whole structure wobbles. The gospel produces patient people because it has already settled the question they would otherwise spend their lives trying to answer.

Neither circumcision nor uncircumcision. After four chapters fighting circumcision, Paul does not say that being uncircumcised is what counts. Neither does: ethnic and religious markers are irrelevant to standing with God. Make your uncircumcision a badge and you are playing the same game with the pieces reversed.

Faith working through love. Four words fought over for centuries. The verb is energeō, at work: faith is the living thing, and love is faith at work. Faith alone justifies, but the faith that justifies is never alone. A faith that produces no love does not need supplementing; it was never real faith at all.

In everyday life. Think of the one person in your home, work or church whom you find hardest to love. Do one concrete thing for their good this week, without telling anyone. That is not earning God’s favour; it is faith, which already has his favour, getting to work.

If love is the evidence, how much love is enough? That is the question the Judaizers’ conditions taught people to ask, and it is the wrong one. Love is not the entrance fee; it is the sign of life. A newborn baby breathes weakly, but the doctor does not ask whether it breathes enough to be human. Look for direction, not quantity: is there a love for God and his people that was not there before, growing however slowly? That is the Spirit’s work. If you are troubled by how little you love, bring that trouble to Christ, whose love for you does not depend on yours for him, and ask him to enlarge your heart.

Where Christians differ: faith working through love. Roman Catholic teaching has used this phrase to argue that we are justified by faith formed by love, so that love is part of the ground of justification; both sides agree that living faith always loves. This commentary’s view: Paul says what counts is faith, and describes that faith as one that works through love. Love is the fruit of justifying faith, not part of its ground, and the grammar agrees: love is not what qualifies faith, it is what faith does. We are justified by faith alone, receiving Christ’s righteousness; the faith that receives Christ then works through love (Ephesians 2:8–10; James 2:17; the Westminster Confession 11.2; the 1689 London Baptist Confession 11.2).

verseByVerse.quote: You were running well. Who hindered you from obeying the truth? This persuasion is not from him who calls you. A little leaven leavens the whole lump.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Galatians were running well until someone cut in, and the teaching that tripped them did not come from the God who called them; a little of it will change everything. Paul writes like a coach watching a runner who was going to finish.

Who hindered you from obeying the truth? To hinder (enkoptō) is to block the way; in a race it is a runner cutting in across another’s lane. The runner did not tire or lose heart; somebody stepped in front of him. And obeying the truth means believing and living the gospel: for Paul the truth is something you do as well as something you hold.

This persuasion is not from him who calls you. Verse 8 is quiet and decisive: God, who called them by grace, is not the source of this teaching. Paul names him carefully as “him who calls you”: present tense, still calling. You know the voice that called you, and this is not it.

A little leaven leavens the whole lump. A pinch of sour dough (leaven) goes into a large batch, and in time the whole mass has changed. Quantity is irrelevant: a gospel with one small condition attached is not mostly the gospel; given time, it is a different loaf. And the change is invisible while it happens. In a church that is losing the gospel the sermons and the language are unchanged; what alters first is the atmosphere, the quiet arrival of measurement into a room that used to be full of relief.

Leaven and the Lamb. Paul uses the same proverb in 1 Corinthians 5:6, and there he gives at once the reason leaven has no place in the church: “Christ, our Passover lamb, has been sacrificed” (1 Corinthians 5:7). At Passover Israel cleared every crumb of leaven from their houses and ate the lamb with unleavened bread, as a people leaving slavery (Exodus 12:15–20). A gospel with a condition added is old leaven carried back into the house where the Lamb has died. The issue is not fussiness about doctrine but loyalty to the one who was sacrificed.

Who got in front of you? Christians who have gone backwards usually blame themselves for a failure of stamina, and often it is not that at all. Somebody cut in: a teacher, a book, a friend with strong opinions, a season under a ministry that made the gospel conditional. So ask of any cooled faith not “Why did I run out of energy?” but “Who got in front of me, and when?” Very often there is a date.

A test for ordinary believers. The test of a teaching is not whether it is strict; God is often strict. It is whether it comes to you the way he came to you: with a gift, to someone with nothing to offer, and the effect was relief. When a teaching leaves you feeling measured, watched and slightly behind, you may not be able to refute it, but you can recognise that it is not the voice that called you. “My sheep hear my voice,” Jesus said (John 10:27).

How do I tell whether a teaching is leaven or just a different emphasis? Ask what it does to the gospel of free justification in Christ. Christians differ honestly on baptism, church government, the end times and much else, and those differences, important as they are, need not touch the heart. Leaven changes what makes a person right with God, adds a condition to Christ, or quietly moves the weight from his work to yours. Does it leave me resting wholly on Christ? Does it make grace more amazing or less? Does it fit Scripture read as a whole? If a teaching makes Christ smaller and you larger, it is leaven, however small it looks.
verseByVerse.note: Leaven (yeast) spreads through the whole lump of dough.

verseByVerse.quote: I have confidence in the Lord that you will take no other view, and the one who is troubling you will bear the penalty, whoever he is. But if I, brothers, still preach circumcision, why am I still being persecuted? In that case the offense of the cross has been removed. I wish those who unsettle you would emasculate themselves!
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul is confident that the Lord will hold the Galatians, leaves their troubler to God’s judgment, and refuses any gospel that takes the offence out of the cross.

Confidence in the Lord. After the leaven, a surprise. He has called them foolish, bewitched, severed from Christ, and now he is confident about them: not in their good sense, nor in his own arguments, but in the Lord.

Whoever he is. One ringleader or each false teacher: either way, however important, God will judge him. Paul does not organise a campaign; he leaves him to God.

But if I, brothers, still preach circumcision, why am I still being persecuted? Verse 11 lets slip what was being said: that Paul himself taught circumcision when it suited him (perhaps pointing to Timothy, or to his past as a circumcising Pharisee), so the Galatians were only being asked to do what the apostle really wanted. Paul answers with evidence: look at my life. Nobody stones a man for preaching what everybody already accepts. The scars are the argument.

The offense of the cross. The word is skandalon, a stumbling block. What offends is not the suffering; the world has always admired a martyr. It is what the cross says about the person looking at it: that he could not be saved by any other means, that his religion and decency contributed nothing, that he had to be rescued like a criminal, and that the Judge stepped down from the bench and took the sentence himself. Add any requirement and the offence drains away, because now there is something for the man to do. A religion you can contribute to is one the world will tolerate. A gospel nobody is annoyed by has usually been adjusted.

I wish those who unsettle you would emasculate themselves! This reads as a crude outburst until you know the region. Across Asia Minor, with its chief shrine at Pessinus in Galatia itself, the mother goddess Cybele was served by priests who castrated themselves in ecstatic worship. So Paul is saying: you want to cut flesh to be accepted by God? You already know what that religion looks like; it is on your own doorstep. If cutting wins God’s favour, why stop where Moses stopped? The road they are on ends somewhere they have already seen.

The stone in Zion. Paul applies Isaiah’s stone to Christ: “Behold, I am laying in Zion a stone of stumbling, and a rock of offense; and whoever believes in him will not be put to shame” (Romans 9:33; compare 1 Peter 2:6–8). So the offence of the cross is finally the offence of a person. The Messiah Israel expected would not hang on a tree under God’s curse (3:13; Deuteronomy 21:23), yet this one did, in the sinner’s place. The stone men trip over is the stone on which a believer stands and is never put to shame.

How to hold on to someone who is drifting. You can be confident in the person, which is optimism and collapses on contact with facts, or write them off. Paul does neither. He tells them the worst honestly and then expects God to keep them, the only ground on which anyone has ever been kept, including him.

What is the offence of the cross today? Much the same, in modern clothes: that we are sinners who cannot save ourselves; that decent, religious and kind people need a Saviour as much as criminals do; that there is only one way to God, through a crucified Jew; that good works earn nothing. People will happily admire Jesus as a teacher; what they resist is being told they needed him to die for them. Do not soften this to be liked. Explain it gently, with tears if need be, but leave the offence where God put it, because it is the same message that saves.

Is strong language ever right for me? Rarely, and with great care. Paul was an apostle writing under inspiration about wolves destroying a flock he had founded, and even here his target is the teachers, not the confused sheep. Scripture tells us to let no corrupting talk come out of our mouths (Ephesians 4:29) and to correct opponents with gentleness (2 Timothy 2:25). If you enjoy biting words, stop. Keep your strongest language for the dangers that most threaten souls, and speak it with sorrow, never against the people being misled.

Uncertain wording. The verb in v. 12 (apokoptō) means to cut off and was used of castration; the form here means to have oneself cut. Almost all modern translations take it as castration, and Cybele’s priests nearby support that. Older versions such as the KJV render it simply “cut off”, which some took as a wish that the troublers be cut off from the church. The likely meaning is the ESV’s.
verseByVerse.note: Paul’s bitter wish may allude to the priests of the goddess Cybele in that region, who castrated themselves.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The freedom Christ gives is freedom to serve one another in love, not a base of operations for the flesh. Paul answers the old fear that grace breeds licence not with rules but with love (v. 13), because love of neighbour is what the whole law was always aiming at (v. 14). The alternative is a church that bites and devours itself until nothing is left (v. 15).
verseByVerse.theology:
Love as the Fulfilment of the Law

For the believer the law’s moral demands are not abolished but fulfilled, from a different source. The law commands from outside; love, produced by the Spirit, moves from within. This is the law written on the heart (Jeremiah 31:33): not a different law, but the same law, obeyed out of love for the God who gave everything, and not as the price of his favour.

Verse 13 also answers the charge, as old as the gospel, that free grace leads to licence (see the note on vv. 13–14), and v. 15 shows how a religion of performance destroys a congregation (see the note on v. 15).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The Galatians were living out v. 15 while arguing about how to be holy, and vv. 13–14 name the one thing that binds a church as rules never can.

Now: A church that makes the Christian life mainly about visible markers produces pride in those who meet the standard, shame in those who do not, and division. The cure v. 13 offers is not a new rule but service (see “The cure is service” in the note on v. 15).

verseByVerse.quote: For you were called to freedom, brothers. Only do not use your freedom as an opportunity for the flesh, but through love serve one another. For the whole law is fulfilled in one word: “You shall love your neighbor as yourself.”
verseByVerse.commentary:
Christ set you free to serve one another in love, not to indulge yourself, and that love is what the whole law was always aiming at.

For you were called to freedom, brothers. Paul now faces the objection waiting since verse 1: if people are genuinely free, what is to stop them doing as they like? Opportunity (aphormē) was used of a military base of operations: the flesh, our sinful human nature, can use your freedom as its base. And its reasoning sounds like good theology: “I am not under law. God has forgiven this already. Grace is greater than my sin.” Each sentence is true, and all three have been used to excuse things that wrecked a family.

No fence, but love. Paul’s answer to this objection, which every preacher of grace meets (Romans 6:1), is not a fence of rules. Having demolished law as the ground of standing, he will not smuggle it back as the ground of behaviour.

Serve one another. Be slaves to one another (douleuete): the verb is deliberately shocking. Having torn the yoke off their shoulders, Paul tells them first to put themselves at each other’s disposal. The freest man who ever lived wrapped a towel round his waist and washed his disciples’ feet.

Free lord, dutiful servant. Luther put the paradox exactly: a Christian is a perfectly free lord of all, subject to none, and a perfectly dutiful servant of all, subject to all. There is no tension, because the slavery Paul has been fighting is slavery to a system in order to be accepted, and this is serving people because you already are accepted.

Fulfilled in one word. Verse 14 quotes Leviticus 19:18 (compare Romans 13:8–10). How can Paul quote the law to people not under it? Not summarised but fulfilled: brought to its intended completion. Every commandment described what love looks like in a particular situation. “You shall not steal” is love meeting your neighbour’s property; “You shall not bear false witness” is love meeting his reputation. So a man who truly loves does what the law was written to produce, not to be justified but because he loves, as a man who loves his wife needs no rule against reading her letters.

A higher standard, not a lower one. A code can be satisfied; you can reach the end of a list. “As yourself” has no end to reach. Nobody has ever gone to bed having loved his neighbour as much as he instinctively looks after himself.

Fulfilled first in him. Before love fulfils the law in us, it fulfilled it in Christ. He came not to abolish the law but to fulfil it (Matthew 5:17), the one man who ever loved his neighbour as himself, and then more than himself: he loved his Father with all his heart, and his enemies all the way to the cross (Romans 5:8). That fulfilment reaches us through him: God condemned sin in the flesh in his Son, so that the righteous requirement of the law might be fulfilled in us, who walk according to the Spirit (Romans 8:3–4). Our love is not a new way of earning but his obedience working itself out in his people.

What it does not mean. Not that love replaces the commandments, so that we decide what love means. Love is defined by the commandments (Romans 13:9). A person who says, “I am doing the loving thing”, while breaking God’s commands about marriage, honesty or life, has redefined love to suit himself.

In everyday life. Pick a specific person and a specific service: the washing-up nobody wants to do, the visit you keep postponing, an hour with a lonely neighbour. Do it as one set free, not as one paying a debt. When your love falls short, as it will, Christ’s perfect love stands in your place, and your poor service is accepted for his sake.

If love fulfils the law, can a kind person fulfil it without Christ? Not in the way the law means. Many unbelievers are kinder than many Christians, a real gift of God’s common goodness. But the law’s first command is to love God with all your heart (Matthew 22:37–40), and its second asks for love as yourself, every day, from the heart, with no gaps. Nobody has managed even the second, so the kind person needs Christ as much as the cruel one. And this frees the religious person too: neither of us generates that love. Christ fulfilled it for us, and the Spirit grows it in us (v. 22).

So does the law still bind the believer? Not being “under the law” (v. 18) means not under it as a way of earning life, as a curse, or as the ground of our standing. God’s moral will has not lapsed: “this is the love of God, that we keep his commandments” (1 John 5:3). The Spirit-led Christian does not need the law to make him acceptable, but he is glad of it as a description of the life the Spirit is producing.

Does loving my neighbour as myself mean I must first learn to love myself? No. The command assumes that we already care for ourselves, without being told to (Ephesians 5:29), and turns that instinct outward. The cure for a crushed sense of self is not self-love but being loved by God, which frees you to stop looking inward at all. And who is my neighbour? Jesus answered with a Samaritan: whoever is in front of you and in need, even if he is not your kind (Luke 10:29–37).

parallels.desc: you shall love your neighbour as yourself

verseByVerse.quote: But if you bite and devour one another, watch out that you are not consumed by one another.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A church that turns holiness into competition will tear itself apart, and nobody wins.

Bite and devour. The three verbs come from animals and escalate: a snap, then eating, then nothing left. The Galatians were apparently already tearing each other apart over how to be holy, and that is no coincidence: the one causes the other, and it is still a common way for a good church to destroy itself.

How it works. Once standing before God is tied to performance, every other believer in the room becomes a measurement. If he keeps more than I do, he is a threat, and I must find the flaw that explains him; if he keeps less, he is a reassurance, and I need him to stay there. Neither is love, and both feel like discernment. Add a genuine doctrinal disagreement and it all gains a righteous vocabulary, so that people defending their own standing believe they are contending for the truth.

Consumed by one another. Not the strong eating the weak: everyone loses. The party that prevails is left holding a smaller, colder, more suspicious congregation than the one it was fighting for.

One for whom Christ died. Paul gives the deepest reason elsewhere: do not destroy the one for whom Christ died (Romans 14:15; compare 1 Corinthians 8:11–12). The believer across the room is someone the Son of God loved enough to die for, and every bite in a church fight lands on a body that belongs to Christ.

What do you want to be true? Here is a test for a disagreement you are inside now: ask what you want to be true about the other person. If you would be disappointed to discover he was right, or that his motives were good, then whatever the merits of your case, you are biting. The verse does not ask whether your position is correct; Paul obviously thought his was.

The cure is service. Paul does not answer biting with a rule; he has just said, through love serve one another. The antidote to devouring a brother is serving him, deliberately and concretely, while you still disagree with him. It is very hard to keep eating a man you are carrying something for. Pressing anger produces strife (Proverbs 30:33), and quarrels come from the passions at war within you (James 4:1–2); service starves them.

What it does not mean. Not that truth does not matter; Paul fights hard for it in this letter. You can contend for the faith without devouring the brother who is confused about it.

My church is already in a fight. What should I do? First, refuse to add to it: no gossip, no forwarding of messages, no recruiting to a side, no conversations about people that you would not have with them present. Second, take any grievance directly and privately to the person concerned, and then if needed to the elders (Matthew 18:15–17). Third, pray for those you disagree with, by name, asking God to bless them. Fourth, look for a way to serve someone on the other side. And if the issue is a real matter of the gospel, speak plainly but without contempt. A church can survive disagreement; it rarely survives malice.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 16–26 — The Flesh and the Spirit
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The Spirit, not the law, is God’s answer to the flesh. Walk by the Spirit and the flesh’s desires will not rule you, though the two are at war within every believer, and those led by the Spirit are not under the law (vv. 16–18). The works of the flesh are plain, and a life given over to them has no share in God’s kingdom (vv. 19–21); the Spirit grows one fruit, the character of Christ, against which there is no law (vv. 22–23). Those who belong to Christ have crucified the flesh, so they keep in step with the Spirit, without the conceit that provokes and envies (vv. 24–26).
verseByVerse.theology:
Putting the Flesh to Death, and Why the Fight Is Evidence of Life

The Christian life has two sides: putting the flesh to death, which v. 24 states as already done to every believer, and coming alive to God, which v. 25 calls keeping in step with the Spirit. Neither is self-powered. The first applies what happened to the old self in Christ’s death (2:20); the second is the Spirit’s fruit.

The tension between v. 17 and v. 24 is resolved by the image of crucifixion (see the note on v. 24), and v. 21 needs the same care (see “The morning after” in the note on vv. 19–21).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The Galatians needed to see that the law and moral chaos were not the only two options, and vv. 16–18 give the third: walking by the Spirit. The middle of Paul’s list (v. 20) described their own congregations. And in v. 25 Paul turns the word for their old bondage round (see the note on v. 25).

Now: Walking by the Spirit (v. 16) is concrete rather than mystical (see “What walking by the Spirit looks like” in the note on vv. 16–18).

verseByVerse.quote: But I say, walk by the Spirit, and you will not gratify the desires of the flesh. For the desires of the flesh are against the Spirit, and the desires of the Spirit are against the flesh, for these are opposed to each other, to keep you from doing the things you want to do. But if you are led by the Spirit, you are not under the law.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Spirit, not the law, is God’s answer to the flesh: walk by him and its desires will not rule you, though the war within goes on. This is Paul’s whole answer to both legalism and licence, and it is neither a law nor a technique.

But I say, walk by the Spirit. Go on walking: the ordinary word for daily conduct, step by step. Not soar, not fight, not achieve: walk. By the Spirit means depending on him, following his lead, relying on his power.

You will not gratify. A promise, not a command, and the Greek is as strong as it can be: you will certainly not carry out the flesh’s desires. It does not say the desires will stop. And the order is the whole strategy of Christian holiness. Paul does not say, “Stop gratifying the flesh, and then you will be able to walk by the Spirit.” He says walk, and the other will follow. Sin is displaced far more often than it is defeated by direct assault, because a man staring at his temptation and gritting his teeth is still looking at it.

What the flesh is. Human nature in its fallen state, set against God: the mind that does not submit to God’s law, and cannot (Romans 8:7). It is not the body as such; several works of the flesh in vv. 19–21, like envy and rivalry, have nothing to do with the body.

Against the Spirit. Verse 17 is honest about the cost: a settled war within every believer. Young Christians often take the conflict to mean that something went wrong at their conversion. It is the reverse. Before conversion conscience might protest (Romans 2:15), but the flesh had the field. The fight is a sign of life: something in you now wants what God wants, and it will not be quiet. You cannot drift into holiness, and you cannot sin with a quiet heart either.

Led by the Spirit. Being led is something done to us (Romans 8:14). The Judaizers offered a code to be kept; Paul offers a person to be followed. Those he leads are not under the law’s condemnation, nor under it as a system of control. A code can only stand outside you and tell you what to do; the Spirit is inside, and he produces the life the law describes.

The Spirit who led the Son. The Spirit who leads us is the Spirit of God’s Son, sent into our hearts (4:6), and he has led this way before. Jesus, full of the Holy Spirit, was led by the Spirit in the wilderness for forty days, tempted by the devil (Luke 4:1–2), and where Adam and Israel gave way to their desires, he refused every one. The Spirit who hovered over the waters at creation now leads Christ’s brothers through the same war, behind a captain who has already won it. He fights in us against everything that would destroy us, and he is not losing.

What walking by the Spirit looks like. Not a mystical state or waiting for a feeling. It means asking him for help rather than relying on willpower (Luke 11:13); filling the mind with his word, since he leads through what he has written (Colossians 3:16); saying no to the flesh at the first stirring, not after a long negotiation (Romans 8:13); saying yes to the next step of obedience he shows you, however small; and staying close to God’s people and the means of grace (the word, prayer and the Lord’s Supper), where he works. No single great experience settles it; daily, ordinary dependence does.

Does being led by the Spirit mean following inner voices and impressions? Not in the sense many mean. Here and in Romans 8:14 it concerns the direction of a life, away from the flesh and toward holiness, not private messages about which job to take. The Spirit speaks in Scripture, which he inspired and which is complete and sufficient (2 Timothy 3:16–17). He does work in our hearts, convicting, comforting, bringing his word to mind and giving wisdom, but an impression is never a new word from God, and nothing that contradicts Scripture is his leading. Christians whose churches expect prophetic words today see some of this differently, and they are brothers and sisters; they too agree that every such word must be tested by Scripture (1 Thessalonians 5:20–21).

Where Christians differ: sinless perfection. Some, especially in parts of the holiness tradition, teach that believers can reach a state where the flesh is eradicated and they no longer sin, and they are moved by a right hunger for holiness. This commentary’s view: Paul describes an ongoing war between flesh and Spirit in the believer. The Spirit gives real victory, and believers grow in holiness, but the flesh is not destroyed until glory (Romans 7:14–25; 1 John 1:8; the Westminster Confession 13.2; the 1689 London Baptist Confession 13.2). The Christian life is a fight, not a state of sinless rest.

Uncertain wording. The last clause of v. 17, “to keep you from doing the things you want to do”, is compressed. Its connecting word may state purpose or simply result, and “the things you want” could mean the good the believer wants (as in Romans 7:15–19), the evil the flesh wants, or both. Most likely it is both: each side blocks the other, so that neither gets its way unopposed. It does not mean the believer is helpless, for v. 16 has already promised which side prevails when we walk by the Spirit.
verseByVerse.note: “Flesh” here means human nature in its fallen state, set against God.

verseByVerse.quote: Now the works of the flesh are evident: sexual immorality, impurity, sensuality, idolatry, sorcery, enmity, strife, jealousy, fits of anger, rivalries, dissensions, divisions, envy, drunkenness, orgies, and things like these. I warn you, as I warned you before, that those who do such things will not inherit the kingdom of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
What fallen human nature produces is plain to see, and a life given over to it has no share in God’s kingdom.

Now the works of the flesh are evident. Works is Paul’s word all through the letter for works of the law, and the echo is deliberate. Law-keeping and licence look like opposites, but both are things a man produces out of his own resources; only the products differ. Fifteen are listed, in four groups.

Sexual immorality, impurity, sensuality. Sexual immorality (porneia) is the broad word for all sex outside marriage. Impurity (akatharsia) is moral uncleanness. Sensuality (aselgeia) is indulgence that has stopped caring who sees.

Idolatry, sorcery. Then religion goes wrong. Sorcery translates pharmakeia (hence pharmacy): potions, spells and drugs used to bend outcomes. Both are attempts to control God or the spirit world: an idol is a god you can locate, and a spell is a result you can arrange.

Enmity, strife, jealousy. Slow down at the long middle, the largest group: eight sins of relationships. Enmity (hostility), strife (quarrelling), jealousy, fits of anger (outbursts of rage), rivalries (selfish ambition), dissensions (splits), divisions (factions, haireseis), envy. Every one thrives in a church meeting as easily as in a tavern, and these were tearing the Galatian churches apart (v. 15). Paul has put the sins of the respectable at the centre of his list, and a congregation horrified by verse 19 will often live with verse 20 as if it were normal.

Drunkenness, orgies, and things like these. Last come sins of excess: orgies (kōmoi) were the drunken processions that ended pagan festivals. The list is a portrait, not a legal code, and nobody can plead that his particular version is not itemised.

Will not inherit the kingdom. Few passages disturb tender consciences more, so read the verb carefully. Do is prassō, practise, and the tense describes a settled habit: those whose lives are characterised by these things and who have made their peace with them. Not the believer who falls and repents, but the one who continues without repentance (1 Corinthians 6:9–11). There is a world of difference between a man who falls into a ditch and a man who lives in it, and Scripture never confuses them.

Heirs through the Son. In this letter nobody earns an inheritance; it comes by being a son, and sonship comes through Christ (4:4–7). The works of the flesh are the life of someone who has never been adopted, and such a life has no share in the estate. But the Son who won the inheritance gives his people the Spirit who cries “Abba! Father!” in their hearts (4:6), and that Spirit makes war on every item on this list.

The morning after. The question is not whether you sinned, but whether the sin still grieves you and you take it to Christ. A man in whom the Spirit lives cannot sin comfortably. The very ache that makes you afraid of this verse is evidence that it is not about you, and the blood of Jesus cleanses the one who brings it to him.

I keep falling into the same sin, a sexual one. Am I one of those who practise it? Ask not whether you have fallen again, but which side you are on. Are you at peace with it, defending it, planning for it? Or do you hate it, confess it and keep fighting, even after many defeats? The second is not the life Paul condemns; it is the war of verse 17. But do not settle for endless defeat. Bring it into the light with a mature Christian friend or pastor (James 5:16), remove what feeds it (devices, places, habits), and ask for help, practical and spiritual. Each time you fall, go straight back to Christ, whose blood cleanses from all sin (1 John 1:7, 9).

Is it not harsh to shut people out of God’s kingdom for envy or drunkenness? Only if the kingdom is a club with a fee. It is the place where God is king and love reigns completely, and a heart set on these things, that will not let them go, does not want it; it wants itself, and heaven would be unbearable to it. Nor does the list let the religious feel safe: jealousy and factions sit beside drunkenness and orgies. God takes every one seriously enough to judge it, and seriously enough to have borne it himself in his Son. No one who comes to Christ is turned away (John 6:37), and the list in Corinthians ends with “such were some of you” (1 Corinthians 6:11).

Is it sorcery to take medicine? No. The word described magic, potions and drugs used to manipulate spiritual powers, often with occult practices attached. Medicine used to heal is a gift of God; Paul told Timothy to take a little wine for his stomach (1 Timothy 5:23), and Luke was a physician. What the verse condemns today includes fortune-telling, spells, seeking spirits, and the misuse of drugs to escape or to alter the mind in the way drunkenness does.

Textual note. Some later manuscripts, followed by the KJV, add adultery at the start of the list and murders after envy; the earliest do not, so most modern Bibles omit them.
verseByVerse.note: “Sorcery” translates a word that also covered magic potions and drugs.

verseByVerse.quote: But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness, self-control; against such things there is no law.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Spirit grows in believers one harvest, the character of Christ himself, which the law could command but never produce.

But the fruit of the Spirit. The flesh has works; the Spirit has fruit. Works are manufactured; fruit is grown, and no apple was ever produced by an apple tree straining. The Spirit produces it as we abide in Christ (John 15:4–5).

One fruit, not nine. Not nine badges to collect, but one fruit with nine facets: a single character, finally the character of Christ himself being formed in a person (4:19). You do not choose patience this year and gentleness next.

Is love. Love heads the list, since verse 14 has just said the whole law is fulfilled in it: the love Christ showed, which seeks another’s good at its own cost. It is the root of the rest (1 Corinthians 13): joy is love rejoicing, peace is love resting, patience is love waiting, and so on down the list.

Joy, peace. Joy (chara) is gladness in God, not a cheerful temperament; it survives circumstances that ruin cheerfulness, because its ground is outside them. Peace (eirēnē) is wholeness: first peace with God, then the inward rest of a man who has stopped negotiating his standing, and harmony with others.

Patience, kindness, goodness. Patience (makrothymia) is a long fuse with people, the word used of God’s forbearance with us. Kindness (chrēstotēs) is gracious tenderness, not mere politeness but active usefulness to somebody. Goodness (agathōsynē) is moral substance and generosity, the quality of a man who is the same when nobody is checking.

Faithfulness, gentleness, self-control. Faithfulness (pistis) is reliability and loyalty: being where you said you would be, keeping your word when it costs. Gentleness (prautēs, meekness) is not weakness; in Greek it could be used of a powerful horse broken to the bridle, strength under control. And self-control (enkrateia) comes last, striking on a list of fruit, since every self-help programme in the world sells it. You do not generate it. You receive it, and then you use it.

Against such things there is no law. A dry piece of understatement that completes the argument of the chapter. The Judaizers feared grace would produce lawlessness. Paul says: look at what the Spirit produces, and find me the legislature that would prohibit any of it. The law was always aiming at this, and the Spirit produces it without the law’s help.

Nine words, one face. Read the nine words again and you will see a face. Love that went to the cross; joy set before him that carried him through it; peace he left to his friends on the night he was betrayed; patience with slow disciples; kindness to lepers and children; goodness that no one could convict of sin; faithfulness to his Father to the end; gentleness that would not break a bruised reed; self-control at his arrest and before Pilate, when twelve legions of angels were a word away. The Spirit is making us like him, and one day the harvest will be complete, and the Son will be the firstborn among many brothers.

How is the fruit of the Spirit different from the gifts of the Spirit? The fruit is character, the same in every believer and growing for a lifetime. The gifts are abilities for service, distributed differently, as the Spirit apportions to each one individually as he wills (1 Corinthians 12:11). The fruit matters more: without love the greatest gifts are nothing (1 Corinthians 13:2), and Jesus warns of people who prophesied and cast out demons in his name and were never his (Matthew 7:22–23). A church should prize holiness above gifting.

I see almost none of this in myself. Have I got the Spirit at all? This list is often used to wound, so three things should be said. Fruit is slow and seasonal, and nobody digs up a tree in March to check. You are the worst-placed person to assess it: the people who live with you will almost always report growth you cannot see. And the sentence does not say the fruit of the diligent Christian but of the Spirit, who is not slow, nor uncertain of the outcome; the growing was never your department.

If I cannot produce the fruit, what do I actually do? Stay connected to the vine, and cooperate with the gardener. Abide in Christ by trusting him and staying in his word (John 15:7). Pray for the fruit you lack. Put yourself where growth happens: the preaching of the word, the Lord’s Supper, the fellowship of believers. Pull up weeds by confessing sin. When an opportunity comes to exercise patience or kindness, take it, trusting the Spirit to give what he asks. This is the effort of a branch staying in the vine, not of a branch trying to grow apples by itself.
verseByVerse.note: “Fruit” is singular: one harvest with many flavours.

verseByVerse.quote: And those who belong to Christ Jesus have crucified the flesh with its passions and desires.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Everyone who belongs to Christ has already had the flesh nailed to his cross; it still shouts, but it no longer rules.

And those who belong to Christ Jesus. All true believers: not unusually consecrated Christians, but everyone who is his.

Have crucified the flesh. The tense is the key: a past action, complete. Paul states what happened to every Christian as a fact before it is a duty. United to Christ in his death, believers have put the flesh to death (2:20; Romans 6:6) and turned decisively against their sinful nature.

If it is dead, what has been fighting? Seven verses earlier Paul described a war inside the believer. The answer is in the image itself. Crucifixion was meant to be slow: a man nailed to a beam could take hours or even days to die, and all that time he was mortally wounded, fixed in place, going nowhere, and still perfectly capable of shouting at people. He was finished. He was not yet silent.

The noise of a dying man. That is the flesh in a believer: mortally wounded, its authority broken, its outcome settled, but audible until the day the body dies. So the voice you hear on a bad Thursday is real and loud, and it is not evidence that nothing happened to you. It is the noise of something that has been executed and has not yet stopped.

When did this happen? Paul has already told us: I have been crucified with Christ (2:20). It happened at the cross, and it became yours when you were united to him by faith. Everything in us that was in love with its own ruin was fastened to that wood in his body; the sentence carried out on him was carried out on it, and it will never get down. That is why the verse begins where it does: those who belong to Christ Jesus.

Relief in the order. If crucifying the flesh were your project, every failure would mean starting again. Because it is Christ’s finished work applied to you, your failures are the noise of a dying man, not the recovery of a victorious one, and you are refusing orders from something already condemned. So believers go on putting it to death daily (Romans 8:13; Colossians 3:5): not to make the execution happen, but because it has.

How do I put the flesh to death in practice? Starve it and refuse it. Starve it by cutting off what feeds it: if a certain website, friendship, habit or late-night hour regularly leads you into sin, remove it, however drastic that seems (Matthew 5:29–30; Romans 13:14). Refuse it at the first stirring, in Christ’s name: “This is not who I am now.” Replace it with the opposite good: generosity for greed, thanksgiving for complaining, service for envy. And do it all by the Spirit (Romans 8:13), in prayer, in the company of other believers, confident that the flesh has already lost.

In everyday life. When the old voice shouts today, answer it out loud if you need to: “You were nailed to the cross with Christ; I do not take orders from you.” Then do the next good thing.

verseByVerse.quote: If we live by the Spirit, let us also keep in step with the Spirit.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Since the Spirit has given us life, let him also set the pace of our daily walk.

If we live by the Spirit. The if is not a doubt: since we live by the Spirit, as we do. He gave every believer new birth and a new heart that wants God (John 3:5–6; Ezekiel 36:26). All New Testament commands have this shape: this is what you are, so live like it.

Keep in step. In verse 16 the word was walk. Here it is stoichōmen: to keep rank, march in line, match the step of the man beside you, following the Spirit’s lead in daily obedience.

The word turned round. The verb shares its root with stoicheia, Paul’s word in chapter 4 for the elementary principles that had the Galatians in bondage (4:3, 9). They had marched to a calendar and a code before. Paul does not tell them to stop marching; he tells them who sets the pace now. The words that once described our chains now describe our march.

Where the Spirit marches. Keeping in step with the Spirit always brings a man to the same place, because the Spirit’s whole work is to glorify Christ: “he will take what is mine and declare it to you,” Jesus said (John 16:14). The new march is set by the Spirit of the Son who bought us out of the old (4:4–6), and he is leading us home.

Ahead or behind. You can march ahead of him, driving a ministry or a decision at a pace nothing has been given to sustain, and calling the exhaustion faithfulness. Or you can lag behind: hearing the small thing you should do, agreeing with it and not doing it, until the agreeing has quietly become a substitute for the doing. Neither looks like rebellion, and the correction is the same: find where he actually is, and be there. He sets a pace a real person can sustain over a whole life, which is exactly what the law never did.

How do I know where the Spirit is leading in a decision, like a job or a move? Begin with what he has already said. Scripture settles the moral boundaries: if an option requires sin, it is not his leading. Within those boundaries he leads by giving wisdom, so ask for it (James 1:5), think carefully, weigh your gifts and responsibilities, consider how each option affects your love for God, your family and your church, and seek counsel from mature believers (Proverbs 15:22). Then decide, and trust God’s providence with the outcome. You do not need a sign or an inner voice: a wise decision made in faith is a step in step.
verseByVerse.note: “Keep in step” is a military word for marching in line.

verseByVerse.quote: Let us not become conceited, provoking one another, envying one another.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Empty glory sets believers competing with one another, and the Spirit’s fruit leaves no room for it. This small verse brings the whole soaring argument down to how you feel about the Christian three seats away, and leads into chapter 6.

Let us not become conceited. Kenodoxoi: empty-glory, a reputation held up by air, often pride in spiritual achievements. A man whose significance depends on something that hollow cannot leave other people alone, because a standing that rests on being better than others can only be kept up by comparing.

Provoking one another, envying one another. Two symptoms of one disease. Provoking, challenging as to a fight, is what the man ahead does: needling, making sure the gap is felt. Envying is what the man behind does: resenting, watching, quietly hoping for a stumble. Both have their eyes fixed on another believer instead of on Christ, and calculate themselves from the difference.

Why we want what they have. The French thinker René Girard spent a lifetime on a simple observation: most of our desires are borrowed. We learn what to want by watching others want it, which is why a toy nobody has touched for months becomes precious the moment a brother picks it up; and the people we copy become our rivals, reaching for the same thing. Advertising sells you the desire of someone you admire, and your phone shows you a thousand lives a day, each a model and each a rival. Girard, who came to faith in Christ, argued that the way out is not to stop imitating, which no one can do, but to find a model who is not our rival.

A model who is not a rival. Christ is that model. Empty glory attracts only while it is the best glory in view. Set beside the Son of God, who had glory in full, laid it down, took the form of a slave and was executed for people who were arguing about rank (Philippians 2:3–7), the competition in the third row loses its grip. He does not hoard what he has; he makes us fellow heirs with him (Romans 8:17). You cannot compete with someone who has already given you everything he won. “He must increase, but I must decrease” (John 3:30).

The flicker. Think of the believer whose ministry, family or reputation is flourishing most visibly in your circle. A flicker of something when his good news is announced, before the congratulation catches up, is verse 26 with your name on it. Paul puts it straight after the fruit of the Spirit because envy cannot coexist with love, joy and peace: it needs somebody else to have less. The cure is not to try harder to be pleased but to look somewhere else, at him.

Is it wrong to admire another Christian, or want to be like them? No. Paul says, “Be imitators of me, as I am of Christ” (1 Corinthians 11:1), and Hebrews tells us to imitate the faith of our leaders (Hebrews 13:7). Admiration thanks God for another’s gifts and wants to grow the same way; envy resents them for having what you lack and is secretly glad when they stumble. The difference shows when they succeed: admiration rejoices, envy aches. If you notice the ache, confess it, and then thank God aloud for the very thing you envied. That is how the Spirit turns envy into love.

In everyday life. Pick the person you most often compare yourself with, and pray for their blessing by name, specifically, for the thing you most envy or most look down on.
