keyVerse.quote: For you were called to freedom, brothers. Only do not use your freedom as an opportunity for the flesh, but through love serve one another.
keyVerse.note: This verse is the hinge of the chapter. It gathers up the call of vv. 1–12 not to surrender the freedom Christ won, and opens vv. 13–26 by saying what that freedom is for: not self-indulgence but love that serves. The freest man who ever lived washed his disciples’ feet, and his Spirit now makes free people servants.

5.reflection:
Paul warns that adding anything to Christ as a condition of being right with God makes Christ “of no advantage” (vv. 2–4). What are the things Christians today are tempted to add? How would you finish the sentence “I am right with God because Christ died for me, and because I …”?

Paul calls the Galatians to stand firm in freedom (v. 1) and then to use that freedom to serve one another (v. 13). Why do you think freedom can feel harder than living by rules? Where could you use your freedom to serve someone this week?

Verse 15 describes a church biting and devouring itself, and v. 26 traces it to conceit and envy. What usually turns Christian disagreement into biting? What helps you rejoice when another believer is doing well?

The fruit of the Spirit is one fruit, the character of Christ, grown rather than manufactured (vv. 22–23), while the flesh still fights (vv. 17, 24). Which part of that fruit do you most long to see grow in you, and what does walking by the Spirit look like for you in practice?

6.title: Boasting Only in the Cross: The New Creation and the Community of Grace
6.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 6 completes the practical teaching begun at 5:13, showing what life by the Spirit looks like inside a church (vv. 1–10); then Paul takes the pen himself and sums up the whole letter (vv. 11–18).

The message. The gospel of free grace makes a church of burden-bearers, not scorekeepers, and leaves only one thing to boast in: the cross of Christ. People who know they were picked up by grace pick up others gently, keep sowing to the Spirit without giving up, and refuse every version of the faith that offers a safer, more impressive religion than a crucified Lord. What counts is not a mark on the body but a new creation.

Why it was said. The Galatians had been biting and devouring one another (5:15), provoking and envying (5:26), while teachers pressed circumcision on them (see the introduction). A church that thinks its standing with God is earned will always grow harsh with the fallen and proud of its own showing. Paul shows the other way, and then exposes what the circumcision campaign was really about.

How the chapter makes its case. Verses 1–5 deal with the fallen brother: restore him gently, carry one another’s burdens, and stop measuring yourself by your neighbour, since each will answer for his own load. Verses 6–10 widen the view: support those who teach you, remember that God is not mocked and every life reaps what it sows, and do not grow weary of doing good. Verses 11–18, in Paul’s own large handwriting, compress the whole letter: the agitators want a good showing and a way round persecution (vv. 12–13); Paul boasts only in the cross (v. 14); new creation is the rule, with peace and mercy on all who walk by it (vv. 15–16); his scars show whose he is, and grace has the last word (vv. 17–18).

Where it leads. Every part of the chapter rests on Christ. He is the gentle restorer who never fell, the Burden-Bearer who carried our sorrows, the one who sowed only righteousness and was handed the harvest of our corruption. And at the end Paul holds up the cross itself, Rome’s shameful gallows, as the one glory of his life, because there the Son of God “loved me and gave himself for me” (2:20), and through it the new creation has begun.

For us. Ask whose burden you are carrying, what you are sowing with your hours and your money, and who you would be if the reputation you have built quietly fell away. Then look at the cross until it is the one thing you boast in.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A church that lives by grace carries its fallen and its burdened instead of judging them. When a brother is caught in sin, those who walk by the Spirit restore him gently, keeping watch on themselves (v. 1), and all are to carry one another’s crushing weights, which is the law of Christ (v. 2). What spoils this is pride: thinking yourself something and measuring yourself against your neighbour (vv. 3–4). Instead, test your own work before God, remembering that each will answer for his own load (v. 5).
verseByVerse.theology:
The Church as a Community of Restoration

The church is a communion of saints, committed to mutual care, discipline and restoration, and verse 1 puts the letter’s teaching on justification into practice. We deal gently with a failing brother because we know we stand only by grace; the man who forgets his own proneness to sin will be a prosecutor, and the man who remembers it will be a restorer. Gentleness without truth becomes sentimentality, and truth without gentleness wounds further.

Verses 2 and 5 keep the balance between the burden others must help carry and the load each must carry himself (see “Two errors” in the note on vv. 3–5).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The Galatian congregations were biting and devouring one another (5:15). Some took freedom as licence and others answered with condemnation; verse 1 corrects both, and v. 3 names what was fuelling the second: men who thought they were something.

Now: A warm and orthodox church can still be carrying nobody’s burdens (see the note on v. 2). And v. 4 asks where our sense of doing well or badly comes from (see the note on vv. 3–5).

verseByVerse.quote: Brothers, if anyone is caught in any transgression, you who are spiritual should restore him in a spirit of gentleness. Keep watch on yourself, lest you too be tempted.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When a fellow believer falls into sin, those who live by the Spirit are to set him gently back on his feet, keeping watch on themselves as they do it. Paul puts five chapters of doctrine to work on the hardest situation in ordinary church life: a Christian who has fallen.

Caught in any transgression. The verb is passive: overtaken, perhaps ambushed by sin before he realised. The sin is no smaller (“any” leaves no kind out), but the posture changes. You are looking at a casualty, not a defector.

You who are spiritual. Not an elite tier: every Christian lives by the Spirit (5:16, 25), and the spiritual are those actually keeping in step with him today. There is an edge in it, though. The Galatians had plenty of people who thought themselves advanced, and Paul quietly says: if you are so spiritual, here is the job.

Restore him. The verb (katartizō) is used of mending torn nets (Matthew 4:21) and of setting a broken bone. Nobody sets a bone by shouting at it. You get close, cause only the pain the job needs, and aim at a limb that works again. A bonesetter who enjoyed the pain would be unfit for the work.

In a spirit of gentleness. Gentleness is fruit of the Spirit (5:23). It is not softness about the sin but strength under control, the strength of a man who could crush and chooses to heal.

Keep watch on yourself. Suddenly singular, in a sentence full of plurals: Paul speaks to the restorer alone. “Let anyone who thinks that he stands take heed lest he fall” (1 Corinthians 10:12). The danger is rarely the obvious one. It is seldom to commit the same sin, but to enjoy the position: to find being the one who is well unexpectedly pleasant, to relay the details as a prayer request, to feel firm ground under you that you lacked last week. That is a worse condition than the one you came to mend, and it is invisible to the man in it.

The only restorer who never fell. The gentleness asked for here is Christ’s own; he is “gentle and lowly in heart” (Matthew 11:29). He alone never needed to keep watch on himself, for he was tempted in every respect as we are, yet without sin (Hebrews 4:15), and his sinlessness did not make him hard with the fallen. He restored Peter by a charcoal fire, after three denials, with three questions and no lecture (John 21:15–17). He came to where we had fallen, the Shepherd who carries the stray home on his shoulders rejoicing (Luke 15:5). We go to a fallen brother as people he picked up, and we handle the brother as he handled us.

The practical shape of it. Go to him, rather than discuss him. First ask whether you would want this conversation conducted on you as you are about to conduct it, and confess to God the sin in yourself most like his. Say the true thing plainly: gentleness that will not name the sin is cowardice wearing its coat. And go knowing that only grace you did not generate separates you from him. A man who has grasped this letter cannot be a prosecutor; he has read the charge sheet with his own name on it.

And if he will not be restored? Gentleness does not give way to indifference. Jesus lays out the steps: go privately, then with one or two others, then to the church (Matthew 18:15–17). Where someone who calls himself a believer persists in serious sin without repentance, the church must act (1 Corinthians 5:11–13), always aiming to bring him back.

What if the sin is abuse, or a crime? Then gentleness toward the sinner must never mean danger for the victim. Restoration concerns a person’s relationship with God and the church; it does not cancel the duty to protect the vulnerable or to report a crime to the authorities, whom God has appointed to punish wrongdoing (Romans 13:1–4). Abuse is never to be hushed up, minimised or handled privately to protect a reputation, and no victim should be pressed to reconcile with an abuser or stay in danger. The church can pray for a repentant offender and seek his good, while keeping him well away from those he harmed and from positions of trust.

Does being restored mean being given back the position he had? Not necessarily. Restoration means being brought back to repentance, forgiveness and fellowship, welcomed at the Lord’s Table, and that should be full and warm. Trust, and especially leadership, is a separate matter. Elders must be above reproach (1 Timothy 3:2), and a man who has gravely fallen may be fully forgiven and still rightly not hold office again, or only after long proof. Forgiveness is a gift; trust is rebuilt.

verseByVerse.quote: Bear one another’s burdens, and so fulfill the law of Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Help to carry the weights that are too heavy for one person; that is what keeping Christ’s law of love looks like.

Bear one another’s burdens. Go on carrying the barē, the weights that press a person down: not minor inconveniences but what is genuinely too much for one. A failing marriage, a diagnosis, a son who has stopped speaking to his parents, the sin from the verse before that a man cannot get free of on his own.

The law of Christ. After five chapters saying the believer is not under law, Paul puts Christ’s name on the word: not the old system smuggled back, nor a new code. The whole law is fulfilled in loving your neighbour as yourself (5:14), and the Lord gave it as a new commandment: “that you love one another: just as I have loved you” (John 13:34; compare 1 Corinthians 9:21). It is a law defined not by a list but by a life, and its standard is no longer only “as yourself” but “as I have loved you”, which costs a good deal more.

Why his name is on it. Christ did not merely legislate burden-bearing. He bore the burden nobody else could lift: “Surely he has borne our griefs and carried our sorrows” (Isaiah 53:4). A Christian who shoulders another’s weight is doing, in miniature and at infinite distance, what was done for him at Calvary. The law of Christ is Christ’s own life poured into his people: the Burden-Bearer making burden-bearers, so that no one in his family carries everything alone.

Whose weight are you under? Not who you pray for: that matters greatly, but can be done entirely at home. Whose burden has cost you a Saturday, money you had other plans for, or a friendship that got harder because you told the truth inside it? A church can be doctrinally immaculate, warm on a Sunday, and carrying nothing at all, because burden-bearing is invisible and voluntary and nobody notices its absence.

How to do it. Notice: burdens are usually carried in silence, so ask the second question: not “How are you?” but “How are you really doing with your father’s illness?”, and listen without rushing to fix it. Offer something specific: “Let me know if you need anything” hands the weight back to the person already bent under it; “I am bringing a meal on Thursday” lifts some of it. Put the person in your diary for the third month, when everyone else has gone quiet. Pray with them, not only for them, and keep what they tell you to yourself. When the burden is a sin, carry it the way verse 1 says. None of this is heroics; it is what carried people do: “Cast your burden on the LORD, and he will sustain you” (Psalm 55:22), and he has, all the way to the cross.

It will not be reciprocal. In a healthy church the carrying evens out over years, but not on any given Tuesday, and the man who keeps accounts will not last. You carry, and sometimes you are carried, and the ledger between you was closed at the cross.

What if I am the one with the burden, and find it hard to ask for help? Ask anyway: the command assumes someone will let his burdens be carried. Pride often hides as independence (“I do not want to be a nuisance”), but refusing help denies others the chance to obey Christ and leaves you crushed under a weight God never meant you to carry alone. Tell one trusted believer the truth about what is happening, and say plainly what would help: a meal, a lift, someone to sit with you or to pray with you weekly. If your burden is a sin you cannot break, tell a mature Christian; confession to one another is a means of healing (James 5:16).

verseByVerse.quote: For if anyone thinks he is something, when he is nothing, he deceives himself. But let each one test his own work, and then his reason to boast will be in himself alone and not in his neighbor. For each will have to bear his own load.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Pride stops us carrying one another’s burdens, so judge your own work before God instead of comparing yourself with others, for each of us will answer for his own. Three verses that look like scattered proverbs make one argument: restoration goes wrong when a man has a wrong view of himself.

He deceives himself. Spiritual pride is the one sin that blinds you specifically to itself. A man knows when he has lost his temper. Nobody has ever thought, “This morning I am puffed up.”

When he is nothing. Not crushing: Paul has called these people sons and heirs of God. He means nothing on your own account, something only in Christ: “by the grace of God I am what I am” (1 Corinthians 15:10; compare 1 Corinthians 4:7). Every gift worth having came through the Son of God, “who loved me and gave himself for me” (2:20). A man who forgets that has mistaken a delivery for an achievement, and taken the credit for a parcel paid for with blood.

Test his own work. As metal is put in the fire to find what it actually is, and the object is his own work, not others’. The Galatians were measuring themselves against one another, which is why the chapter before ends with provoking and envying (5:26).

Not in his neighbor. Paul is not endorsing self-congratulation but saying where the measuring is done. A man who has tested his own work has a modest, real sense of what God has given him to do and whether he is doing it, and any satisfaction comes from God’s work in him. A man who has measured himself against his neighbour has nothing, because his verdict changes whenever the neighbour does.

His own load. This looks like a contradiction of verse 2, and two things resolve it. First, the words differ, though the difference should not be pressed too hard: verse 2’s barē is a weight a man cannot carry alone; verse 5’s phortion is a ship’s cargo or a soldier’s pack, the normal load each must carry, the word the Lord uses in “my burden is light” (Matthew 11:30). Second, the time differs. Verse 2 is about now; verse 5 looks ahead, “will have to bear”, probably to the day when each of us gives his own account (Romans 14:12), and no one can stand in the queue for us. Yet that day holds no terror for those in Christ: we shall each give our account, and the Judge will be the one who bore our sins.

Two errors. What is crushing you, others must help carry. What is properly yours, your own obedience, your own repentance, your own answer at the last day, nobody can carry, and it is no kindness to pretend otherwise. There is the Christian who will not let anyone near a weight that is breaking him, and calls it strength; and the Christian who has quietly transferred his own pack to his church, his counsellor or his spouse, and calls it fellowship.

Arithmetic on other people. When you last felt good, or a failure, about your Christian life, was it because you had compared yourself with someone else? God has not asked you to weigh your pack against theirs. The quieter question is what he has given you to do today, and whether his grace is enough for it.

How do I actually test my own work? Hold it up to God’s word and calling, not to other people. What has God given me to do, in my family, work, church and neighbourhood? Am I doing it faithfully, as for the Lord (Colossians 3:23)? Where have I been lazy, proud or unkind, and where has God plainly helped me grow? Talk it over with an honest, wise friend. Then thank God for the good, confess the bad, and get on with the next task. The aim is not a score but faithfulness.
verseByVerse.note: A “burden” in verse 2 is a crushing weight; a “load” in verse 5 is one’s own pack.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Life is a field, and what we sow we will reap, so keep sowing to the Spirit and do not give up. Paul begins with money: those taught the word are to share their good things with their teachers (v. 6). God is not mocked: sowing to the flesh reaps corruption, and sowing to the Spirit reaps eternal life (vv. 7–8). Weariness is expected, and the one condition of the harvest is not giving up (v. 9); while the season lasts, do good to everyone, especially to the household of faith (v. 10).
verseByVerse.theology:
The Harvest as the Motive of Present Faithfulness

Verses 7–9 read present obedience in the light of a future harvest. The harvest is secured by grace, not earned, but the reaping is real and certain, and knowing it keeps the believer at work. Verse 8 describes a direction of life, not wages (see “A direction of life” in the note on vv. 7–8).

Verse 6 grounds the support of gospel ministry in something older than church order (see “Not a novelty” in the note on v. 6).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The Galatians were weary, and drifting toward the Judaizers’ more comfortable programme would have ended the trouble. Verse 9 is aimed there: the harvest is coming, do not walk off the field.

Now: Sowing is small, repeated and unremarkable (see “Small seeds” in the note on vv. 7–8), and v. 9 is for people at the end of their strength (see the note on vv. 9–10).

verseByVerse.quote: Let the one who is taught the word share all good things with the one who teaches.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Those who are taught God’s word are to share their good things, money included, with those who teach them. Paul turns to money without preliminaries.

Let the one who is taught the word. Taught is katēcheō (hence catechism). Paul does not tell teachers to raise support; he tells congregations to give it. A man who must ask for his own living will find it hard to say the unwelcome thing, and this letter exists because somebody said one.

Share all good things. Share comes from the family of koinōnia, the New Testament’s word for the deepest communion of the church. Giving is fellowship in the form that is easiest to test, and “all good things” is broad: money, food, hospitality, encouragement.

Not a novelty. “If we have sown spiritual things among you, is it too much if we reap material things from you?” (1 Corinthians 9:11, 14); the labourer deserves his wages (1 Timothy 5:17–18). Israel too was told to provide for the landless Levites and welcome them at its feasts (Deuteronomy 12:19; 14:27).

Why here? It is the first thing Paul thinks of after burden-bearing, and the sowing and reaping that follows (“Do not be deceived: God is not mocked”) probably has as its nearest setting what a congregation does with its money. Few things show more exactly what a church believes.

Paul’s own freedom. Paul made tents rather than be a burden, and boasted of preaching free of charge (1 Corinthians 9:15–18). Paid ministry is not the only faithful shape, but a congregation may not use his freedom as an excuse. He chose to go without; he never said the teacher was not owed.

What the teacher hands you. What a faithful teacher hands his hearers week by week is Christ, as the Galatians once had Jesus Christ publicly portrayed as crucified before their eyes (3:1). A congregation that shares its bread with the man who brings that word is not paying for a service but answering, in a small way, the riches it has been given.

What decides your giving? Many Christians give from what is left, so that the teaching of the word is funded by whatever remains of a lifestyle planned without it in mind. Paul’s word is share: not tip, not subsidise, not fund from surplus. It assumes a common life in which what one has is available to the other, a far more disturbing idea than a percentage.

What it does not mean. Not that teachers should demand support or preach for money. Elders serve “not for shameful gain” (1 Peter 5:2), and a teacher who makes money the point has disqualified himself.

Does this mean I must give a tenth? The New Testament lays down no fixed percentage for Christians; it calls for giving that is regular, proportionate, generous and cheerful (1 Corinthians 16:2; 2 Corinthians 9:6–7). Christians differ on whether the tithe still binds, and many find it a wise starting place. The question is not how little you can give but how gladly you can share. Give first, not last, from each pay; support your own church and those who teach you; and let your giving grow as God provides. Christ, though he was rich, became poor for your sake (2 Corinthians 8:9).

In everyday life. Do something this week for the one who teaches you, beyond money: a note of thanks for one specific thing you learned, a meal, a promise to pray for him by name.

verseByVerse.quote: Do not be deceived: God is not mocked, for whatever one sows, that will he also reap. For the one who sows to his own flesh will from the flesh reap corruption, but the one who sows to the Spirit will from the Spirit reap eternal life.
verseByVerse.commentary:
No one can make a fool of God: what a person sows with his life he will reap, ruin from the flesh or eternal life from the Spirit.

God is not mocked. The tone hardens without warning. The verb comes from the word for the nose: to turn up the nose, to sneer. The point is not that God takes offence but that nobody gets away with it: treat him as a system to be worked around, and it simply does not work.

Whatever one sows. The farmer’s principle runs through Scripture (Job 4:8; Proverbs 22:8; Hosea 8:7), and it carries three certainties. You reap what you sow: no farmer is surprised by the species of his crop. You reap more than you sow, which cuts both ways. And you reap later than you sow, the certainty that deceives, because the gap makes a man think the connection is not real.

The gap. Nobody sneers at God at harvest. The sneer comes in month four, when nothing has visibly followed and the warning seems overwrought. But the ground keeps the account whether or not anyone is watching, and it is not a machine but the moral order of a holy God, before whom no creature is hidden and to whom we must give account (Hebrews 4:13), and he is not a fool.

Sows to his own flesh. To invest your life, time, money and energy in sinful desires (5:19–21). The harvest is phthora, corruption, ending in ruin and eternal destruction. The flesh pays out less in catastrophe than in slow decay: a marriage that goes quietly hollow, an appetite that needs more each year to do the same work, a conscience that stops registering, a man in his sixties who cannot say what he built. Nothing dramatic happened; it simply went bad, and in the end not merely a life but a soul.

Sows to the Spirit. To invest in what pleases the Spirit: prayer, Scripture, worship, love, service; and the harvest is eternal life. That is not wages for services rendered, which would contradict the whole letter. Nothing you sow can purchase eternal life, which is the life of the risen Christ: “God gave us eternal life, and this life is in his Son” (1 John 5:11). Verse 8 describes a direction of life: a person indwelt by the Spirit of Christ sows to the Spirit as a living tree puts out leaves, and the harvest is not his wages but the full growth of Christ’s life in him. Nor is the warning aimed at the believer who falls and gets up and fights again: the war between flesh and Spirit (5:17) is itself a sign that the Spirit is there. The one in danger has stopped fighting and no longer cares.

Small seeds. Sowing is small, repeated and unremarkable. This morning’s twenty minutes with the Bible open, the apology you made instead of the point you were entitled to make: none of it felt like anything, which is what seed is like in the hand. We look for a cause of our spiritual dullness the size of the effect, and there never is one: only a field, and what has gone into it for years. And the Spirit who raised Jesus lives in you and makes the seed grow.

God is not stingy. The one who sowed most perfectly to the Spirit reaped what we had sown. Christ planted nothing but righteousness and was handed the harvest of our corruption on the cross, so that his obedience is counted ours and our patchy sowing accepted for his sake. Then he went into the ground like seed and came up as “the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep” (1 Corinthians 15:20). God is not mocked, and God is not stingy: he gives eternal life as a gift to those who could never have grown it.

Is this karma? No. Karma is an impersonal law no one can escape. Here a personal God speaks, who forgives, and who laid the penalty of his people’s sin on Christ. But forgiveness does not always remove sin’s earthly consequences: David was forgiven (“The LORD also has put away your sin”), and yet the child died (2 Samuel 12:13–14); and the Lord disciplines the one he loves (Hebrews 12:6). Nor does every hardship mean a person is reaping a particular sin; Job and the man born blind (John 9:3) show otherwise. A parent who has lost a child should never read that loss as God’s payment for their sin: David’s case was named by a prophet, and yours has not been. The verse warns against thinking we can sow to the flesh and escape the harvest.

I sowed to the flesh for years. Is it too late? Not if you are turning to Christ now. The harvest of eternal life depends not on the length of your sowing but on the grace of the giver: the thief on the cross sowed nothing and was with Christ in paradise that day (Luke 23:43), and God can restore the years the swarming locust has eaten (Joel 2:25). Face honestly any earthly consequences, and put right what you can; Christ has borne the eternal harvest of your sin. From today, sow to the Spirit in small seeds, and trust God with the crop.

Where Christians differ: is eternal life earned by sowing? Some take this verse to mean salvation is a reward for good living. This commentary’s view: eternal life is God’s free gift in Christ (Romans 6:23), received by faith (the whole message of Galatians). But the life of faith shows itself in sowing to the Spirit, and that life leads to its harvest. Sowing to the Spirit is not the root of salvation but its fruit and its path (Romans 2:6–7; 8:13). Those who sow persistently to the flesh, without repentance, show they do not have the Spirit.

verseByVerse.quote: And let us not grow weary of doing good, for in due season we will reap, if we do not give up. So then, as we have opportunity, let us do good to everyone, and especially to those who are of the household of faith.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do not give up doing good, for God’s harvest will come in his season; and while the season lasts, do good to everyone, especially to fellow believers.

Let us not grow weary. Paul has mostly said “you”; here, as in 5:25–26, he says “us”: the apostle knew what it was to be tired of doing good. The verb means losing heart, going slack (as in 2 Corinthians 4:1). The warning is against a very ordinary exhaustion: a Christian worn out from carrying burdens, restoring the fallen and giving away money.

In due season. At God’s appointed time. No farmer resents June for not being September. He works a field that shows him nothing for months, because the timetable was never his, and he knows the difference between “nothing is happening” and “nothing is visible”.

If we do not give up. The one condition, and it is not achievement. Paul does not say we shall reap if we sow enough, or well, but if we do not go limp and stop. The risk is not failure but abandonment: walking off the field after years of work, three weeks before something comes up.

As we have opportunity. Verse 10 turns the tired worker’s eyes outward. Opportunity is the same word as the season in verse 9: the sowing season is now. Not when it is convenient, but while there is still time.

Do good to everyone, and especially. “Everyone” rules out a church that does its good only where it will be appreciated by people who share its views. “Especially” rules out general goodwill toward mankind as a substitute for helping the believer two streets away whose boiler has failed. Fellow believers come first, as one cares first for one’s own family: first, not only. And a household runs no application process. The claim on you is not that the person deserves it, but that he is kin.

Consider him. Hebrews uses the same verb for going limp and gives the remedy: “Consider him who endured from sinners such hostility against himself, so that you may not grow weary or fainthearted” (Hebrews 12:3). Jesus did good for some three years against rejection, and at the end his field looked like a cross, a borrowed tomb and eleven frightened men. He did not give up. For the joy that was set before him he endured the cross (Hebrews 12:2), and the harvest of that sowing has been coming in ever since. A tired Christian keeps going not by staring at his own furrow, but by looking at his Lord’s.

The people this verse belongs to. It belongs to people reading it at the end of their strength, and the God who never grows weary gives power to the faint (Isaiah 40:28–29). The mother who has prayed for a son for twenty-two years and has stopped expecting the phone to ring. The man who teaches eight children in a back room while the church around him talks about growth. The wife who has been gentle with a hard husband for a decade with nothing to show for it. The small-town pastor who has buried more people than he has baptised. Paul’s answer to every one of them is a fact about the world God made: sowing is followed by reaping, and the season is his.

I am exhausted. Is resting the same as giving up? No. Giving up is abandoning the field; resting is what keeps you in it. God built rest into creation, Jesus took his tired disciples away to rest a while (Mark 6:31), and Elijah under the broom tree was given sleep and food before he was given a task (1 Kings 19:5–8). You may need to sleep, share the work, say no to something good, or ask for help; none of that is unfaithfulness. Paul warns against losing heart: concluding that doing good is pointless and walking away. Rest, and then go back to sowing.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 11–18 — The Cross and the New Creation
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: In his own hand Paul sums up the letter: the cross is the only boast, and new creation is all that counts. He writes large to expose the agitators’ motives, a good showing, escape from persecution and converts to boast about (vv. 11–13). He boasts only in the cross, through which the world is dead to him and he to it (v. 14). Circumcision is nothing and new creation everything, and peace and mercy rest on all who walk by that rule, and on the Israel of God (vv. 15–16). His scars show whose he is, and he ends with grace, calling them brothers (vv. 17–18).
verseByVerse.theology:
The Cross as the Permanent Centre, and the Israel of God

Paul’s boast in v. 14 sums up the letter. The cross, where the law’s curse was borne and the new creation began, is not only the entrance to the Christian life but its permanent centre. This is Luther’s theology of the cross against a theology of glory: God’s ways are read from below, through shame and suffering, not from above through human notions of power and success.

On v. 16 much turns on the small word kai, which can mean and or even; read as even, which fits the letter’s argument best (3:29; 4:26), it makes the Israel of God the whole people of God in Christ. The two readings are weighed in the note on vv. 15–16 and its box “Where Christians differ: who is the Israel of God?”.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The Judaizers wanted social safety, and vv. 12–13 name it bluntly (see the note on vv. 11–13). Verse 17 answers it with the marks Paul carried from his sufferings (see the note on vv. 17–18).

Now: Verse 13 puts a test to any softened conviction (see “What does the adjustment cost you?” in the note on vv. 11–13), and v. 17 honours anyone whose faithfulness has cost them something unglamorous (see “Marks that are honoured” in the note on vv. 17–18).

verseByVerse.quote: See with what large letters I am writing to you with my own hand. It is those who want to make a good showing in the flesh who would force you to be circumcised, and only in order that they may not be persecuted for the cross of Christ. For even those who are circumcised do not themselves keep the law, but they desire to have you circumcised that they may boast in your flesh.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul writes the end of the letter in his own large hand to expose what the circumcision party really wanted: to escape persecution and to have converts to boast about.

With my own hand. Letters were normally dictated, the author adding a line at the end in his own hand as a signature (2 Thessalonians 3:17). Here Paul writes the whole closing paragraph, and writes big, the ancient bold type: this is the letter compressed, and he does not want it missed.

A good showing in the flesh. The first thing he writes large is not doctrine but motive: to make a good showing is literally to present a fine face in public.

That they may not be persecuted. Circumcising the Galatians bought escape from persecution by non-Christian Jews. This is diagnosis, not insult. Judaism had a measure of tolerance under Rome, and circumcised Jews who followed a Messiah could shelter under it; uncircumcised Gentiles worshipping a crucified Jew could not, and Jewish Christians seen to erase the line between Jew and Gentile paid for it among their own people. If the Gentile converts were circumcised, Christianity looked like a Jewish sect, and the offence of the cross disappeared (5:11). These teachers were less theologians than men under pressure, with a solution any reasonable committee might reach: the synagogue satisfied, Rome uninterested, nobody beaten.

Do not themselves keep the law. Circumcision obligates a man to the entire code (5:3), and the men selling it were not keeping it either. This was never a serious attempt at law-righteousness, but safe belonging dressed in Scripture.

Boast in your flesh. The second motive is uglier: converts as trophies, something done to another man’s body that can be counted and reported. Every generation of ministry has its version: the number, the person turned into a credential. Christ counts his people not as trophies but as children; he does not boast in our flesh, but gave his own flesh for the life of the world (John 6:51).

Get behind me. The Lord met this reasoning in his own disciples. When he first spoke of his cross, Peter rebuked him: “Far be it from you, Lord! This shall never happen to you.” Jesus answered, “Get behind me, Satan! … For you are not setting your mind on the things of God, but on the things of man” (Matthew 16:22–23). Following the Messiah without the cross is the temptation Jesus refused most sharply, and for us. The Judaizers wanted to keep the name of Christ and lose his cross; he took up the cross so that we might bear his name.

What does the adjustment cost you? That is the question for anyone who has softened a Christian conviction and given a theological reason. The test is not whether the reason is defensible (the Judaizers had excellent reasons, one of them avoiding a beating) but what the adjustment costs you. Every change these men proposed made their lives easier, and the flesh has never once recommended a course that would get its owner persecuted. Paul’s alternative is a cross, which is exactly what the whole manoeuvre was designed to avoid.

What it does not mean. Not that all Jewish Christians were insincere. Paul speaks of these particular teachers; many Jewish believers, like Peter, James and Barnabas, shared his gospel and suffered for it.

Is it wrong to avoid persecution if I can? Not in itself. Jesus told his disciples to flee from town to town when persecuted (Matthew 10:23); Paul escaped Damascus in a basket and appealed to his rights as a Roman citizen; we are to pray for peaceful lives (1 Timothy 2:1–2). Wisdom, tact and lawful protection are good. What is wrong is avoiding persecution by changing the message: dropping what offends, keeping quiet about Christ when silence is denial, bending God’s commands to fit in. Are you avoiding trouble, or avoiding Christ? The first may be wise; the second is the Judaizers’ path.

Uncertain wording. Two details are not certain. Why the letters were large: perhaps Paul’s eyes were poor (compare 4:15) or his hand untrained, but most likely for emphasis. And “those who are circumcised” (v. 13) could mean the teachers or Gentile converts who had accepted circumcision and now pressed it on others; the likely meaning is the teachers, since the sentence is about what they want from the Galatians.
verseByVerse.note: Paul dictated his letters, then took the pen himself to finish; his large letters may reflect poor eyesight or simply emphasis.

verseByVerse.quote: But far be it from me to boast except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, by which the world has been crucified to me, and I to the world.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul’s only boast is the cross of Christ, which has ended the world’s hold on him and his standing in its eyes.

Far be it from me to boast. They boast in flesh; Paul boasts in a gallows. The phrase is mē genoito, as at 2:17 and 3:21: may it never be. Not his conversion, record, learning, visions or suffering: one thing, done for him rather than by him. “Let the one who boasts, boast in the Lord” (1 Corinthians 1:31).

How strange it sounded. The cross was not yet jewellery but Rome’s public death for slaves and rebels, so shameful that polite writers avoided the word; Cicero said the very name of the cross should be far from a Roman citizen’s body, thoughts, eyes and ears. And a Pharisee knew Deuteronomy 21:23 (3:13): a hanged man is cursed by God. To boast in a crucifixion was, in Jewish terms, blasphemy, and in Roman terms, disgusting.

The world has been crucified to me. The world is the whole system of values, status and religion opposed to God, religious achievement included. Through the cross it is dead to Paul. What it holds out, standing, security, the approval you were raised to want, is not all evil, but its offers have lost their power: it cannot buy a man who has seen the cross.

And I to the world. The harder half: the world no longer has a claim on him, and he has lost his standing in its eyes, the very thing the false teachers were desperate to avoid. A man dead to the world is no longer being ranked, which is precisely why he was free to write this letter and they were not. Isaac Watts built “When I Survey the Wondrous Cross” on this verse: “Forbid it, Lord, that I should boast, save in the death of Christ my God.”

Three crucifixions. This is the letter’s third. The old self under condemnation died with Christ (2:20); the flesh’s rule within is broken (5:24); and here the world’s hold from outside is broken. One cross deals with guilt, the flesh and the world, which is why it is the only thing left to boast in.

The universe has one boast. The Son of God hangs on a beam outside a city, stripped, mocked, numbered with criminals, bearing a curse that belonged to others; and no throne in history has ever been so completely a throne. There the love of God was shown at full strength, his justice was satisfied in full, the powers were disarmed and put to open shame (Colossians 2:15), and the Lamb who was slain was found worthy (Revelation 5:12). The universe has one boast in it, and it is a man on a cross.

What it looks like with a mortgage. Not withdrawal; Paul had a trade and cared greatly about money for the poor. The world can still take things from you but can no longer set your price. Ask what would happen if the reputation you have built quietly collapsed, not through sin, just through being overlooked. If you would lose something painful but survivable, the crucifixion has been done; if you would not know who you were, the world is still very much alive. That is a reason not for despair but for another look at the cross; the world loosens its grip slowly.

What it does not mean. Not that Paul hated the created world or other people. “God so loved the world, that he gave his only Son” (John 3:16), and everything created by God is good, to be received with thanksgiving (1 Timothy 4:4).

How do I boast in the cross in practice? Make it the first thing you say about yourself before God: not what you have done, but what Christ did. When you are praised, quietly give the credit to his grace; when you are accused, run to the cross rather than to your record. Speak of Jesus crucified and risen more than of your experience or your church. Sing the hymns that look at the cross, and look at it yourself each day, slowly, until its glory crowds out the smaller glories you are tempted to chase.

verseByVerse.quote: For neither circumcision counts for anything, nor uncircumcision, but a new creation. And as for all who walk by this rule, peace and mercy be upon them, and upon the Israel of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
What counts before God is not a mark on the body but the new creation he works in Christ, and Paul pronounces peace and mercy on all who live by that rule.

Neither circumcision nor uncircumcision. The verdict that ends the argument. Paul finishes this sentence three ways: in 5:6 what counts is faith working through love; in 1 Corinthians 7:19, keeping the commandments of God; here, a new creation. Three answers, one thing: the question is never the mark on the body but whether God has done something.

A new creation. Kainē ktisis is new in kind, not merely recent. Paul is reaching back to Genesis 1 and to Isaiah’s new heavens and new earth (Isaiah 65:17). The gospel produces not a reformed version of the old thing but the age to come arriving early in a person, the life of the renewed world already begun in everyone joined to the risen Christ. Jesus called it being born again, and Paul the washing of regeneration (John 3:3–8; Titus 3:5): a heart dead to God made alive by God. “If anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation” (2 Corinthians 5:17). The Judaizers proposed alterations to someone God had already made new, as if renovating a house were the same as being born. The God who said, let there be light, has shone in our hearts “to give the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ” (2 Corinthians 4:6).

This rule. A measuring rod (kanōn): what he has just said, not circumcision, not uncircumcision, but new creation, the rule of grace alone.

Peace and mercy be upon them. A blessing echoing Psalm 125:5 and 128:6: “Peace be upon Israel!” Paul’s greetings put peace last; here it comes first, with mercy beside it, as if at the end of so severe a letter he wants the last word to be kindness.

The Israel of God. The most argued-over phrase in the letter, and much turns on the small word kai, which can mean “and” or “even”. Read “even the Israel of God”, and the phrase caps the sentence: those who walk by this rule, Jew and Gentile together in Christ, are the Israel of God. Read simply “and”, and a second group is in view, most naturally Jewish believers, the believing remnant, singled out for blessing at the end of a letter that has been hard on their nation’s badge.

What everyone agrees on. Whoever the Israel of God is, no one gets into that number by ancestry or by a mark. The Galatians had been told they were second-tier members of God’s people; Paul’s final blessing rests on everyone walking by this rule, and checks nobody’s papers.

I do not feel like a new creation. Am I one? Being a new creation is first something God declares and does, not something you feel. If you are united to Christ by faith, it has begun: God has given you a new heart, his Spirit lives in you, and you belong to the age to come. But the old body, memories, habits and remaining flesh are still there, which is why it does not always feel new. Look for the marks, however small: a new love for Christ, a new hatred of sin, new desires to please God, a new family in the church. A newborn does not feel like a person either, but he is one, and he will grow.

Where Christians differ: who is the Israel of God? Some take it to be ethnic Israel, or believing Jews, distinct from Gentile believers; others, the whole church. The reading of kai as “and”, with believing Jews in view, is held by serious readers who love this book, including many who expect a future for ethnic Israel on the strength of Romans 11 and honour the Scriptures as fully as anyone. This commentary’s view: Paul has spent the whole letter arguing that all believers, Jew and Gentile, are Abraham’s offspring and heirs (3:7, 29), that the Jerusalem above is our mother (4:26), and that ethnic markers count for nothing; it would be strange to end by setting believing Jews apart as a special group. The Israel of God is best understood as the whole people of God in Christ, the true Israel (Romans 2:28–29; Philippians 3:3). This does not cancel God’s purposes for ethnic Israel (Romans 11), but describes the church as the fulfilment of Israel.
verseByVerse.note: Interpreters differ over whether “the Israel of God” means believing Jews or the whole church, Jew and Gentile together. The more persuasive reading is the whole church (compare 3:29).

verseByVerse.quote: From now on let no one cause me trouble, for I bear on my body the marks of Jesus. The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with your spirit, brothers. Amen.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul closes the case by pointing to the scars he bears for Jesus as proof of whose he is, and commends the Galatians, still his brothers, to the grace of Christ.

From now on let no one cause me trouble. Abrupt, almost weary: the case is closed. After six chapters of argument, Paul simply shows the scars.

The marks of Jesus. Stigmata were brands put on a slave, soldier or temple servant to show whose he was. Paul’s were almost certainly the scars of beatings and stoning, put there by people trying to stop him (2 Corinthians 11:24–25), some perhaps at Lystra, in Galatia, where hearers of this letter may have watched him dragged out and left for dead (Acts 14:19). The false teachers wanted a mark cut into Gentile flesh to prove belonging. Paul’s marks settle whose he is far more conclusively than circumcision ever could.

With your spirit, brothers. After all the sharp words, the Greek sentence ends, just before the Amen, with “brothers”. The man who pronounced an anathema, a solemn curse, on the false gospel (1:8–9) signs off calling them family.

Grace at both ends. The letter that began with grace (1:3, 6) ends with grace, and everything between is an argument that nothing may be added to it. There is nowhere else for a Christian to stand.

Everything was paid. So the last thing Galatians does is hold up its subject one more time: a Son sent in the fullness of time, born of woman, born under the law; who kept every clause of it and was made a curse on a tree, so that the blessing of Abraham could reach a farmer in Lystra with no ancestry and nothing to bring; who bought slaves out of the market, put his Spirit in their hearts and taught them to say Father. He bears marks too, in his hands, his feet and his side, the price of everything this letter defends. Nothing was cheapened. Everything was paid. And from first to last it was grace.

Marks that are honoured. That matters for anyone whose faithfulness has cost something unglamorous: a career that went nowhere because of a conviction, a family that cooled, a body worn out in a small work nobody counted. Those marks are not evidence of a failure to manage life well. Paul called his the marks of Jesus, and expected them to be honoured.

In everyday life. Before you sleep tonight, say the last verse of Galatians over yourself and over the people you love.

I have never suffered for Christ like this. Am I a lesser Christian? No. Your standing rests on Christ’s wounds, not yours, and God assigns different paths; many live long, quiet lives without beatings or prison and are not second-class. But every believer bears some marks: the cost of honesty at work, a friend lost over your faith, self-denial nobody sees, patience in a hard marriage. Do not despise those small marks, and do not go looking for dramatic ones. Be faithful where you are, pray for those who suffer more (Hebrews 13:3), and be ready if the cost rises.

Where Christians differ: the stigmata. Some medieval saints, such as Francis of Assisi, were said to receive the stigmata: wounds like Christ’s, miraculously appearing on their hands and feet, seen as a sign of special holiness. This commentary’s view: Paul’s marks were the ordinary scars of persecution suffered for preaching Christ, not miraculous wounds. Scripture nowhere teaches miraculous stigmata or treats them as a sign of holiness. The true marks of belonging to Christ are faith, love, holiness and willingness to suffer for him.
verseByVerse.note: The “marks” were the scars left by beatings and stoning — like the brands on a slave showing whom he belonged to.

6.text: <sup>1</sup>Brothers, if anyone is caught in any transgression, you who are spiritual should restore him in a spirit of gentleness. Keep watch on yourself, lest you too be tempted.<sup>2</sup>Bear one another’s burdens, and so fulfill the law of Christ.<sup>3</sup>For if anyone thinks he is something, when he is nothing, he deceives himself.<sup>4</sup>But let each one test his own work, and then his reason to boast will be in himself alone and not in his neighbor.<sup>5</sup>For each will have to bear his own load.<sup>6</sup>Let the one who is taught the word share all good things with the one who teaches.<sup>7</sup>Do not be deceived: God is not mocked, for whatever one sows, that will he also reap.<sup>8</sup>For the one who sows to his own flesh will from the flesh reap corruption, but the one who sows to the Spirit will from the Spirit reap eternal life.<sup>9</sup>And let us not grow weary of doing good, for in due season we will reap, if we do not give up.<sup>10</sup>So then, as we have opportunity, let us do good to everyone, and especially to those who are of the household of faith.<sup>11</sup>See with what large letters I am writing to you with my own hand.<sup>12</sup>It is those who want to make a good showing in the flesh who would force you to be circumcised, and only in order that they may not be persecuted for the cross of Christ.<sup>13</sup>For even those who are circumcised do not themselves keep the law, but they desire to have you circumcised that they may boast in your flesh.<sup>14</sup>But far be it from me to boast except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, by which the world has been crucified to me, and I to the world.<sup>15</sup>For neither circumcision counts for anything, nor uncircumcision, but a new creation.<sup>16</sup>And as for all who walk by this rule, peace and mercy be upon them, and upon the Israel of God.<sup>17</sup>From now on let no one cause me trouble, for I bear on my body the marks of Jesus.<sup>18</sup>The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with your spirit, brothers. Amen.

keyVerse.quote: But far be it from me to boast except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, by which the world has been crucified to me, and I to the world.
keyVerse.note: Paul writes this in his own hand at the close of the letter, and it gathers up everything he has argued: nothing can be added to Christ, so nothing but his cross is worth boasting in. It also explains the rest of the chapter, because people whose only boast is the cross can restore the fallen gently, carry others’ burdens and keep sowing without needing to be admired.

6.reflection:
Verse 1 asks those who are spiritual to restore a fallen brother gently while keeping watch on themselves. What makes this hard to do well? What does the way Jesus restored Peter (John 21:15–17) teach us about how to go?

Whose burden are you carrying at the moment in a way that costs you something (v. 2)? And is there a burden of your own that you need to let someone help you carry?

Paul says we reap what we sow, often long after the sowing (vv. 7–9). Where are you tempted to think the harvest will never come, whether from the flesh or from the Spirit? What small seed could you sow this week?

The false teachers wanted a good showing; Paul would boast only in the cross (vv. 12–14). What are you tempted to boast in, before God or before others, and what would it look like for the cross to be your only boast?
